## The two defects the real run left alone - 2026-08-04

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **the "1 transactions" plural and the evidence panel's
inconsistent rendering**, both observed during the first real run three handovers
above and neither chased at the time.

One of them turned out to be a different defect from the one reported, and saying
so is the more useful outcome than a fix that matched the guess.

### The plural: eight sentences, not one

The reported symptom was one line in the shift panel. Searching for the class
rather than the instance found **eight** unpluralised counts across the shift and
reporting surfaces, several sitting beside counts that were already correct:

| Where | Was |
| --- | --- |
| `shift_panel` confirmed sales | `1 transactions, 1 minor units` |
| `shift_panel` expected cash | `1 minor units over 1 sale` |
| `shift_panel` unattributed tender | `worth 1 minor units. They are inside...` |
| `shift_history_panel` recorded sales | `over 1 transactions` |
| `daily_metrics_panel` daily sales | `over 1 transactions in 1 shift` |
| `daily_metrics_panel` cost data | `1 sale lines have no cost recorded` |
| `sales_totals_panel` category basis | `0 of the 1 sales read` |
| `sales_totals_panel` cost data | `1 sale lines have no cost` |

The daily summary line is the sharpest example: it pluralised `shiftCount`
correctly and `transactions` not at all, **in the same sentence**, so it could
produce both "12 transactions in 1 shift" and "1 transactions in 2 shifts".

Two decisions worth recording:

- **The agreement rule covers pronouns and verbs, not only nouns.** The
  unattributed-tender line now reads "It is inside the confirmed sales above" for
  one sale, matching what the unsettled-sales line beside it already did. That
  line was checked and is correct as written: `count == 1 ? 'sale names' :
  'sales name'` pairs a singular subject with "names" and a plural subject with
  "name", which reads wrong at a glance and is right.
- **"minor unit" was pluralised too**, even though the money presentation is
  part of the excluded currency work. Fixing "1 transaction" while leaving "1
  minor units" in the same sentence would have been worse than either.
- **Inline ternaries, not a helper.** The codebase already expresses this rule
  inline in a dozen places; a new shared helper would have made these eight sites
  the odd ones out.

**Every plural form is byte-identical to what it produced before**, which is why
the 979 existing shift, reporting, sales, checkout, and tenancy tests passed
unchanged after the edit. That is also the finding: **no test pinned any of these
sentences at a count of one.** Seven new tests do now.

### The evidence panel: the reported symptom was not the defect

The report was that the panel "sometimes lists all five states with their counts
and sometimes only `Saved offline: 0`, with at least one record present."

**There is no such state.** `_EvidenceContents` renders either the empty sentence
or all five lines as siblings of one `Column`; no input produces a subset. A test
now pins that, so an omission can never become the explanation. The most likely
reading of the screenshots is the landing screen's layout: the panel sits inside a
`Center` within a `SingleChildScrollView`, so tall content is cut off at both ends
and the lines below "Saved offline: 0" were simply below the fold. That is
recorded rather than changed - it is a deliberate look for a mostly-empty screen,
and the content is reachable by scrolling.

> **Corrected on 2026-08-05, after rendering it.** The conclusion - below the
> fold - was right. The mechanism stated here is wrong in two ways, and acting on
> it would have changed nothing. Only the **bottom** is cut, never both ends: a
> scroll view starts at offset zero. And the `Center` is not the cause: it passes
> loose constraints down, so content taller than the viewport fills the height and
> starts at the top, which makes centred and top-aligned the same layout in
> exactly the case being complained about. See the last handover in this file.

**But looking for it found a real defect beside it.** Every refresh signal changes
the loader's identity, which restarts `TenantRouteGuard` and puts it back into its
loading state - and that state was `SizedBox.shrink()`. So **the whole panel
vanished and reappeared on every signal**, and `CheckoutSyncPass` reports a change
more than once per sale, so a cashier watching for their sale saw the counts
flicker away repeatedly. That matches "sometimes lists all five states and
sometimes does not" at least as well as the layout does.

The fix keeps the last counts on screen while a fresh read is in flight, and says
they may be a moment old rather than leaving that to be inferred. Two safety
properties came with it:

- **The retained counts are dropped the instant the session key moves.** One
  business's local work shown under another business's name would be a worse
  defect than the blanking it replaces. Pinned by a test that switches business
  mid-read and asserts the previous counts disappear and nothing is shown until
  the new read answers.
- The cache is written by assigning a field inside the guard's builder, not by
  `setState`, so it adds no build cycle.

Confirmed by reverting the `loading` widget to `SizedBox.shrink()`: the refresh
test fails, the other ten pass.

## The shift half of the pipeline, proved end to end - 2026-08-04

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **the reconciliation integration runner now carries a real sale
through the shift-verification phase and out the other side through
`amendShiftSummary`.** Its five tests stopped after the metrics phase; there are
now seven, and the whole chain - sale, dirty day, job, metric, shift
expectation, verification, difference, correction - is proved by tests rather
than by the one manual run recorded four handovers above.

No production code changed. The two new tests exercise code that was already
shipped and already unit-tested; what they add is the first evidence that it
does what the pure tests say when a real Firestore, a real task queue, and a
real callable are involved. That is the same gap that let
`mergeSaleReconciliationJob` throw on every sale for eleven sessions.

### What the shifts phase had never actually done in this harness

The fixture seeded a tenant and a product and no `shifts` document at all. Every
run therefore *did* reach the shifts phase - and found the shift its own
expectation named missing, recorded `invalid_or_missing_shift`, and moved on
without a single assertion noticing. **The variance path had never run against a
real server**, which is the reason this chunk existed.

The seeded shift records 0.00 over 0 transactions: the state a shift is left in
when it closes before the sale filed against it reaches the server, which is
what `scripts/plant-late-sale.js` engineers by hand. Both recorded figures are
then wrong, so the verifier's two comparisons, the two figures it records, and
the amendment's two rewrites are each individually observable. A fixture that
got one of them right by accident would have proved half as much.

Decisions worth recording:

- **The anomaly is found by querying `shiftId`, not by recomputing its digest.**
  The verifier and the amendment callable derive `shiftAnomalyId` in two
  different modules from the same shift and generation. A test that recomputed
  the digest would agree with whichever one it copied; a test that queries by
  field and then asserts `clearedAnomalyId` equals the ID it found proves the
  two modules agree with *each other*. If they ever stopped agreeing, the listed
  difference would survive its own correction and that assertion fails.
- **The counted cash is asserted unchanged.** `closingCashMinor` is a physical
  count of a drawer and the single property that makes this path safe to expose
  is that it can never rewrite one. The fixture uses 12000 minor units so a test
  would notice it moving.
- **The job's completion is waited for, not sampled.** The file's existing rule
  is that anything the pipeline is still writing must not be asserted; the new
  test extends that rule rather than bending it, by waiting until the job is
  `completed` - after which nothing rewrites its counters - and only then
  asserting `shiftsProcessed` and `shiftVarianceCount`.
- **Idempotency and non-repeatability are different properties, and both are
  asserted.** Replaying the same `requestId` returns the stored answer and leaves
  `summaryAmendmentCount` at 1. A *fresh* `requestId` is refused with
  `FAILED_PRECONDITION`, because settling the expectation as `amended` in the
  same transaction makes a second correction of that generation impossible
  rather than merely pointless.
- **The seeded actor is an `admin`, not an `owner`.** `amendShiftSummary` admits
  both, but an `owner` staff record must also be named by the tenant's
  `ownerUid`, and these fixtures are owned by a uid with no Auth account. The
  authorization path is otherwise identical.

### The fixture's third export, and the rule it had to satisfy

`functions/reconciliation-integration/index.js` now exports `amendShiftSummary`
beside the trigger and the task worker. Its require closure was checked first:
`core/authorization`, `core/idempotency`, `core/validation`,
`operations/domain`, `reconciliation/model` - and not one reaches
`firebase-functions/params`. That matters because a `defineSecret` or
`defineString` without a default makes the emulator stop at startup to ask for a
value, and with no terminal to answer it looks like a run that hangs forever
after `Serving at port ...`. The rule and how to check it are now written in the
fixture and in the README rather than being folklore.

### Meaningful failures and their resolutions

- **The first full run failed, and the failure was a real flake this chunk made
  more likely.** `TRIGGER_TIMEOUT_MILLISECONDS` was 30 seconds, and the *first*
  trigger delivery of a cold run is the only one that pays for the Functions
  emulator starting a Node worker: it was measured at 25.4 and 23.0 seconds on
  this host, while every later delivery in the same run appeared in about 310ms.
  Adding one more function to the fixture was enough to take the first test over
  the bound. Raised to 60 seconds with the measurement written down. The bound
  exists so a trigger that never runs fails with a description of what it was
  waiting for rather than hanging; it was never a performance assertion, and the
  diagnostic line still reports the time actually taken.
- **A callable error's `status` is `FAILED_PRECONDITION`, not
  `failed-precondition`.** The wire contract uppercases it, which the invitation
  suite already knew and this one had to learn.
- No assertion in the shipped code failed. Both new tests passed on their first
  focused run.

## One shift's correction, reachable from the shift itself - 2026-08-05

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **shift history now says on the row when a closed shift's
recorded sales were corrected, how many times, and when - and opens the
corrections trail narrowed to that one shift.**

Step 1 of that chunk said to confirm the field was on the document the panel
already reads before designing around it. It was on the document and **not in
the read model**, so widening `TenantShiftHistoryEntry` was part of the work
rather than a lookup.

### The row says it before it offers anything

The link was never the point. `amendShiftSummary` rewrites `totalSales`,
`totalSalesMinor`, and `transactionCount`, so **the "Recorded sales" figure on a
corrected row is the rewritten one** - and until this chunk nothing on that row,
or on the whole page, said so. A manager reading a corrected shift saw a figure
presented exactly like every uncorrected one beside it.

So the row now states the correction first, and the link is offered after it:

```text
The recorded sales above were corrected 2 times after this shift closed, to the
total its own sales prove. The counted cash was not changed. Last corrected
2026-07-31 19:00 UTC.
```

Decisions worth recording:

- **A cashier is told, and is not offered the trail.** The trail is
  owner/admin/manager by both `firestore.rules` and its repository, deliberately
  excluding the cashier whose shift it is. But the *shift document* is readable
  by that cashier and carries the correction fields, and the figures on their own
  row are the rewritten ones. Hiding the correction from the person accountable
  for the shift would have been worse than withholding the reason, so the
  sentence is shown to every role that can read the shift and a second sentence
  names the roles that may read the record of who asked and why. This is the same
  shape the differences list already uses for a manager who may read it but not
  act on it.
- **The counted cash is named in the sentence, not left to be inferred.** It is
  the figure a cashier is accountable for and the one thing the amendment path
  guarantees it never writes. "This shift was corrected" alone would leave a
  reader wondering whether their drawer count had been rewritten too.
- **The gate is the trail's own repository, not this surface's management set.**
  `TenantShiftAmendmentFeedRepository.canReadInSession` and
  `TenantShiftHistoryRepository.canReadEveryCashier` name the same three roles
  today. They mean different things, and the authority on who may read the trail
  is the trail.
- **The page header was corrected too.** It claimed figures were "shown exactly
  as they were closed", which a corrected row makes false. It now says they are
  shown as the server holds them, never recomputed here, and that a corrected
  shift says so on its own row.
- **No injected capability, no route builder.** `_openCorrections` sits beside
  `_openSales` and is built the same way: the trail is a read of the same
  business through the same reader, so there is nothing for a composition root to
  grant or withhold. `main.dart` did not change.

### What the read model had to refuse

The four fields (`summaryAmendmentId`, `summaryAmendedGeneration`,
`summaryAmendmentCount`, `summaryAmendedAt`) are written by one transaction and
by one writer. **No client can write any of them**: the close rule restricts a
cashier's single update to the seven closing keys, and
`rules-tests/test/shift-amendments.test.js` already proves a forged
`summaryAmendmentId` is denied to both the cashier and the owner. So a partial or
incoherent set is either a server that changed its contract without this client
knowing or a document no server wrote, and it is refused rather than read as an
uncorrected shift - reporting a rewritten total as an original one is the single
outcome this surface must not produce.

Three lines drawn deliberately:

- **The three deterministic fields are required together; the instant is not.**
  `summaryAmendedAt` is a server timestamp, and every instant in this read model
  is decoded as absent-or-valid for that reason. Its absence limits what the row
  can say about *when*; it never puts the correction itself in doubt, and the row
  says so in words.
- **A corrected shift with no summary is refused**
  (`amended_shift_without_summary`). The correction rewrites the three summary
  fields, so this document could not have come from one, and the row would
  otherwise have to say both that no totals were recorded and that the totals
  were corrected.
- **`summaryAmendmentCount` below 1 is refused.** The server writes the ID and
  increments the count in the same update, so a corrected shift has had at least
  one correction.

## The stock half of the runner, entered for the first time - 2026-08-05

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **the reconciliation integration suite now enters the stock
phase.** It had never been entered by any test, and it could not have been:
`processStockPage` is unreachable from a sale.

That is the finding, and it is the same shape as the one two handovers above.
A sale-trigger job advances metrics then **shifts** - the runner's own
`advanceReconciliationJob` chooses `job.source === "sale_trigger" ? "shifts" :
"stock"` - so every sale this suite has ever written skipped the phase entirely.
The file even said so in a comment, used as a reason an absent `productCursor`
was a stable fact. The only entry point that starts a job whose phases include
stock is `requestTenantReconciliation`, which is why the fixture now exports it.

### Why it takes two runs, and why that is not a workaround

A product with no carried `stock_reconciliation_state` is **baselined**, not
compared: the run records what it found as the truth to measure the next one
against, sets `expectedQuantity = observedQuantity`, and writes
`baseline_established`. So a stock variance is unreachable in a single run *by
construction*, and a test that expected one from a first run would be asserting
something the design forbids.

The test therefore tells one story in two runs:

1. A manual **`full`** run baselines both seeded products and checkpoints what it
   read. `full` is what makes `checkpointKind` `manual` rather than `none`, so it
   is the only manual mode that writes a `stock_checkpoints` record at all.
2. A sale files three units against one product. The trigger writes the ledger
   movement and deliberately nothing else - the till is what decrements a product
   - so this is the state left behind when that never happened.
3. A manual **`incremental`** run is the first comparison that can disagree. It
   finds the ledger accounting for three fewer than the product holds and records
   the `stock_variance`.

Decisions worth recording:

- **The second run is `incremental` on purpose, and it is the sharper of the
  two.** It takes no checkpoint of its own, so it has to read the earlier
  checkpoint, recompute its hash, and agree with it while writing nothing that
  could paper over a disagreement. `checkpointChainValid: true` on a run that
  wrote no checkpoint is the chain actually being verified. The test also asserts
  that run wrote **no** checkpoint document.
- **The checkpoint hash is never recomputed by the test.** `stockCheckpointHash`
  is one function in one module; a test that derived the hash would agree with
  whatever it copied. What is asserted instead is that the *next* run recomputed
  it and agreed, and that the carried state points at the exact checkpoint path
  the earlier run wrote. Same reasoning as the shift anomaly being found by query
  rather than by digest.
- **Two products, one sale.** The product no sale named is asserted `matched`
  with no listed difference, and the job's `stockVarianceCount` is asserted to be
  exactly 1 of 2 products processed. A phase that reported a difference for
  everything would be as broken as one that reported none, and only a second
  product makes both observable in one run.
- **The stock the run disagreed with is asserted unmoved.** `mutatesStock: false`
  is on the job, the verification, and the anomaly, and the product's `quantity`
  is re-read and asserted unchanged. Reconciliation reports a stock difference;
  correcting one is a stock adjustment made from the product.
- **The fixture export needed no closure check.**
  `requestTenantReconciliation` lives in the same `reconciliation/handlers`
  module the task worker already comes from, so exporting it loads nothing that
  was not already loaded and cannot reach a new `defineSecret` parameter. That is
  recorded in the fixture beside the rule it satisfies.

### The guard that would have made the whole test vacuous

`reconcileProduct` defers any product whose `updatedAt` is inside the last five
minutes and records `recent_write_deferred` instead of comparing it. It exists so
a sale's own product decrement is not read as a variance during the window before
its movement lands.

Every fixture in this file seeded `updatedAt: now`, which is inside that window.
**The stock phase would have run, deferred both products, and asserted nothing
about stock** - a green test proving only that the phase can decline to answer.
The fixture now seeds a settled product ten minutes in the past behind an
explicit `settledStock` option, with the reason written at the constant.

Confirmed by mutating the fixture back to `updatedAt: now`: the test fails with
`recent_write_deferred` where it expects `baseline_established`.

## The same narrowing, from the other side - 2026-08-05

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **the differences list now opens the corrections trail narrowed
to the shift the row names**, and keeps it reachable after the row has been
deleted.

`openTenantShiftAmendments` has taken a `shiftId` since the trail was written and

### Three places it is now offered, and one where it deliberately is not

- **Per row, for every row that names a shift** - not only the one kind that can
  be corrected. A shift corrected at a later generation can still be listed under
  an earlier one, because a `reconciliation_anomalies` record is keyed by shift
  *and generation* and a correction deletes only the generation it settled. So
  "has this already been dealt with?" is a real question on an
  `invalid_or_missing_shift` row, and the answer - including "never" - comes from
  the trail rather than from this list. A test pins that row offering the link
  while offering no correction.
- **Beside the notice, after a correction succeeds.** The row it resolved has
  been deleted by the server, so without this the correction just made would be
  reachable only by opening the whole business's trail and reading down. It is
  narrowed to the shift **the server's answer named**, not the shift this page
  asked about, which is the same rule the notice text already follows.
- **Beside the notice, after an outcome nobody knows.** Whether a correction was
  recorded is precisely the open question there, and the trail is the only place
  that answers it. Both the ambiguous refusal and the untrustworthy-answer path
  now offer it, and the untrustworthy-answer sentence was reworded to say so.
- **Not after a refusal that certainly changed nothing.** A definite refusal left
  the shift exactly as it was, so there is nothing new to look at, and a link
  there would imply otherwise. Pinned by its own test.

Two more decisions worth recording:

- **No role check was added, and adding one would have been wrong.**

## A stock difference, where the correction is made - 2026-08-05

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **the product stock surface now states what reconciliation
recorded against the product**, narrowed to that product, with the figures the
ledger and the product actually differ by.

The integration suite proved earlier in this session that the record exists with
real figures, and the differences list renders it business-wide. But the surface
where somebody answers for a product's on-hand - and where the adjustment that
resolves it is recorded - said nothing about it. The operator who can act on a
stock difference was the one who could not see it.

### The read is a secondary one and is not allowed to fail the page

The recorded quantity and the stock ledger are what that route exists for. So the
difference read is carried as a value, not thrown:

- **A failed or refused read reports itself in place** - "Whether reconciliation
  recorded a difference for this product could not be read. The stock and ledger
  below are unaffected." - and the route guard's failure state is never entered.
  The same degrade-rather-than-fail rule the staff-name resolver beside it already
  follows.
- **Unreadable and empty are different answers and the surface never conflates
  them.** `_ProductDifferences` carries an explicit `readable` flag for exactly
  that reason.
- **A broken boundary degrades the same way.** The repository refuses a page that
  answers with another product's record, and that refusal becomes "could not be
  read" rather than a foreign product's figures on this page. A test drives it
  with a filter-ignoring transport and asserts the other product's ID never
  appears anywhere on screen while the stock figure stays readable.

### Nothing is shown for a product with nothing recorded

This is an exception report. A permanent "no differences" line on every product
would make the one that matters easier to miss rather than harder, so a clean
product renders no section at all.

### The wording had to answer a question the shift trail does not

A shift correction deletes the difference it resolved. **Nothing deletes a stock
one.** `reconcileProduct` writes `stock_{digest(productId, jobId)}` per run that
found a difference and never removes an older record, so a product put right
months ago still lists what was found then. Presenting those as open differences
would be false, so the section says so:

> A record is kept for each run that found a difference here, and none is ever
> removed: a later run that agrees simply records nothing new. So an older entry
> may already have been put right. Each one names the run that found it.

Each row therefore names its `jobId` and its own instants, and the bounded page
says plainly that what it shows is neither everything nor the most recent - the
order is by digest, so it carries no time information at all.

### Only one of four kinds is a difference an adjustment resolves

A product can hold `stock_variance`, `invalid_stock_movement`,
`checkpoint_chain_invalid`, and `invalid_product_quantity`. Only the first is a
quantity disagreement:

| Kind | What the row says |
| --- | --- |
| `stock_variance` | the ledger's expected figure, the product's, which way they differ, and that an adjustment below is how it is put right |
| `invalid_stock_movement` | the expected figure does not account for everything that moved; **an adjustment will not resolve this** |
| `checkpoint_chain_invalid` | the chain does not join up so the expected figure cannot be trusted; not a quantity disagreement |
| `invalid_product_quantity` | the quantity could not be read as a whole number, so nothing can be added to it |

The `stock_variance` sentence is byte-identical in wording to the differences
list's, so the two surfaces describe one record the same way. It is written
locally rather than shared: the panels are in different domains and a shared
string would have made one of them depend on the other for a sentence.

### The narrowed read, and why it takes no kind

`loadProductPage` filters on `productId` and nothing else. Two equality filters on
this ascending key order would need a composite index, and the surface wants every
difference listed against the product rather than one kind of them. A new Rules
emulator test issues the exact shape, proves an unknown product answers with an
empty page rather than an error - which is what lets the surface say nothing at
all - and proves a cashier still cannot reach it.

The product stock surface and the differences repository are granted the same
three roles, so no session that reaches this panel is refused the read. The
refusal path is still handled rather than asserted away, because that equality is
a fact about today's two role lists and not a property either surface owns.

## The kind that could never be recorded - 2026-08-05

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **the stock phase's other two outcomes, against a real server.**
Writing the test found that one of them was unreachable, and that is the result -
a fix worth more than the coverage that produced it.

### `invalid_stock_movement` had never been written and could not be

`reconcileProduct` chose the difference's kind like this:

```ts
anomalyType: !chainValid ? "checkpoint_chain_invalid" :
  cumulativeInvalidMovementCount > 0 ? "invalid_stock_movement" : "stock_variance",
```

Twelve lines above it: `if (cumulativeInvalidMovementCount > 0) chainValid = false;`

So the second branch required `chainValid && cumulativeInvalidMovementCount > 0`,
which the line above made impossible. **Every unreadable ledger entry was
reported as a broken checkpoint chain** - a different and more alarming finding
that points an operator at the wrong evidence entirely: at a tamper-evident chain
of checks rather than at the one ledger row that could not be read.

The string appeared exactly once in `functions/src`, in that expression, and
nowhere in any test. `processors.ts` has no unit-test file at all - `amendment`,
`jobs`, and `model` each have one - so the integration suite is its only coverage,
which is why a dead branch survived there and not elsewhere.

Confirmed empirically **before** changing anything: the new test failed with
`actual: 'checkpoint_chain_invalid', expected: 'invalid_stock_movement'` against a
real server, and passed after the reorder.

### The fix, and what it deliberately does not change

The most specific cause is now tested first:

```ts
anomalyType: cumulativeInvalidMovementCount > 0 ? "invalid_stock_movement" :
  !chainValid ? "checkpoint_chain_invalid" : "stock_variance",
```

- **`chainValid` is still set false by an unreadable movement.** That is correct
  and was never the bug: no checkpoint can claim to describe a ledger part of
  which could not be read. The comment there now says why the kind must
  nevertheless name the movement.
- **The chain's verdict is not lost.** `checkpointChainValid: false` is recorded on
  the verification record and the carried state either way, and the new test
  asserts it on the unreadable-movement product.
- **No client change was needed.** Both kinds were already modelled, and the
  product stock surface built earlier in this session already words them
  differently - "the ledger entry is what needs looking at" against "not a
  quantity disagreement". That wording was written for a kind that could not
  occur; it can now.

### Two products, one run, so the distinction is what is observed

The test engineers both outcomes in the same run on different products, so the
phase telling them apart is the property under test rather than an assumption:

- One product's ledger gains a movement whose `quantityDelta` is a string, with a
  real `recordedAt` so the cursor still advances past it. That makes the count of
  unreadable movements exactly one, which the test asserts.
- The other product's checkpoint from the first run is corrupted by changing its
  `expectedQuantity` so its stored hash no longer describes its contents. The hash
  itself is left alone: this is the next run recomputing it and disagreeing, not
  the test asserting a digest.

Neither product's quantity changed, so both records carry `variance: 0` and exist
only because the comparison could not be trusted. The test asserts `variance ==
observedQuantity - expectedQuantity` on both, which is the identity the Dart read
model refuses a record for breaking, so these two server-written shapes are known
to be decodable by the surfaces that render them.

### One thing observed and deliberately left alone

The corrupted-chain product's verification record has `status: "matched"` while
`checkpointChainValid` is `false`. The status describes the quantity comparison,
which did match, and the chain has its own field - but "matched" for a product
whose chain does not verify reads wrong at a glance. Nothing in the app renders
that field today, and changing what `status` means is a second decision rather
than part of this chunk. It is recorded as the next chunk's first question.

## One decision, in one place, with tests - 2026-08-05

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **the stock comparison's conclusion is now one pure function
with unit tests**, and the question the previous chunk left open - what `status`
should say when the chain does not verify - is answered.

### The status question, answered

A product whose quantity agreed with its expected figure while its checkpoint
chain did not verify was recorded as `matched`.

**It is now `checkpoint_chain_invalid`.** The argument for `matched` was that the
field describes the quantity comparison, and the quantities did agree. The
argument against it wins: they agreed with a figure derived from evidence that did
not verify, and nothing else in this codebase records a check as passed while
recording that its own evidence could not be trusted. The status now agrees with
the difference recorded beside it instead of contradicting it.

Two facts made this safe to change rather than a judgement to defer:

- **No client can read the field.** `stock_verifications` and
  `stock_reconciliation_state` are not matched by any rule in `firestore.rules`, so
  the catch-all `allow read, write: if false` covers them. The change is
  observable only to the server and to anyone reading Firestore directly.
- **Nothing reads the stored `status` back.** `baselineStatus` is recomputed from
  the carried state's own validity on every run; the only field read back across
  runs is `lastVerificationHadVariance`, and its meaning is unchanged.

### The extraction, and what it is for

`stockComparisonOutcome` in `model.ts` takes the four facts that settle a stock
comparison - the baseline status, the chain verdict, the count of unreadable
movements, and the variance - and returns the status and the kind of difference to
record, or no kind at all when there is nothing wrong.

It replaces three separate expressions in `reconcileProduct` that each restated
the same condition: the status ternary, the anomaly-kind ternary, and
`!chainValid || cumulativeInvalidMovementCount > 0 || variance !== 0` written out
twice more for whether to write the record and what to return. **That duplication
is how the previous chunk's defect survived**: one copy could be reordered
without the others noticing, and the branch it made unreachable looked live.

Decisions worth recording:

- **It went in `model.ts`, not a new `processors.test.ts`.** The previous
  handover asked for the latter. `model.ts` is where the pure reconciliation
  decisions already live and `model.test.ts` already tests them; a
  `processors.test.ts` that only tested a function defined elsewhere would have
  been the odd one out, and it still could not have touched the transaction.
- **`reconcileProduct` was not restructured.** The extraction is the decision and
  nothing around it; the transaction, its reads, and its writes are untouched
  apart from consuming the result.
- **The absent kind is `undefined`, not a sentinel.** "There is nothing to record"
  is exactly the shape a caller needs - `if (outcome.anomalyType)` - and it made
  the two duplicated conditions disappear rather than move.

## The last thing the stock phase can conclude - 2026-08-05

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **`invalid_product_quantity`, against a real server.** All four
outcomes of the stock phase now have end-to-end evidence, and the phase that no
test could reach at the start of this session is completely covered.

No production code changed. The test exercises a path that was already shipped,
and what it adds is the first proof that the path behaves as the pure reading of
it says when a real Firestore and a real task queue are involved.

### The one stock difference that does not accumulate

Every other stock difference is addressed `stock_{digest(productId, jobId)}`, so a
neglected product collects one record per run that found it - which is why the
product stock surface built earlier in this session has to say that an older entry
may already have been put right.

This one is addressed `product_quantity_{digest(productId)}`: **one record per
product, forever, rewritten in place by each run that still finds it.** That is a
different contract from its four siblings, and the test proves it by running twice
and asserting there is still exactly one record, with the same ID, now naming the
later run.

The second run is a manual `full` one rather than another `incremental` one
because manual admission control holds one cooldown per mode, and a second
incremental request inside five minutes is refused by design. That is worth
knowing before writing any test that wants two manual runs of one business.

### Two things this outcome does differently, recorded rather than endorsed

- **It writes no `stock_verifications/{jobId}` parent document.** Every other
  outcome creates it before writing the product's record beneath it; this branch
  returns before that. Firestore is content with a subcollection under a
  non-existent document, so nothing breaks - but anything that ever lists runs by
  that parent would miss exactly the runs that found an unreadable quantity. The
  test asserts the current behaviour and says so, so a change either way is a
  decision rather than a surprise.
- **It records no quantity figures at all**, and the test asserts their absence.
  There was no figure to compare, and a zero here would be a number the phase
  never read. The Dart read model requires only the product for this kind, which
  is what makes that shape decodable.

  earlier. Nothing was wrong - the suite genuinely got slower and this host is
  variable - but a wrapper set from the old measurement would have killed a
  healthy run and orphaned an emulator, which is the failure pattern the test
  discipline near the top of this file warns about.
- **`Out-String` buffers everything until the command exits**, so a background run
  filtered that way shows an empty output file while it is running. Read the task
  output when it completes rather than trying to watch it.
- No assertion in the shipped code failed. The new test passed on its first
  focused run.

## Saying there is more, after looking at it - 2026-08-05

### Completed in this session

The chunk deferred for four sessions: **the landing route now says when its
content runs past the fold.** It was answered by rendering the screen rather than
by reasoning about it, and the rendering corrected the recorded diagnosis before
anything was changed.

### The recorded diagnosis was wrong, and acting on it would have fixed nothing

Four handovers in this file describe the defect as "the panel sits inside a
`Center` within a `SingleChildScrollView`, so tall content is cut off at both
ends". A widget test rendering the real `TenantSafeLandingScreen` at 411x731 with
real fonts loaded shows otherwise:

- **Only the bottom is cut, never both ends.** A scroll view starts at offset
  zero, so the top is never clipped; the branding panel sits flush under the app
  bar in the rendering.
- **The `Center` is not the cause.** It passes loose constraints down, so a scroll
  view whose content overflows sizes to the full height and starts at the top -
  centred and top-aligned are *the same layout* in exactly the case being
  complained about. The `Center` only has an effect when the content is short,
  which is the case that already looks right.

So the change that four handovers pointed at - replace the `Center` with a top
alignment - would have produced a pixel-identical screen. The correction is
marked inline at the original claim as well as recorded here.

What is actually wrong is narrower and duller: content taller than the viewport,
with **nothing on screen saying so**. What a cashier saw was a heading sliced
through mid-glyph and no counts under it, and the fold is ~120 logical pixels
higher than it needs to be because the two buttons below the scroll area are
pinned outside it.

### What was changed

`_LandingScrollArea` replaces the bare `Center(child: SingleChildScrollView(...))`
and fades the bottom 32 pixels into the surface the screen is already drawn on,
**only while something is below the fold**. The centring is kept exactly as it
was: a mostly-empty landing screen with one panel in the middle is what it is
for, and a permanent "there is more" on a screen with nothing more would be worse
than the silence it replaces.

Decisions worth recording:

- **The position is asked, not awaited.** The first implementation listened for
  `ScrollMetricsNotification`, and it worked in a unit test and silently did
  nothing on the real screen: the notification is dispatched when metrics
  *change*, and the first layout of this route does not reliably produce one.
  That is the case that matters, because a screen is over the fold from the
  moment it opens or not at all. It now reads `extentAfter` from its own
  `ScrollController` in a post-frame callback scheduled by every build, which
  answers for every frame including the first.
- **The notification listener was kept anyway, for the one case the controller
  misses.** This route's content changes height on its own - the checkout counts
  are re-read on every sync signal - and that relayout rebuilds the panel rather
  than this widget, so its own build never runs. A metrics change is the only
  signal for that, and a test pins it.
- **The fade is behind an `IgnorePointer`.** It is drawn over the bottom edge of a
  scrollable, which is exactly where a thumb lands; swallowing that drag would
  make the content it points at harder to reach than before it existed. Asserted
  by dragging from the fade and checking the content moved, not by looking for an
  `IgnorePointer` in the tree - Material puts several of its own in there, so the
  structure proves nothing and the behaviour proves everything.
- **The scroll view now has an explicit controller**, so it is no longer eligible
  to be the `PrimaryScrollController`. On iOS that removes tap-status-bar-to-top
  for this one route. Recorded rather than worked around; this is an Android
  point-of-sale app and the route is one screen tall.

### How the rendering was produced, since it is worth repeating

A throwaway widget test built the real screen at `411x731` logical pixels with
`FontLoader` reading Roboto and MaterialIcons from
`<flutter>/bin/cache/artifacts/material_fonts`, and captured it with
`matchesGoldenFile` under `--update-goldens`. **Without loading those fonts a
widget test renders every glyph as a filled box**, which is useless for looking at
a layout. The shift panel's slot held a stand-in of representative height - the
real one needs Hive, a temp directory, and a fake server - which is honest here
because the container's behaviour depends on the height of its child and nothing
else. The test and its goldens were deleted afterwards; they are not part of the
suite.

The first rendering after the change was **pixel-identical** to the one before it,
which is how the notification defect above was found. Comparing the two PNGs
rather than trusting a green test is the reason this chunk shipped something that
works.

## What the pinned buttons cost, measured - 2026-08-05

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **the landing route's navigation buttons now scroll with its
content instead of being pinned below it.** The previous handover asked for the
measurement first, and the measurement decided it - the number was far worse than
the estimate that motivated the question.

### The measurement

Rendered from the real `TenantSafeLandingScreen` at 411x731 logical pixels, with
the shift panel slot filled and the checkout evidence panel resolved:

| Who | Pinned row | Scroll viewport | Content | Hidden |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cashier, before | 108 | 519 | 700 | 181 |
| **owner, before** | **288** | **339** | 700 | **361** |
| cashier, after | - | 627 | 832 | 205 |
| owner, after | - | 627 | 1012 | 385 |

The previous handover estimated the row at "about 120 pixels". For an owner it is
**288 of the 631 pixels the body has**, because eight buttons are offered and at
411 wide the longer labels do not pair up, so the `Wrap` runs to four rows.

What that left an owner looking at was the branding panel and the first two lines
of the shift card. **"Open shift" - the one thing somebody about to trade opens
this screen for - was below the fold, behind seven navigation buttons**, and the
checkout evidence panel was not on screen at all.

After the change the viewport is the whole body, 627, for everyone. An owner now
sees the entire shift card including both of its actions, and four of the five
checkout counts. More total content is below the fold than before (385 against
361) because the buttons are now part of that content - which is the trade, and
it is the right way round: the primary information is above the fold and the
navigation is below it.

### Nothing was pinned in their place

"Change business" had the claim, as the route's escape hatch. It was not kept:

- Signing out is already in the app bar, so the route is not a trap without it.
- Switching business is the rarest control on the screen.

  least-used thing on it.

If anything is ever pinned here it should be **"New sale"** - the only
write-capable action and the one this screen exists to start. That is a product
decision about the till, not a layout one, and it is deliberately not made here.

### What the short screen looks like now

Unchanged in spirit and slightly better: with no shift panel the content is 532
of 627, nothing is hidden, no fade is shown, and the whole column - buttons
included - is centred. The buttons sit with the content they belong to rather
than floating against the bottom edge.

## The narrowing that was not worth having - 2026-08-05

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **a `productId`-narrowed entry point into the stock movement
feed - or the deletion of the parameter.** Step 1 said to answer the question
before writing anything, and answering it changed what got built.

### The answer, and what it cost to reach it

**A `productId`-narrowed collection group answers nothing the per-product page
does not, so it was not built.** The two reads are the same read:

| | per-product page | `productId`-narrowed group page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| documents | `tenants/{t}/products/{p}/stock_movements` | the same |
| order | ascending document ID | the same |
| roles | owner, admin, manager | the same |
| decoded by | `TenantStockMovement` | the same |
| index | Firestore's automatic single-field | a **new** `(tenantId, productId, __name__)` composite; `firestore.indexes.json` carries only `(tenantId, __name__)` and `(tenantId, sourceType, __name__)` |
| boundary | bounded by path prefix | the one read in this app that Firestore does not bound by a path prefix |

So the group version costs an index and the widest boundary in the codebase to
return rows a bounded read already returns. The chunk's own instruction - "the
honest chunk is to delete the narrowing and say why, not to build a second
surface onto the same rows" - applies directly, and **no index was added**.

There was no literal parameter to delete: `TenantStockMovementFeedRepository`
never grew one. What was left unbuilt for three sessions was the entry point,
not a dangling argument, and the record above is what stops it being reopened a
fifth time.

### The candidate the chunk named is real, and it is an entry-point defect

Step 2 said to check whether the group feed can see movements the per-product
page cannot. It can, and the reason is three facts that compose:

- `firestore.rules` allows `delete` on `products/{productId}` to an **owner or
  admin**.
- The `stock_movements` below it are `allow write: if false`, and Firestore does
  not cascade a delete into a subcollection. The ledger therefore outlives the
  product **permanently**.
- `TenantProductStockScreen` requires an already-decoded `TenantProduct` and is
  reachable only from the catalog, which no longer lists the product;
  `loadStock` refuses with `product_unavailable` before reading the ledger at
  all.

A deleted product's ledger was therefore visible in exactly one place - the
business-wide feed - as a bare `Product {id}` line with nothing behind it and no
hint that the product was gone. That is not a narrowing problem. It is the
entry point missing from the read that could always have answered it.

### What shipped

- **`TenantProductStockRepository.loadLedger`** returns a `TenantProductLedger`
  carrying the product ID, the product **or null**, and the ledger page. Null is
  a real answer rather than a failure.
- **`loadStock` still refuses the same absent product**, and a test pins that.
  The distinction is the whole design: reading what moved a product is safe once
  it is gone, and correcting the stock of a product that does not exist is not.
- **`findProduct` is a separate method rather than a flag on `readProduct`.**
  Every existing caller wants a missing product to be a refusal; turning that
  into a nullable they must remember to check is how a deleted product ends up
  rendered as one with no stock.
- **The product ID is validated before it reaches a path.** It arrives from a
  feed row, not from a decoded catalog record, so it has never been checked;
  `invalid_product_id` refuses `''`, `a/b`, `.`, `..`, and an over-long ID
  before any read is issued.
- **`TenantProductLedgerScreen` is read-only.** It offers no adjustment form, no
  filter, and - on a single-page ledger - no control at all, which a test
  asserts by widget type. That is what lets it open for a product that cannot be
  corrected because it no longer exists.
- **A deleted product is named as one.** The title reads `Deleted product`, the
  page says the ledger is kept permanently and that there is nothing left to
  correct, and **no stock figure is shown** - there is no document to read one
  from and inventing one would be a fiction.
- **The row labels are now shared, not copied.** `stock_movement_labels.dart`
  holds the six sentences both movement surfaces describe one entry with. Two
  copies of "Before and after were not recorded" is two chances to change one
  and not the other. They are in the same domain and render the same document,
  which is what makes sharing right here and wrong between domains - the
  opposite call to the one recorded for the anomalies sentence further up this
  file, for the opposite reason.
- **The route is injected, like every other one.** While the composition root
  supplies none, the feed is exactly the read-only list it was before, and a
  test asserts the row is a plain `Text` with no button anywhere on the page.
- **It opens under the same session scope**, so a tenant switch invalidates it
  rather than leaving a detached screen behind. A test reads the scope back out
  of the pushed route and asserts it is the same controller.

## The largest module's first unit tests - 2026-08-06

### Completed in this session

The chunk above: **`processors.ts` has unit tests.** It was the oldest untouched
item in this file - four handovers - and, exactly as two chunks ago, most of it
was already in the tree. Three untracked files were waiting at `HEAD`:

```text
functions/src/reconciliation/processors.test.ts
functions/src/testing/fakeFirestore.ts
functions/src/testing/fakeFirestore.test.ts
```

They were read before anything else, and the answer was **finish them** - the
same call, and for the same reasons, as the reconciliation-run surface. What was
there was coherent rather than abandoned: `npm --prefix functions test` was
**247/247** against it before a character was changed, up from the 211 recorded
at the end of the last session, and discarding it would have thrown away the
queued item four handovers had asked for.

### What was already there, and what it is worth

- **`fakeFirestore.ts`** - an in-memory Firestore the processors can be run
  against as units. The four page sizes are 5, 25, 200, and 50, so every boundary
  assertion against a real emulator would mean seeding tens or hundreds of
  documents per run; this is what makes "a page that ends exactly on its own
  boundary" and "a lease revoked between two products of one page" cheap enough
  to assert at all.
- **`fakeFirestore.test.ts`** - the double's own semantics, fifteen cases, each
  named for the processor behaviour that depends on it. This is the part that
  makes the rest trustworthy. Three panel fakes in this repository have already
  made a Dart test pass for the wrong reason by answering a question they were
  never asked, and this is the largest fake in the project; its claims about
  Firestore are written down as assertions rather than left as comments.
- **`processors.test.ts`** - twenty-one cases over the four exports, covering the
  four behaviours the previous handover named: the cursor a partial page resumes
  from, a page that ends exactly on its own boundary, a lease lost mid-page, and
  a phase that finds nothing.

The double's design decision worth repeating: **where Firestore's semantics
decide an outcome it implements them, and everything else throws.** A document
with no value at an ordered field is invisible to that query; a transaction
refuses a read after its first write; `FieldValue.delete()` is rejected in an
unmerged `set`; `update` refuses a document that does not exist. Any operator but
`==`, any `FieldPath` but `documentId()`, any unrecognised sentinel, and any
unorderable value stop the test instead of being guessed at. A silently-ignored
`where` clause is the single worst thing a Firestore double can do.

### The three branches it left, now closed

Reading `reconcileProduct` against the new file found three paths nothing
reaches - not this file, not the integration suite, not `model.test.ts`:

- **A product this job already finished is counted again but not verified
  again.** A task queue retries a *page*, not the product it stopped at, so the
  second attempt meets products this job's own generation already settled. The
  carried state is what says so. The new test asserts the page re-counts the
  difference from what the earlier attempt concluded - dropping it would leave the
  job's own `stockVarianceCount` short of the records it wrote - and that **nothing
  at all is written a second time**. Its second half proves the guard is scoped to
  this job *at this generation*: a rerun compares the product again, which is also
  the only route that reads a ledger from the beginning.
- **A product written moments ago is deferred rather than compared.** The trap
  every fixture in this file is settled to avoid, and the one that already cost
  this repository a whole integration test that asserted nothing. It is now pinned
  where pinning it is cheap, including that the deferral carries **nothing**
  forward - no expectation for the next run to measure against, and the ledger
  below it was never read.
- **Carried state that names no ledger position is re-baselined and reported.**
  The one stock status nothing had ever covered, over five shapes of broken state.
  It is the branch that quietly forgives a difference: a state that cannot say
  where in the ledger it stopped cannot be resumed from, so the run takes the
  product's own quantity as the new expectation and the comparison then agrees
  with itself by construction. The test seeds a movement that *would* have made
  the expectation 7 if it had been replayed, and asserts it is 10 - and that the
  run records `checkpoint_chain_invalid` rather than reporting agreement it never
  established.

### Every new assertion was proved to fail against the behaviour it names

Five mutations, each built and run, each failing exactly what it should and
nothing else:

| Mutation to `processors.ts` | What failed |
| --- | --- |
| the generation dropped from the already-finished guard | the retry test, alone |
| the deferral window collapsed from five minutes to zero | the deferral test, alone |

### One finding, recorded rather than fixed

**`retryDelayMilliseconds` has no producer anywhere in the pipeline.**
`ProductResult` declares it, `processStockPage` forwards it,

it into `nextAttemptAt` with `Date.now() + Math.max(0, advance.retryDelayMilliseconds ?? 0)`.
Nothing ever assigns it a value, so every continuation this pipeline schedules is
scheduled for now.

It was not deleted, and the reason is that the default it produces is the correct
one: a movement backlog has more work waiting and should be picked up
immediately. Whether *anything* should ever ask for a delay - the deferral is the
only candidate, and it returns `completed: true` rather than asking to be retried
- is a design question about the job-advance contract across three modules, not
something to settle inside a test chunk. The current behaviour is pinned by an
assertion with the reasoning written at it, and the decision is the next chunk.

neighbourhood in two sessions, after the unreachable `invalid_stock_movement`

## A hook with no producer, and three bounds nothing had counted - 2026-08-07

### Completed in this session

Three chunks, in the order the previous handover queued them. The first was the
one it named; the second it also named and this session could not finish, for a
reason recorded in full below; the third it had declined once, on a premise that
had stopped being true.

### 1. `retryDelayMilliseconds` is gone

**The decision: the deferral stays as it is, and the field loses its excuse to
exist.** The previous handover left this as an open design question across three
modules. It has one answer, and the code now says so in one place.

The field could only ever be *forwarded* on a `completed: false` product result,
because those are the only two returns in `processStockPage` that carried it.
`reconcileProduct` has exactly one such return - `movement_backlog` - and a
backlog means the next two hundred movements are **already committed and
waiting**. Delaying that continuation is not conservative, it is just slower.

The one branch with any claim to asking for a delay is `recent_write_deferred`,
and asking would mean holding the page: returning `completed: false` with the
product as `pendingProductId` so the phase stalls until `safeAfter`. The previous
handover asked for that cost to be measured before choosing. Measured, it is worse
than a delay:

- **A held product blocks every product after it.** The page is ordered by
  document ID, so one hot product early in the catalog stops the other 9,999 from
  being verified at all in that job. Stepping past it verifies 9,999 and re-reads
  the hot one on the next run.
- **The five-minute window is not a five-minute wait.** Every sale stamps
  `updatedAt` on every product it decrements -
  `lib/checkout/checkout_sale.dart:419`, `stockServerTimestampFields: ['updatedAt']`
  - so a product selling more often than once every five minutes never leaves its
  own window. The hold is unbounded, and it is unbounded for exactly the products
  a stock check exists to watch.
- **Stepping past costs nothing.** The deferral writes the two
  `stock_verifications` documents and never touches
  `stock_reconciliation_state`, so no movement cursor advances, the
  already-finished guard does not fire, and the next job reads the product from
  the same ledger position. Nothing is lost by deferring; something is lost by
  waiting.

So the field is removed from `ProductResult`, `StockPageResult`, and `JobAdvance`,
the pass-through in `handlers.ts` is gone, and `nextAttemptAt` is
`Timestamp.now()`.

**`advanceReconciliationJob` still writes the field rather than clearing it, and
that is now under test for two reasons it turned out to have.** Both were
discovered while working out what a test of it should say:

1. **A backoff a failed attempt left behind must not outlive it.**
   `recordReconciliationFailure` writes `nextAttemptAt` 15 seconds to an hour out
   and `claimReconciliationJob` throws `unavailable` while it is live. Without
   `advance` overwriting it, a job that failed once would have *every remaining
   page* refused for being early - and past the sixth consecutive failure, refused
   for a full hour per page.
2. **`FieldValue.delete()` would strand the job.**
   `listRetryableReconciliationTasks` finds a lost dispatch with
   `where("nextAttemptAt", "<=", now)`, and Firestore returns nothing for a
   document with no value at a filtered field. A queued job without the field is
   invisible to the only sweep that can recover it.

`jobs.test.ts` had no coverage of `advanceReconciliationJob` at all - the previous
handover's step 4 said it did, and it did not; the file was five pure cases over
`saleTriggerJobFields` and `mergeDirtyJob`. It now has three Firestore-backed
cases, and the fixture is built by `createManualJobInTransaction` rather than
hand-seeded, so it cannot drift from what production creates.

**That needed one addition to the double: `create`.** `FakeTransaction` had no
`create`, which is the write Firestore rejects a delete sentinel in and the exact
shape of the defect `sentinelAudit.ts` exists to find - the one that threw on
every sale for as long as it lived. The double could describe that refusal in a
comment and not reproduce it. Now it reproduces it, and `ALREADY_EXISTS` besides,
which is the whole of every idempotent creator's idempotency in this codebase.

### 3. The three metrics bounds, all asserted

The previous handover recorded two bounded limits in `regenerateDailyMetric` as
"unasserted anywhere", with the caveat that proving them "requires the page sizes
to become injectable, which is a change to production code for a test's benefit".

**That caveat was written against an emulator, and it stopped being true when the
double landed.** Five thousand sales and two hundred expectations are seeded in
memory in about three seconds, so the bounds are asserted at their real figures
and the production constants stayed private. There are three, not two, and none of
them had ever been counted:

| Bound | Where | What it limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5,000 sales per business date | `processors.ts` | documents **read** |
| 200 stale shift expectations | `processors.ts` | documents **deleted** |
| 200 distinct shifts | `model.ts`, `aggregateDailySales` | documents **written** |

**They are one budget, and that is now written down where the constant is.** One
regeneration is a single transaction: at most 200 deletions, plus 200 expectations
written, plus the daily metric, plus the dirty-day row - **402 writes against
Firestore's limit of 500**. Raising either 200 moves the widest regeneration past
that limit, and on the day it does, a busy date stops being republishable rather
than getting slower. The inline `201`/`200` literals are now
`SHIFT_EXPECTATION_LIMIT`, carrying that reasoning.

The half of each test that matters is not that it throws but **when**: both
refusals are raised before the transaction opens, so a date over either bound
keeps its previous daily metric and stays dirty. A bound checked one line later
would publish an aggregate over the first 5,000 sales of the day and mark the day
clean, and nothing downstream could tell that figure from a complete one. Each
test asserts `db.writes` is empty and the day is still `dirty`.

Both bounds are asserted on both sides of the comparison, because the query reads
one more than the bound precisely so a date sitting exactly on it is still a
complete read - `>` and not `>=`, and each direction is a separate test.

### Practical notes carried forward

- Everything in the previous nine sessions' lists still applies, with one
  correction: **do not revert a mutation with `git checkout -- <path>` in a session
  that also changes that file.** Copy to the scratchpad and restore from the copy.
- **The Auth emulator reserves three ports, not one:** `port`, `port + 200`, and
  `port + 400`. Two suites 200 apart cannot run while the other is held, and the
  failure names a port no config mentions.
- **Never free a port by killing an emulator you did not start.** A held
  `emulators:exec` may be holding seeded data. Read its command line first - the
  `--hold` flag is the tell - and move your own port instead.
- **A double's fidelity is what makes a bound testable at its real figure.** The
  standing advice was to make three page sizes injectable to test them. Ten
  thousand in-memory documents cost three seconds and left the constants private,
  which is strictly better than a production seam that exists for a test.
- **When three constants share one budget, say what the budget is at the
  constant.** 200 + 200 + 2 = 402 against Firestore's 500. None of the three
  numbers is safe to raise alone, and nothing said so until now.
- `node --test` needs `--test-reporter=tap` before its output is filtered; the
  Firebase emulator runners use the default reporter, whose totals are `pass N`
  behind an information glyph.

### 2. The reconciliation job lifecycle is watched

`jobs.ts` had three exported functions with no unit coverage. All three now have
it, over the same in-memory Firestore the previous session used for
`advanceReconciliationJob`, and the eleven tests are the *refusals* rather than the
happy paths.

**The premise, written down once at the top of the new section: a Cloud Tasks
queue guarantees at-least-once delivery.** So the same dispatch arrives twice, a
dispatch the job has already moved past arrives late, and a worker killed at its
deadline leaves a job that looks running and is not. Three fields decide every one
of those - `generation`, `revision`, `leaseToken` - and a claim granted when it
should not be is two workers writing one tenant's stock verifications from two
different ledger positions.

**`claimReconciliationJob`** - five refusals:

- A job that no longer exists ends the dispatch quietly. The queue will not stop
  delivering a task for anything short of a success, so this cannot throw.
- A task naming a superseded `generation` or `revision` is refused. Both
  directions, because a finished page bumps one and a rerun bumps the other.
- A live lease is not stolen by a duplicate dispatch, and the refusal writes
  nothing - not even an attempt count.
- **The lease is ten minutes against a seven-minute worker.** `handlers.ts`
  enqueues with `dispatchDeadlineSeconds: 420` and runs with `timeoutSeconds: 420`.
  The three-minute margin is what stops a worker still inside its own deadline
  from having its lease expire underneath it, which is the only way two workers
  reach one job's processors at once. Two constants in two modules, now pinned by
  one assertion.
- **An expired lease is recovered with a *new* token, and that is the fence.** The
  boundary is asserted on both sides - refused one millisecond early, granted at
  the instant. The worker that lost the lease may still be alive and still holding
  a half-finished page, so the test then proves both `advanceReconciliationJob`
  and `finalizeReconciliationJob` refuse it and write nothing.

**`finalizeReconciliationJob`** - both branches:

- A finished job is unqueued from **both** routes that could redispatch it, and
  they are independent. The status refuses the queue redelivering the task that
  finished it; deleting `nextAttemptAt` is what makes it invisible to
  `listRetryableReconciliationTasks`. That is the exact mirror of what `advance`
  does - `advance` *writes* the field so a job whose dispatch was lost stays
  findable - and the pair is now one assertion each.
- **A sale that lands mid-run reruns the job instead of completing it**, and the
  fixture is built by running two sales through `registerSaleReceipt` rather than
  by seeding `rerunRequested`. Seeding the flag would prove that `finalize` reads
  a field; running the sale proves the sale is not lost. The job is advanced one
  page first so it has a real cursor to lose: a rerun starts a fresh pass from the
  metrics phase, so keeping `productCursor` would silently skip the first five
  products. And it is `generation`, not `revision`, that the rerun bumps - the
  returned payload is claimable and the finished pass's is not.

**`recordReconciliationFailure`** - the schedule and its two ends:

- **The whole reachable backoff ladder is 15s, 30s, 60s, 120s, 240s, 480s, 960s.**
  Seven rungs, asserted at their real figures.
- **Earlier notes in this file said the backoff reaches an hour. It does not.**
  The formula names 15 seconds, eight doublings, and a one-hour cap - deliberately
  the same shape as the queue's own `retryConfig` in `handlers.ts` - but quarantine
  at eight consecutive failures fires at the seventh rung, so neither the exponent
  clamp nor the hour cap is reachable. Both stay, because raising the threshold
  must not also uncap the wait; that reasoning is now a comment at the constant,
  along with the other half of the relationship: **the threshold has to stay below
  the queue's `maxAttempts: 12`**, or the queue abandons the task before the job
  quarantines itself and nothing ever writes the alert.
- **A dispatch refused for being early is not a failure.** The queue retries on its
  own schedule and knows nothing about the job's, so early arrivals are routine.
  The refusal is thrown by the claim, which sits *above* the `try` in
  `executeReconciliationTask` that records failures - and it has to stay there. If
  an early dispatch counted, a job would quarantine itself out of retry noise
  alone, without ever having run a page a second time.
- **The eighth consecutive failure quarantines and raises one platform alert**, at
  a deterministic document ID with `merge: true`, and the quarantined job is then
  locked by both routes at once: refused by status, invisible to the sweep. A job
  that stops retrying silently is a tenant whose figures quietly stop being
  verified, so the last failure is also the one that tells somebody.
- **A failure from a worker that has lost the job writes nothing.** It returns
  rather than throwing, because it is called in a `catch` and a failure handler
  that throws replaces the error the caller was already reporting. The late error
  must not fail a job somebody else is running, put a backoff on it, or spend one
  of its eight lives.

**No production behaviour changed in this chunk.** The only edit to `jobs.ts` is
the eight-line comment recording why the hour cap is unreachable and what the two
thresholds owe each other.

### Meaningful failures and their resolutions

- **The mutation harness could not spawn `npm.cmd`: `EINVAL`, with empty stdout
  and stderr, for all thirteen mutations at once.** Node 20 and later refuse to
  spawn a `.cmd` or `.bat` through `execFileSync` without `shell: true`. The empty
  error text is the tell - a build that actually failed prints diagnostics. It was
  diagnosed with one direct reproduction before any retry, and resolved by
  invoking the compiler the way `npm run build` would have:
  `node functions/node_modules/typescript/bin/tsc -p functions/tsconfig.json`.
  That is also several seconds faster per mutation, which matters at thirteen.
- **The mutation harness never used `git checkout --` to revert.** It holds the
  original file in memory and restores from that in a `finally`, then verifies the
  restore byte-for-byte and rebuilds. This is the previous session's correction
  turned into something that cannot be forgotten - and it mattered here, because
  `jobs.ts` carries a real edit this session that `git checkout --` would have
  destroyed.
- **No assertion failed that was not made to.** Every red run in this session was

### Next bounded chunk

**Cover `registerSaleReceipt`'s own defences.** It is the entry point every
reconciliation job comes from - one Firestore trigger per sale - and it now runs
against the double (the rerun test above drives it), but only down its simplest
path. Every branch below is one it takes on real data and none is asserted
anywhere:

1. **The receipt is the idempotency key.** A redelivered `onDocumentCreated` must
   return the *first* delivery's task and invalid-line count without writing a
   second movement or double-counting the dirty day - and a receipt whose
   `tenantId`, `businessDate`, or `jobId` disagrees with the retry must throw
   `already-exists` rather than be trusted.
2. **`saleMovements` combines lines per product and rejects the rest.** Two lines
   of the same product become one movement with `lineCount: 2`; a non-object line,
   a missing or over-long or slash-bearing `productId`, a non-integer or
   non-positive quantity, and an unsafe integer sum each count as invalid. `items`
   that is not an array is one invalid line, and anything past the hundredth line
   is counted and dropped.
3. **Invalid lines write a `reconciliation_anomalies` document**, and only when
   there is at least one. The dirty day's `invalidLineCount` increments by the same
   figure, which is the only place a malformed sale is visible to an operator.
4. **A bucket that belongs to another source throws.** `dirty_<bucket>` is a
   predictable ID, so a job created there by anything but the sale trigger has to
   be refused rather than merged into.
5. The movement document ID switches to a hash past 120 characters of sale ID -
   the branch that keeps a Firestore path legal.

Do not add `collectionGroup`, `in`, or `<=` to the double for this; none of the
above needs them.

## A business can set what it sells in - 2026-08-07

### Why this chunk and not the queued one

The queued chunk was branch coverage for `registerSaleReceipt`. It was declined
for this session in favour of the capability directly above it on the board,
because the board said the app could not function without it: **"Set the currency
/ checkout configuration - Read-only. Without it the till refuses to sell at
all."** That is not a coverage gap, it is a business that cannot trade. The
`registerSaleReceipt` chunk is carried forward unchanged and needs no decision.

The other red row from the same finding - catalog management - was left alone
deliberately, and not only for size. Its halves have different costs, which the
Firestore rules settle rather than the plan:

| Half | Rule today | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create a product | `allow create: if hasTenantRole(['owner','admin','manager']) && quantity is int` | reachable now, client-only |
| Delete a product | `allow delete: if hasTenantRole(['owner','admin'])` | reachable now, client-only |
| **Edit** a product | `allow update` permits **only** a strictly decreasing `quantity` with `affectedKeys().hasOnly(['quantity','updatedAt'])` | needs a rules change or a new callable - a separate decision |

So "a shop can stock itself" is a client-only chunk, and "a shop can correct a
price" is not. That split is recorded in `PLAN.md` as the next chunk and its open
half. Configuration writing had no such split: `configuration/{documentId}`
already carries `allow write: if hasTenantRole(tenantId, ['owner','admin'])`, so
this session added no rule, no callable, and no export.

### Completed behaviour

**One route publishes `configuration/checkout`, and only that document.** Reached
from the safe landing screen as "Checkout settings", beside the read-only catalog
rather than beside the till, because it decides what every price in that catalog
means. Offered to owner and administrator only - the same pair the Firestore rule
allows - and the route itself is guarded by that pair, so a manager or cashier is
denied and issues no read at all.

**The surface is built around whether a till can sell, not around whether a
document exists.** `TenantPublishedCheckoutConfiguration` has three states:
`published`, `absent`, and `malformed`. The third is the one that mattered: the
strict read model refuses a document whose `currency` is not `^[A-Z]{3}$`, the
catalog refresher then answers `configurationUnavailable`, and every device in the
business stops selling. Showing the cashier's refusal to the one person who can
correct it would have left them with nothing to do, so the publishing repository
catches `FormatException` and reports the state, while `TenantScopeViolation` is
deliberately **not** caught - a reader answering outside the tenant is a broken
boundary, never "nothing is published".

**The write merges.** `set(data, SetOptions(merge: true))`, not a whole-document
`set`. `configuration` is one collection with a document per concern and the read
model deliberately ignores fields it does not know, so a whole-document write from
this build would silently delete a setting a later one added. The rules test proves
both halves: an unknown `receiptFooter` on the same document survives, and
`configuration/branding` beside it is untouched.

**There is no request ID, and that is a property rather than an omission.** Every
other write in this client derives a deterministic document ID from
`actorUid + operation + tenantId + requestId` so a retry addresses one document.
This write names one fixed path and one fixed value, so it is idempotent by
construction: an ambiguous outcome is reported as "publishing the same code again
is safe", and the page re-reads rather than warning the operator off a retry.

### The safety decisions

1. **A sale carries the currency it was priced with, so nothing is ever
   re-priced.** `checkout_draft.dart:302` copies `snapshot.configuration.currency`
   into the sale payload, and that payload is hashed. Changing the published code
   therefore rewrites no history and converts no amount. The confirmation says so
   in those words, and the route repeats it as a standing sentence: "It converts
   nothing: this app runs no exchange rate, and no recorded sale is ever
   re-priced."
2. **An unsynced device keeps pricing in the old code, and the operator is told
   so.** The till prices from the encrypted Hive snapshot, which is only re-read by
   the catalog refresh inside a sync pass. Two devices can therefore record the
   same day's sales in two currencies, and `daily_metrics` carries no code at all -
   the reporting label comes from the *current* configuration. This is stated in
   the confirmation rather than prevented, because preventing it would mean
   blocking a correction: a business that published `KSE` for `KES` must be able to
   fix it.
3. **A commit asks for a full sync pass.** `CheckoutSyncSignals` gained
   `requestSyncAfterConfigurationChange()`, which emits the same unnarrowed `null`
   a reconnect does rather than a `CheckoutSaveSyncRequest`. A save-shaped request
   sets `refreshDerivedData: false`, and the catalog refresh is the only thing that
   re-reads the document - so a save-shaped signal would have left this device
   pricing with the code it had just replaced. It emits nothing on
   `evidenceChanges`: no local checkout state moved.
4. **Only a warned change is confirmed; a refused one is never asked about.** The
   intent is built *before* the dialog, so `invalid_currency` and
   `currency_unchanged` are reported as sentences instead of being confirmed and
   then refused, and the confirmation describes the intent that would be written
   rather than the text that was typed. `intent.changesPublishedCurrency` is the
   only thing that decides whether the strong warning is shown, and it is false for
   both `absent` and `malformed` - neither replaces anything usable.
5. **Republishing the identical code is refused.** It would rewrite the provenance
   fields and ask every device to re-read a catalog that cannot have changed. A
   malformed or absent document is never "unchanged": clearing it is exactly what
   the surface exists for.
6. **`kes` is a spelling of `KES`, not a different setting.** Normalization is in
   the repository rather than the widget, so the one casing an ISO 4217 code has is
   decided at the boundary that validates it. Reading is never a repair, though: a
   stored lowercase code stays `malformed`, because the till would otherwise price
   a sale with a code no rule and no report agrees about.
7. **The committed/rejected/ambiguous/unavailable split is the return writer's,
   unchanged.** Offline attempts nothing; a failing connectivity check counts as
   offline; the seven proven-refusal codes are `rejected` and everything else is
   `ambiguous`; only a rejection leaves the page unread, because only a rejection
   proves nothing was written.
