## A shop can stock itself - 2026-08-07

### Why this chunk

It was the queued one, and checking it against the board confirmed it rather than
displacing it: **"Add or retire a product - No write path exists anywhere in the
migrated code"** was the last red row that stops a business operating. Everything
downstream of a product existing already worked - the till, stock, returns,
receipt lookup, reporting, reconciliation - and nothing but
`rules-tests/scripts/seed-dev-emulator.js` could put one there. No capability the
app needs in order to function was found missing and unqueued ahead of it.

Client-only, exactly as the previous chunk predicted from the rules:
`allow create` on `products` is `hasTenantRole(['owner','admin','manager']) &&
quantity is int`, `allow delete` is `hasTenantRole(['owner','admin'])`, and
`categories` allows create, update, and delete to all three. No rule, callable,
export, or index changed. The **edit** half stayed out, and is still the open
decision it was opened as.

### Completed behaviour

**One route adds to and retires from the catalog.** `TenantCatalogManagementScreen`
and `TenantCatalogManagementPanel` in `lib/inventory/`, reached from the safe landing
screen as "Manage catalog", beside the read-only catalog because it is the same
catalog seen by the person who may change it. The guard's role list is the
**create** list - owner, administrator, manager - so a cashier is denied and issues
no read at all. Retiring is decided separately, per render, from the guarded
session, so an administrator sees the action and a manager does not.

**Six safety decisions, each of which could have gone the other way:**

1. **The create writes exactly the shape the strict read model demands.** The rule
   checks only `quantity is int`, so nothing on the server stops a client writing a
   product the till cannot parse - and one unparseable product makes the *whole*
   cached catalog a miss, which stops the business selling.
   `TenantProductCreateIntent` is therefore the only thing preventing it, and the
   unit suite proves it by feeding `documentData()` straight back through
   `TenantProduct.fromDocument` rather than by comparing it to a hand-written
   expectation.
2. **A price is proved through the till's own function.** The typed value is bounded
   to a plain decimal amount with at most two places - two is all `unitPriceMinor`
   holds - and the derived minor units are then round-tripped through
   `checkoutMinorUnitsFromMajor`, the same function the cart and the draft service
   use. The stored major-unit figure is derived from the minor units rather than
   from what was typed, so the two can never disagree about what a line costs.
   `1e3`, `0x10`, `-5`, `1.005`, and an amount past `maximumCheckoutMinorAmount` are
   all refused where they are typed instead of at the till, where the refusal is
   `price_not_representable` with a customer standing there.
3. **A product is always created holding nothing.** The rule would accept any
   integer. Stock that appears without a `stock_movements` entry has no recorded
   origin, and `adjustStock` already carries an `opening_balance` type whose whole
   purpose is to put the first units in and say where they came from - so the create
   names `quantity: 0`, and both the confirmation and the success notice say to
   record the opening quantity from the product itself.
4. **Categories are part of the chunk, create-only.** A product needs a `categoryId`
   and the till already reports products whose category a device does not hold, so a
   surface that could add a product but not a category would not be usable. Renaming
   and deleting a category are **not** offered even though the rule permits both:
   deleting one orphans the `categoryId` on every product filed under it, and nothing
   in this app repairs that. The rules test records what the rule allows, so the gap
   between rule and surface is deliberate rather than forgotten.
5. **Retiring says what survives it.** The confirmation states that the stock ledger,
   every past sale line, and every reported figure keep naming the product; that it
   still holds *n* in stock and retiring moves that nowhere and records no movement;
   and - the part that matters - that this is **not** how a mistake is corrected,
   because a replacement gets its own identity and this one keeps its whole history.
   Retiring is not blocked on non-zero stock: that would invent a rule nothing else
   in the app has, and the figure is stated instead.
6. **The document ID is deterministic and scoped by request, not derived from the
   SKU.** `pd_<40 hex of sha256("createTenantProduct tenantId createdBy requestId")>`,
   and `ct_` for a category, mirroring `_deterministicReturnId` exactly. Two reasons a
   SKU slug was refused: the ID is permanent - `stock_movements` hangs below it, every
   sale line names it, `daily_metrics` aggregates by it - while a SKU is neither
   unique (two products may legitimately carry one, which the till refuses to resolve)
   nor correctable (no client rule and no callable can change it). Deriving the
   permanent identity from the one field this app cannot fix would make a typo
   permanent in the ledger key. The panel retains the request ID **only** across an
   ambiguous outcome, so a retry addresses the same document and a genuinely new
   product gets a new one.

**A replay cannot stock the shelf twice, and the rules prove why.** A `set` onto a
document that already exists is an *update*, and `allow update` on `products` permits
nothing but a strictly decreasing quantity with
`affectedKeys().hasOnly(['quantity','updatedAt'])`. So a replayed create is refused by
the server rather than quietly rewriting a product that has already sold. That is the
whole reason the deterministic ID is safe, and it is now asserted in
`rules-tests/test/catalog-management.test.js` rather than assumed.

**A committed change asks for a full sync pass.** `requestSyncAfterCatalogChange()`
was added beside `requestSyncAfterConfigurationChange()` and emits the same
unnarrowed reason: the catalog refresh is the only thing that re-reads `products` and
`categories`, and a save-shaped request sets `refreshDerivedData: false`. Without it
this device could not sell a product that now exists and could still sell one that no
longer does.

**The form lives above the guard.** Paging and reloading both replace the guarded
subtree with the loading indicator - the standing `TenantRouteGuard` trap - so the
four `TextEditingController`s and the selected category are owned by the panel state
rather than by the guarded contents. A half-typed product survives a page change, and
only a committed create clears it.

**Products page.** The read-only catalog states "More products are available." and
stops; a management surface that could not reach the twenty-first product could not
retire it, so this one pages by document-ID cursor as the returns history does.

### Deliberately not done

- **No SKU uniqueness check.** Nothing on the server enforces one, the seed script
  seeds a deliberate collision, and the till already refuses an ambiguous scan rather
  than picking a product. A client-side check against the loaded page would be a
  guarantee the next device breaks, so the confirmation *states* the hazard instead:
  if another product already scans as that code, the till will refuse that scan.
- **No currency on the confirmation.** The amount is shown as a plain figure and
  labelled "in the currency this business publishes". Reading `configuration/checkout`
  here would couple the inventory domain to the checkout domain for a label.
- **Editing anything.** Still the open decision, and this chunk makes it sharper
  rather than smaller: a catalog typed in by hand is where a wrong price comes from.

## The trigger every reconciliation job comes from - 2026-08-07

### Completed in this session

The chunk the previous handover queued, taken unchanged: **`registerSaleReceipt`'s
own defences**. It was checked against the status board first and kept. No red row
stops a business operating; the sharpest one left - editing a product - is an open
decision rather than a chunk; and this one needs no decision at all.

Fifteen tests in one new file, and **no production change of any kind**.
`functions/src/reconciliation/jobs.ts` is byte-identical to its committed state at
the end of this session, and `git diff` over it is empty.

### Why this function and not another

`mergeSaleReconciliationJob` is `onDocumentCreated` on
`tenants/{tenantId}/sales/{saleId}`, declared `retry: true`. It is the entry point
every reconciliation job in the system comes from: one Firestore trigger per sale,
one transaction, four kinds of document written from a payload composed by a till
that may have been offline for a day.

It already ran against the in-memory Firestore double - `jobs.test.ts` drives it
twice to build a `rerunRequested` fixture - but only down its simplest path: one
sale, one valid line, one new bucket. Every branch below is one it takes on real
data, and none of them was asserted anywhere.

The new file is `saleReceipt.test.ts` rather than more of `jobs.test.ts`, because
the two are about different things: `jobs.test.ts` is the job lifecycle - who may
claim, advance, finalize, and fail a job - and this is the sale that creates one.

### The five groups, and what each is actually protecting

**1. The receipt is the idempotency key.** `reconciliation_sale_receipts/{saleId}`
is written with `create`, and it is the only write in the transaction that can
refuse. Three tests:

- A redelivery writes **nothing** and answers exactly as the first delivery did.
  Both halves of the answer come off the stored receipt - the task the caller
  enqueues and the invalid-line count it reports - and the two counters that would
  show a double count (`saleReceiptCount`, `invalidLineCount`) use
  `FieldValue.increment`, which has no idea a delivery is a repeat.
- A redelivery whose `businessDate` or bucket disagrees with the stored receipt is
  refused with `already-exists`. Both are reachable: the same sale ID with a
  corrected business date, and the same sale ID arriving in a different five-minute
  bucket. Returning the first delivery's task there would enqueue a pass over the
  wrong day.
- Two deliveries that **both** read no receipt cannot both commit. Started together
  and deliberately not awaited in turn, so both transactions read before either
  writes.

**The honest limit of the third one is written into the test.** A real Firestore
aborts the losing transaction and retries it, and the retry then takes the free
path. The double does not retry, so what is proved is the half that holds either
way: the loser is refused outright and nothing it staged reaches the store - no
half-written movement, and no receipt that would make a later redelivery believe
the work was done.

**2. `saleMovements` combines lines per product and rejects the rest.** Two lines of
one product become one movement with `lineCount: 2` and the summed quantity, which
matters because the movement ID is derived from the sale: two documents at one
deterministic ID would mean the second silently replacing the first, and the sale
recorded as having sold three of five.

Fifteen rejected line shapes are tabulated in one test - `null`, a string, a number,
an array, no `productId`, an empty one, a non-string one, one of 129 characters, one
carrying a path separator, no `quantity`, a fractional one, a string one, zero,
negative, and one past `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. Each is counted and dropped; the
sale is still marked dirty and its pass still enqueued, because the metrics and
shift phases read the sale document itself rather than this validation's opinion of
it. The trigger cannot refuse the sale - it is already committed - and throwing
would leave the day permanently unreconciled behind a poison delivery.

Two boundaries are pinned on the passing side as well: a `productId` of exactly 128
characters is legal, because 128 is Firestore's own document-ID limit and the line
becomes a ledger path; and the unsafe-sum check is on the **running total**, so two
lines that are each safe and sum past the range reject only the second, leaving the
first one's movement intact.

`items` that is not an array is one invalid line, not zero - asserted for a missing
field, `null`, an object, and a string. A sale with no readable lines is not a sale
with no stock effect; it is a sale whose stock effect is unknown.

Anything past the hundredth line is counted and dropped: 100 lines of one product
plus five of another gives one movement of 100 and `invalidLineCount: 5`. The bound
is on the transaction, not on the sale - a hundred products is a hundred movement
documents against Firestore's 500-write limit.

**3. Invalid lines write one anomaly document, and only when there is one.** It is
the only place a malformed sale is ever visible to an operator. One sale writes at
most one anomaly however many lines failed; its ID is a digest of the sale, matched
against `/^sale_[0-9a-f]{40}$/`; and the dirty day's `invalidLineCount` carries the
same figure, written in the same transaction, so the day can never report malformed
lines that no anomaly document accounts for. A clean sale writes no anomaly at all -
the collection is read by the differences surface, and an empty record per sale
would bury the ones that mean something.

**4. A bucket belonging to another source throws.** `dirty_<bucket>` is derived from
the clock alone, so unlike every other job ID in this pipeline it is predictable.
Two tests: a *manual* job created at that ID by the production creator, and a
*sale-trigger* job whose `sourceKey` is a different bucket. Both are refused, and
the assertion that matters is that the whole transaction is - the movement, the
dirty day, and the receipt are staged with the job write, so a sale that cannot
claim its bucket leaves no ledger entry and no receipt behind.

**5. The movement ID stops being the sale ID at 120 characters.** Asserted on both
sides of the boundary: at exactly 120 the movement is addressed by the sale itself,
which is what makes a ledger entry traceable by reading its ID; past it, the ID is
`sale_` plus a 40-character digest. Two sale IDs differing in one character get
different digests - sharing one would mean the second sale replacing the first's
ledger entry at a document nothing would look at again - and `sourceId` still holds
the whole sale ID, because once the ID stops naming the sale the document has to.

### One thing observed, and deliberately not changed

**A redelivery always returns a task, including for a sale whose first delivery
returned none.** A sale landing while its bucket's job is already running gets
`enqueue: false` from `mergeDirtyJob`, but the receipt still records the job's
`generation` and `revision`, and the redelivery path returns a task built from them
unconditionally.

It is safe, for two reasons that are both outside this function.
`enqueueReconciliationTask` names the task `reconciliationTaskId(payload)` - a
digest of tenant, job, generation, and revision - and swallows `already-exists`, so
a duplicate enqueue is a no-op. And if the pass has since moved on, the dispatch
names a superseded revision and `claimReconciliationJob` refuses it; if the pass
died, this is exactly the lost-dispatch recovery the lease is for.

So it is recorded rather than fixed. This chunk excluded production changes, and
the behaviour is now pinned by the redelivery test, so a future session changing it
will have to mean to.

A test written after the code it describes is worth nothing until it has been seen
to fail. Three mutations were applied to `jobs.ts` together, and the failing set was
checked against what each should catch:

| --- | --- | --- |
| `businessDate` dropped from the receipt identity check | the disagreeing-redelivery test | 4 |
| `saleId.length <= 120` becomes `<= 1200` | the movement-ID boundary test | 15 |
| `if (invalidLineCount > 0)` becomes `>= 0` | the two no-anomaly assertions | 1, 5, 12 |

## The sweep that decides who is reconciled tonight - 2026-08-07

### Completed in this session

The chunk the previous handover queued, taken unchanged: **`ensureSweep` and
`processTenantDiscoveryPage`**. It was checked against the status board first and
kept. No red row stops a business operating, the sharpest one left - editing a
product - is an open decision rather than a chunk, and this one needs no decision
at all.

Fourteen tests in one new file, and **no production change of any kind**.
`functions/src/reconciliation/jobs.ts` is byte-identical to its committed state at
the end of this session, and `git diff` over it is empty.

With this, `jobs.ts` has unit coverage over every export except the two the previous
handover already ruled out: `listRetryableReconciliationTasks`, which needs
`collectionGroup`, `in`, and `<=` and is out of the double's reach, and
`reconciliationJobDocument`, which is dead inside its own module. Neither was
touched.

### Why these two and not another

`ensureSweep` is what all three schedulers in `handlers.ts` call - nightly at 05:30,
weekly at 04:30 Sunday, staggered monthly at 04:45 - and `processTenantDiscoveryPage`
is the paginator that turns one sweep into one deterministic reconciliation task per
active tenant. Between them they are the only route by which a tenant nobody sold
anything through today is reconciled at all. The sale trigger is the other route, and
it was covered in the session before this one.

The integration suite reaches both, but only down the path where every boundary in
them is invisible: one tenant, one page, one kind. Seeding fifty-three tenants per
assertion against a real Firestore is what the double exists to avoid.

The new file is `sweep.test.ts` rather than more of `jobs.test.ts`, for the same
reason `saleReceipt.test.ts` was: `jobs.test.ts` is the job lifecycle - who may
claim, advance, finalize, and fail one - and this is what decides a job exists.

### The four groups, and what each is protecting

**1. The page boundary, in both directions.** `TENANT_DISCOVERY_PAGE_SIZE` is 50. A
page that ends exactly on it must return a continuation and a page that ends short
must not, and both halves are silent when wrong: a full page returning nothing
strands every tenant after the fiftieth, unreconciled, under a sweep marked
`completed`; a short page returning one enqueues a task that scans nothing forever.
Both are asserted in one chain over fifty-three tenants, together with the page
documents - `pages/00000000`, `pages/00000001` - which are zero-padded so a sweep's
history sorts in the order it ran.

The empty last page is asserted separately, because it is the shape a sweep whose
tenant count is an exact multiple of fifty always ends on: no documents, so no `last`
to take a cursor from, and `outputCursor: last?.id ?? payload.cursor ?? null` is what
stops the completed record claiming it never got past the first tenant.

**2. The monthly shard filter.** The staggered monthly schedule fires *daily* and
reconciles a twenty-eighth of the estate each time. Without the filter it is a second
nightly sweep, in `full` mode, over every tenant at once - the most expensive thing
this pipeline can do. Three assertions: today's shard gets jobs and the rest of the
month does not; the same fixture on a nightly sweep admits everybody, so the filter
is monthly's alone; and a full page holding one eligible tenant still continues,
because `hasMore` is decided by what the *query* returned and not by what the filter
kept. That last one is not a detail - on a twenty-eight-way split, most pages of a
monthly sweep are pages the filter almost empties.

The fixture partitions tenant IDs by calling `monthlyShardDay` rather than hard-coding
a digest, and asserts both halves non-empty so it cannot pass vacuously. The function
is pinned separately in `model.test.ts`; here it is the oracle, not the subject.

**3. Page idempotency.** Cloud Tasks is at-least-once and `enqueueDiscoveryTask`
swallows `already-exists`, so one page running twice is ordinary. The second delivery
must write nothing at all - and it does: the tenant jobs already exist and are read
rather than rewritten, and the `pages/{page}` guard returns before the sweep update.
The tasks *are* re-returned, which is safe only because `reconciliationTaskId` is a
digest of tenant, job, generation, and revision, so the test asserts the two
deliveries produce identical task IDs rather than assuming it.

**4. Sweep identity.** `sweepRunId` is a digest of kind and local date, so two
schedule firings for one date land on one document; the second re-enters it and does
not drag a completed sweep back to `running` or reset a counter. The same
predictability is what would let anything else occupy the ID, so a document there
disagreeing about either kind or date throws `already-exists` rather than being
adopted.

Two more went in beside them, because both are reached only from here: which tenants
are scanned at all - `status == "active"`, so `tenantsScanned` is active tenants and
not tenants - and the shape `scheduledJobDefinition` gives a tenant's job, where
monthly is the only `full` pass and the two checkpoint kinds are what a chain
verification is keyed by. A tenant whose job for today is already running, completed,
or quarantined is read and not redispatched; a failed one is resumed at the generation
and revision the document holds rather than at zero.

### Each of the four was checked by breaking it

A test that passes is not evidence until it can fail. Four mutations were applied to
`jobs.ts`, built, run, and reverted:

```text
hasMore from eligible.length instead of snapshot.size  -> 1 fail (the monthly full page)
monthly shard filter disabled                          -> 2 fail
pages/{page} guard removed                             -> 2 fail
sweep identity check weakened to &&                    -> 1 fail
```

One result is worth keeping. The `hasMore` mutation is **not** caught by the
fifty-three-tenant boundary test, because on a nightly sweep `eligible` and
`snapshot.docs` are the same array. Only the monthly full-page test catches it. If a
later session trims that test as redundant, the page-size source goes unguarded.

`jobs.ts` was restored by reverting each edit exactly, and confirmed with
`git diff --stat functions/src/reconciliation/jobs.ts` (empty) and a byte comparison
against a copy taken before the first mutation and held in the session scratchpad. It
was never reverted with `git checkout --`, per the standing trap.

### What the tests found

**A page creates its tenant jobs before it records itself.** If the sweep document
has disappeared under a live page, the transaction throws `not-found` - after
`ensureScheduledTenantJob` has already created that page's tenant jobs. The test
asserts the honest outcome rather than a tidy one: the throw is what the queue
retries on, the orphaned jobs are queued and valid, and the retry resumes them at the
generation they hold rather than duplicating them, because the job ID is a digest of
kind and date. Nothing is lost; it is just not the order the code reads as having.

**`tenantsEligible` is never initialized.** `ensureSweep` writes `pagesProcessed`,
`tenantsScanned`, and `tenantJobsCreated` at zero and not `tenantsEligible`; the page
transaction increments it into existence. That is correct - Firestore sets a missing
field to the operand rather than treating it as zero - but a sweep read between
opening and its first page reports three counters and not the fourth. Recorded, not
changed: this chunk excludes `jobs.ts`.

### Addendum, same day: how a price is corrected, resolved — and App Check started

Two of the three open decisions moved after the chunk above was committed. Neither
involved any code; both are recorded so a later session inherits the answer rather than
the argument.

**How a price is corrected: an `updateProduct` callable, not a wider rule.** The
product owner asked for a recommendation between the two survivors — delete-and-
re-create having never been viable, since the product ID is what `stock_movements`,
`daily_metrics`, and every past sale line refer to — and accepted the callable. The
three grounds are written up at the decision in `PLAN.md`. The first was **not** in the
original framing and is the one that flipped it:

- **A wider rule means editing the tightest clause in `firestore.rules`.** The current
  `allow update` on `products/{productId}` is the whole guarantee that no client can
  inflate stock. Widening it means OR-ing a second clause onto it, where a mistake is a
  stock-integrity hole rather than an audit gap. A callable writes through the Admin
  SDK, which bypasses rules entirely, so it changes `firestore.rules` **not at all**.
  The rule route was chosen-looking on cost; this is the cost it hid.
- **A price is money and the rule route records nothing** — no actor, no previous
  value, no reason. `adjustStock` changes a mere quantity and writes three documents.
- **Only a server can validate the price.** A rule can check `price is number`; it
  cannot check two-decimal representability, so `19.999` passes and then fails
  `checkoutMinorUnitsFromMajor` at the till with a customer standing there.

The cost estimate in the original framing — "the most work" — was checked and is wrong.
`functions/src/operations/stock.ts` is **128 lines** end to end including imports,
types, and audit writes, and `updateProduct` is that skeleton minus the ledger entry.

Two constraints were settled with the decision so the chunk cannot reopen them: it must
not touch `quantity`, and its role split is its own choice rather than one inherited
from create or delete.

**App Check was started in the Firebase console**, which puts the third open decision
in motion. Nothing was implemented; two facts were checked and recorded against it,
because both bear on the option this file called "by far the most work":

- **`firebase_app_check` lists Windows as a supported platform** as of 0.4.6 on
  pub.dev. That is plugin support and not proof that a built-in attestation provider
  exists for Windows, so the "structurally unreachable on Windows" claim in this file
  is flagged for re-checking rather than retracted. Retracting it on a pub.dev badge
  would be exactly the inheritance-without-measurement this log keeps punishing.
- **The Windows app is registered as a *web* app.** `DefaultFirebaseOptions.windows`
  carries a `1:...:web:...` app ID, because Firebase has no native Windows app type.

The operational warning attached to it: nothing in the client sends a token today, so
console enforcement must stay off until a build that initializes the SDK is in users'
hands. The one enforcement already live is code rather than console —
`requestPasswordReset` declares `enforceAppCheck: true` itself, which is why that single
callable rejects everything while no other callable is affected.

## The callable that corrects a price - 2026-08-07

### Chunk chosen, and why not the queued one

The queued "next bounded chunk" was the intermittent Flutter failure at
`test/checkout/checkout_sync_signals_test.dart`. `PLAN.md` explicitly allowed taking
`updateProduct` first — "if a session would rather move a capability than chase a
flake, take `updateProduct` first and come back to this" — and that is what happened,
for two reasons the queued text already names. The flake hunt is bounded by a
deliverable rather than a duration and may end in a written diagnosis with no code;
`updateProduct` is a `functions/` chunk that is blocked on nothing, whose decision was
settled the same week, and which does not need the Flutter suite to be trustworthy.
The flake still blocks any *Flutter* capability chunk, which is why it goes straight
back to the head of the queue: the surface that calls this callable is the next
capability, and it is Dart.

### Completed in this session

**`updateProduct`, the only way a product's descriptive fields ever change.** Before
it, a product's name, code, price, and category were permanent once written: `allow
update` on `products/{productId}` permits a strictly decreasing `quantity` with
`affectedKeys().hasOnly(['quantity', 'updatedAt'])` — the checkout decrement — and no
callable touched a descriptive field. A mistyped price needed an operator with the
Admin SDK.

It is the **twenty-fourth callable and the forty-seventh export**. It changes
`firestore.rules` **not at all**, which was the first of the three grounds the decision
turned on and is now a verified fact rather than an intention: `git status` shows
`firestore.rules` unmodified, and the 160-test rules suite was run anyway to say so
with a measurement.

```text
updateProduct({tenantId, productId, name?, sku?, price?, categoryId?, requestId})
```

Split in two, following `amendment.ts` / `amendments.ts` rather than `stock.ts`:
`operations/productUpdate.ts` holds every decision as pure functions, and
`operations/products.ts` is the callable, the shared authorization and idempotency
wrappers, and the two writes. `stock.ts` has never had a unit test because its logic
and its Firestore calls are one function; this chunk deliberately did not repeat that.

### The eight things it is responsible for

1. **It never writes `quantity`, and refuses a payload that mentions it.** This is the
   guarantee everything else rests on: a callable that could write a price *and* a
   quantity would be a second way to move stock with no `stock_movements` entry, which
   is the property `adjustStock` exists to provide. The refusal names `adjustStock` in
   its message.
2. **An unknown key is refused rather than dropped.** Silently ignoring one would make
   "this never writes `quantity`" something a caller takes on trust instead of
   something it can observe from outside.
3. **A price is validated against the till's own arithmetic.**
   `productPriceMinorUnits` is `checkoutMinorUnitsFromMajor` from
   `lib/checkout/checkout_draft.dart`, tolerance included, so `19.999` is refused where
   it is typed rather than at the till with a customer standing there. The stored
   major-unit figure is derived from the minor units, never from what was sent.
4. **The *resulting* document must parse and be sellable, not just the fields being
   written.** `readSellableProduct` is the server-side twin of
   `TenantProduct.fromDocument` plus the price conversion, run against the document as
   it will exist. One unparseable product makes the whole cached catalog a miss, so
   quietly making an already-broken product less broken would report success while the
   business stayed unable to sell anything. The contract is: name every broken field in
   one request, or none of them.
5. **A price change needs an owner or an administrator; everything else needs the
   operational three.** This is its own decision, not one inherited from create
   (owner/admin/manager) or delete (owner/admin). It is read from the *requested*
   fields, not from the resulting diff — a manager whose permission depended on the
   value already stored would be a rule nobody could explain, and would let a manager
   discover a price by binary search over refusals.
6. **A named category is checked against this business, whenever it is named.** Nothing
   on the server enforced this before; the client create surface could only file a
   product under a category it had read. A product filed under a category that does not
   exist is invisible to every grouped catalog surface without being unreadable, which
   is the hardest kind of wrong to notice.
7. **A stored legacy `category` alias moves with `categoryId`.** The client's read model
   refuses a product whose two category fields disagree, so leaving the alias behind
   would take the whole cached catalog down. A product filed only under the alias is
   read through it, and asking for the category it already holds records no change.
8. **The before and after of every changed field is audited.** One `audit_logs` entry
   at `pu_<40 hex>`, carrying `changes`, `changedFields`, actor, request ID, and
   `mutatesQuantity: false` — the same idiom `amendShiftSummary` uses for
   `mutatesCountedCash`. Without it a price correction would be the one money-changing
   operation in this system that leaves no record of what it replaced. No
   `stock_movements` entry and no `stock_adjustments` record, because nothing moves.

Two smaller decisions, recorded so they are not re-litigated. A request that changes
nothing is **refused** rather than audited as a no-op; it is reachable only with a
fresh request ID, because a genuine retry answers off the idempotency record. And a
product whose stored `quantity` is not an integer, or whose `image` is not an HTTPS
URL, is refused with a message saying it needs an operator — neither this callable nor
`adjustStock` can correct either, and saying so beats a green result that changes
nothing the till can observe.

### The tests were proved able to fail, and one of them could not

Five guarantees were mutated in turn, rebuilt, and re-run. Four were caught
immediately. **The fifth was not, and it was the most important one:**

```text
the quantity refusal is removed             -> 32 pass, 0 fail   <-- caught nothing
a manager may change a price                -> 30 pass, 2 fail
the legacy alias is left behind             -> 30 pass, 2 fail
the product is replaced instead of patched  -> 29 pass, 3 fail
```

Deleting the dedicated `"quantity" in data` refusal changed no test result, because
`quantity` is refused twice over — once by name and once as a key outside the accepted
set — and the test asserted only the error *code*, which is `invalid-argument` either
way. The behaviour stayed correct; what would have been lost silently is the message,
which is the only thing telling a caller that stock moves through `adjustStock`. The
test now asserts the message, and the mutation is caught:

```text
the quantity refusal is removed             -> 31 pass, 1 fail
```

One mutation was rejected by the compiler rather than by a test and had to be
reshaped: stubbing out the price-representability branch left `priceMinor` possibly
undefined downstream, so `tsc` refused it under `strict`. Widening
`PRICE_REPRESENTATION_TOLERANCE` from `1e-6` to `1` tests the same guarantee and
compiles:

```text
the price tolerance is widened past two decimals -> 29 pass, 3 fail
```

fix, and it is the same lesson as the existing `Select-Object -First N` trap: filter
the capture, not the stream.

## The flake was the test's own clock - 2026-08-07

Chose the queued chunk: chase the one intermittent Flutter failure at
`test/checkout/checkout_sync_signals_test.dart`. The status board has no red row that
stops a business operating and no unqueued capability the app needs in order to
function, and the next capability - the Flutter surface that calls `updateProduct` - is
Dart, so a suite that is green six times in seven cannot certify it. This chunk comes
first for exactly the reason the handover gave.

### It reproduced, and it is not what the plan said to look for

The queued lead was the outbox's **static** per-box lock, on the grounds that the same
mechanism had deadlocked this file once before. **That lead is wrong and is retracted.**
`HiveCheckoutOutbox._serialized` completes its `release` in a `finally` and removes its
own tail; nothing in this file contends on one key from two instances; and, decisively,
a deadlock means a transition that never happens, while what was measured is a
transition that happens **late**.

The fault is in the test, not in anything it tests. `_settle()` waited a fixed **20
event-loop turns** of `Future<void>.delayed(Duration.zero)`. What it was waiting for is
three sequential writes to a real encrypted Hive box on a real filesystem -
`beginSubmission`, `markAwaitingConfirmation`, `recordConfirmation` - each of which
Hive's VM backend dispatches to the IO thread pool as a real `writeFrom`. **A turn count
is not a wait; it is a race against the disk.**

A temporary probe (`test/checkout/zz_seam_probe_test.dart`, deleted before the commit)
ran the seam pipeline one save at a time and read the record after every turn:

```text
172 runs.  Turn at which the record reached `confirmed`:
  median 3    p90 6    p99 9
  tail: one run at 19, one run at 26
  the run that needed 26 turns read `awaiting_confirmation` at turn 20
```

Turn 26 is the failure, exactly as reported: past the 20 turns the helper allowed, with
the record still `awaiting_confirmation` at the assertion. Two runs in 172 at or past
the limit matches roughly one full-suite failure in seven, because a full suite is where
the disk is busiest - and it is why the file passed 15/15 run alone.

### What was changed, and why it is not simply a bigger margin

Raising the turn count would have been the wrong fix: the tail has no bound in turns,
because it is not measured in turns. So **nothing in the seam group counts turns any
more.**

- Three of the four seam tests now hold the future the signal listener starts, and await
  it. The listener still fires and forgets, exactly as the composition root does; the
  future is the test's own. `CheckoutSyncPass.run` settles the record before its own
  future completes, so for the test that used to fail this is the whole of the wait, and
  it is deterministic.
- The fourth - a save arriving during an in-flight run - cannot await the first run
  before releasing it, and the rerun the worker schedules for itself in its `finally` is
  `unawaited`, so it has no future to hold at all. Those two points poll a **condition**
  under a ten-second wall-clock deadline. A genuinely broken seam still fails, just
  later, and it fails naming what it was waiting for.
- The negative assertion - a save is not submitted for a session the device has left -
  now waits for the run to be *over* rather than merely for it to be unlikely, which is
  the other thing a turn count could not give it.

### The flake, made permanent

`a slow disk decides nothing about whether the seam worked` is a new group holding one
test. It wraps the real Hive box in `_SlowBox`, which delays every `put` by 60 ms -
longer than any plausible run of zero-duration turns - and asserts the same `confirmed`
outcome the seam group asserts. It adds no new claim about the pipeline; its whole job
is to fail if this file ever goes back to guessing.

**It was verified to fail without the fix.** The probe file was rewritten to run the
same slow box against the old 20-turn helper, and did fail, deterministically:

```text
Expected: CheckoutOutboxState:<CheckoutOutboxState.confirmed>
  Actual: CheckoutOutboxState:<CheckoutOutboxState.savedOffline>
```

`savedOffline` rather than `awaiting_confirmation` because 60 ms a write is far past the
real stall. Same mechanism, larger dose.

### The same fault in a sibling file, and one that is not

`_waitForState` in `test/checkout/checkout_recovery_test.dart` had the identical shape -
20 `Duration.zero` turns, then `fail(...)` - and was waiting for a `recordConfirmation`
write to the same kind of real box, in a rerun path with no future to hold. It had never
been seen to fail; it was one bad disk stall away from it. It now polls in real
milliseconds against a ten-second deadline.

**`_settle()` in `test/checkout/checkout_sync_test.dart` was examined and deliberately
left alone.** It has the same 20-turn shape, but what it waits for is a coalesced rerun
that finds the record already `awaiting_confirmation` and skips it: no `put`, no disk,
no race. Changing it would be churn. Recorded here so the next session does not
re-derive it.

**No file under `lib/` was changed, and none needed to be.** Production awaits its own
futures throughout, and `CheckoutSyncPass` is sequential and fully awaited. The bug was
never in the pipeline.

### Files changed

```text
test/checkout/checkout_sync_signals_test.dart   `_settle` replaced by `_settleUntil`
                                                and `_runsFinished`; four seam tests
                                                rewired; `_slowDiskGroup` and
                                                `_SlowBox` added
test/checkout/checkout_recovery_test.dart       `_waitForState` given a wall-clock
                                                deadline and real millisecond turns
```

A temporary `test/checkout/zz_seam_probe_test.dart` carried the measurements above and
was deleted before the commit. It is not in the diff.

### Tests

```text

flutter test --no-pub --concurrency=1 --reporter=failures-only test/checkout/
                                                              247 pass  (246 + 1 new)
flutter test --no-pub --concurrency=1 --reporter=failures-only
```

## A product records what it cost, and a sale freezes it - 2026-08-07

Not the queued chunk. The product owner asked whether buying price was captured, was
told it was not, and asked for it - **with one requirement attached: a change to a
buying price must never move a profit figure already reported.** That requirement is
what shaped the whole design, so it is recorded first.

### The requirement was already structurally satisfiable, and that decided the design

Four facts were checked in source before anything was promised, because the answer
"yes, and here is why it cannot be otherwise" is worth more than a new mechanism:

1. **Profit reads the sale line, never the product.** `lineCost()` in
   `functions/src/operations/domain.ts` looks at `line.cost`, then `line.unitCost`,
   then `line.buyingPrice`. There is no product join anywhere in the metrics pipeline.
2. **Sales are immutable.** `allow update, delete: if false` on
   `tenants/{tenantId}/sales/{saleId}`.
3. **Regeneration re-reads sales, not products.** `processors.ts` reads
   `tenantRef.collection("sales")`, so a nightly reconciliation recomputes the same
   figure from the same frozen lines.
4. **The offline record is hash-sealed.** `checkoutPayloadHash` covers the whole
   payload and `_parseRecord` re-derives it on every read.

So the answer was: capture the cost **onto the sale line at the moment of the sale**,
and the guarantee follows from machinery that already exists rather than from a new
rule anyone could later relax.

### Two decisions, both taken by the product owner

- **One cost per product, snapshotted at sale**, rather than stock-lot FIFO or weighted
  average. Lot costing would have meant a unit cost on every stock receipt, a change to
  the `adjustStock` contract, a consumption algorithm inside the checkout batch, and a
  backfill - a large change to a frozen area, for accuracy this business does not need.
  Restocking at a new price now forward-dates itself: old lines keep the old figure.
- **Cost lives on the product document**, where every active member can read it. This
  was raised as a *privacy* decision rather than buried, because it is one: `products`
  is readable by any active member - the till cannot price a sale otherwise - and
  Firestore cannot hide one field of a document. The alternative was a trigger stamping
  cost onto the sale server-side, which keeps buying prices off cashier devices but
  costs a write per sale, leaves a window where the sale has no cost, and cannot work
  offline, which is the platform the whole Hive design exists for. **What was bought
  instead is a surface boundary: no manager is shown a cost, and a client that sends
  one without the role is refused rather than ignored.** That limit is documented at
  `MONETARY_PRODUCT_FIELDS` and at `TenantCatalogManagementRepository.costRoles` so
  nobody later mistakes it for secrecy.

### The half that was already built

Worth recording, because it changed the size of the chunk: the *consuming* half was
finished and idle. `_allowedLineKeys` in `lib/checkout/checkout_sale.dart` already
contained `unitCostMinor`; `CheckoutSaleLine` already carried `unitCostMinor` and
`lineCostMinor` and already emitted `unitCost`, `cost`, and their minor-unit twins;
the parser already read them optionally; the server already computed
`profit = revenue - cost` with an `incompleteCostLineCount` beside it; and the daily
summary already rendered "N sale lines have no cost recorded". The legacy mono-tenant
island still has a working "Buying Price" field in `lib/pos/goods.dart`, which is
where the server's `buyingPrice` alias comes from.

**Two consequences.** No payload schema version bump was needed - `unitCostMinor` is an
optional key within v2, so `validSaleTender`'s `payloadSchemaVersion == 2` branch is
untouched. And **no `firestore.rules` change was needed**: `validSaleLine` constrains
only `productId` and `quantity` and names no key list, and `allow create` on `products`
checks only `quantity is int`. `firestore.rules` is byte-identical, and the rules suite
was run to say so with a measurement.

### What was built

- **`TenantProduct.cost`**, nullable. Null is the normal case and the test says why: no
  product created before this existed carries one, and this read model is strict enough
  that a single refusal makes the *whole* cached catalog a miss, so requiring it would
  have stopped every existing business selling. A *present but unusable* cost is still
  refused, because dropping it would report that product's entire revenue as profit.
- **The encrypted catalog cache carries it**, because the till stamps the cost with no
  network and the cache is the only place it can come from.
- **The till freezes it.** `checkout_draft.dart` converts `product.cost` through
  `checkoutMinorUnitsFromMajor` - the same function the price goes through - and writes
  `unitCostMinor` onto the line. An absent cost stays absent rather than defaulting to
  zero, which would claim the business paid nothing. A cost the till cannot represent is
  refused as `cost_not_representable` rather than dropped. **A missing cost never
  refuses a sale**: that would stop a till trading over a reporting field.
- **Creating a product accepts an optional cost**, owner/admin only, validated through
  the till's own arithmetic so a refusal happens where the number is typed.
- **`updateProduct` gained `cost`** as its fifth editable field and second monetary one.
  It is the only field where an explicit `null` is meaningful: it *clears* a cost, which
  is also the escape hatch for a stored cost too malformed for the callable to correct.
  The audit keeps the unreadable previous value verbatim rather than flattening it to
  null - "who set this to `nine`" is exactly the question a cleared cost leaves behind.

### Files changed

```text

lib/checkout/checkout_catalog_cache.dart            cost written to and read from cache
lib/checkout/checkout_draft.dart                    unitCostMinor frozen onto each line
lib/inventory/catalog_management.dart               costMinor on the create intent,
                                                    costRoles, canRecordCostInSession
lib/inventory/catalog_management_panel.dart         the optional cost field, its
                                                    confirmation text and refusals
functions/src/operations/productUpdate.ts           cost in EDITABLE_PRODUCT_FIELDS,
                                                    MONETARY_PRODUCT_FIELDS, the clear
                                                    path, readSellableProduct
rules-tests/test/catalog-management.test.js         the create rule still permits cost;
                                                    the checkout update rule still does
                                                    not
test/tenancy/tenant_catalog_test.dart               absent is normal, broken is not
test/inventory/catalog_management_test.dart         optional, converted, role-gated
test/inventory/catalog_management_panel_test.dart   shown to an owner, not to a manager
test/checkout/checkout_draft_test.dart              the frozen-cost group
functions/src/operations/productUpdate.test.ts      13 cost cases
```

### The test that is the requirement

`correcting the buying price cannot reach a sale already recorded`, in
`test/checkout/checkout_draft_test.dart`. A sale is rung up against a product costing
60, the catalog is then rewritten with the same product costing 90 - exactly what
`updateProduct` plus a refresh leaves on a device - and a second sale is rung up. The
first sale is **re-read from storage** rather than trusted from the value returned at
save time, because the claim is about what is durable. It still says 60, the second says
90, and the first record's payload hash still verifies, which is what would have refused
it as `malformed_record` had anything rewritten it in place.

### Tests

```text
flutter test --no-pub --concurrency=1 --reporter=failures-only
                                                              1358 pass
npm --prefix functions test                                   346 pass, 0 fail
```

### One failure worth keeping

`clearing is the escape hatch for a cost too broken to correct` was written asserting
that clearing a stored `"nine"` records `previous: null`. It records `previous: "nine"`,
because `describePrevious` returns a string unchanged. **The code was right and the
test was wrong**, and the assertion was corrected rather than the behaviour: an audit
entry that flattens an unreadable previous value to null destroys the only record of
what was there.

## Bulk catalog and return scoring are scoped as rewrites - 2026-08-08

No code changed. The product owner asked whether the previous app's bulk upload, bulk
update, and fraud detection were scoped in this one, and the answer was **no for all
three** - with an asymmetry worth recording:

- **Bulk import was excluded**, so it was a decision.
- **Suspicious-return scoring was never named anywhere** - not a board row, not a
  rollout step, not an exclusion. A 555-line capability of the previous app had simply
  never been written down. "Not excluded" and "not noticed" are indistinguishable in a
  file like `PLAN.md`, and only one of them is a decision.

All three are now scoped as **rewrites**: the idea and the flow carry over, the code
does not.

### What was found in the old app

```text
lib/services/bulk_upload_service.dart    320 lines   reachable only from lib/pos/goods.dart
lib/services/bulk_update_service.dart    468 lines   reachable only from lib/pos/goods.dart
lib/services/fraud_detection_service.dart 555 lines  reachable only from lib/screens/returns_*
lib/model/return_analysis.dart            64 lines
```

`lib/main.dart` imports `tenancy`, `checkout`, `inventory`, `reporting`, `returns`,
`sales`, `shift`, and `audit` - never `services/`, `screens/`, or `pos/`. All of it runs
nowhere.

### The finding that decided the bulk shape

`bulk_update_service.dart` does `batch.update(docRef, arbitraryFields)` from the client.
On `tenants/{tenantId}/products/{productId}`, `allow update` permits
`['quantity', 'updatedAt']` with a strictly decreasing quantity - the checkout decrement
and nothing else - and widening it is precisely what "How a price is corrected" rejected.
**So bulk change is not a batch that needs porting; it is N × `updateProduct` executed
on the server.** A different program, not a modified one. The consolation is that
`planProductUpdate` is already a pure function from stored document plus request to a
validated plan, audit entries included, so the expensive half exists.

Four more reasons a port fails, recorded in the standing decision: the root `alcohol`
collection, four bypassed create guarantees (`TenantProductCreateIntent`, the
deterministic `pd_<hex>` ID, request-ID idempotency, and "created holding nothing" -
`BulkProduct.quantity` writes straight through), and **two field names that drift
silently**. The uploader writes `buyingPrice`, not the `cost` field added the day
before, so an import's cost data would be invisible to `TenantProduct.cost` - the server
reads `buyingPrice` only as a legacy alias on *sale lines*, never on a product. And it
writes `category` as a display name where the model wants a `categoryId`: "Bakery"
passes document-ID validation, matches no category document, and leaves the product
invisible to every grouped surface without being unreadable.

### The improvement, not just the port

The old flow validated then committed. The rewrite is **validate → preview → commit**,
and the preview is the point: a spreadsheet is the one input nobody proofreads, and the
first time a person should see what 400 rows will do is before they do it. With it: name
every broken row at once rather than one round trip per discovery, state partial success
per row, bound and chain the work the way the reconciliation sweep already does, write
one audit entry per product correlated by the import's request ID, and route opening
stock through `adjustStock` semantics so imported units have an origin.

### Return scoring, and why it waits

Sequenced **after the first deployment** at the product owner's direction. The
supporting reason improves the work: every threshold in the feature is a judgement about
what normal looks like, and normal is not knowable from seed data - a ruleset tuned
against fixtures is a guess that gets re-tuned the week real returns arrive.

Six signals carry over as an idea: quick return under 4 hours, late over 72, seller
return rate, void behaviour, refund amount past a z-score of 2, and velocity at 3
returns in 4 hours. Four things must change. It is **client-side and keeps nothing** -
zero Firestore access, and the score lands in `_riskCache`, widget state that dies with
the screen - so it can never be reviewed or acted on, while the gate that matters,
`verifyReturnAndRestoreStock`, is on the server. **One signal has no input at all**: the
void signal keys on `type == 'void'` and this app has no void concept, so voids get
modelled first or that signal is dropped rather than ported as dead code. Thresholds
cannot be global constants across tenants - three returns in four hours is an ordinary
afternoon for a bar. And **the destination already exists**: `reconciliation_anomalies`
is a server-written collection with a live surface at
`lib/reporting/reconciliation_anomalies_panel.dart`, and a risky return is an anomaly.

### A retraction

The exclusion list claimed bulk import "describes a pre-migration flow that ~~reaches no
code in `lib/`~~". **False in letter** - 788 lines are in `lib/services/`. True in
effect, since nothing live reaches them, which is exactly the kind of half-right claim
that makes a later session conclude the feature was never built. Corrected inline.

```text
            decisions, three queue entries, the Flutter track line, an unreachable-table
            pointer, the retraction, and the note that return scoring was never excluded
            because it was never named
HISTORY.md  this entry
```

None run, and none needed: no file outside these two documents was touched. The suites

## A price is corrected from the app - 2026-08-08

### Chunk chosen, and why the queued one was right

Took the queued chunk: **the Flutter surface that edits a product**. Checked against
the board first, as required. Every other red row is blocked on something no session
resolves by working harder — password reset on the App Check decision, the printed
body on an interface nobody has shared, subscription on a schema that does not exist,
profit display on its own reporting chunk, and the three rewrite rows on this one
landing first. No unqueued capability the app needs in order to function is missing.
The bolded row was the only half-built thing on the board: `updateProduct` had been
built, tested, and called by nothing since 2026-08-07.

### Completed in this session

**"Correct" on every product in "Manage catalog", and the row goes green.** A
mistyped price no longer needs an operator with the Admin SDK. The route offers all
five editable fields at once, states every before and after in a confirmation, and
sends only the fields that moved.

Nothing in `functions/` changed, `firestore.rules` is untouched, no export was added,
and no callable's contract moved. `git status` shows it, and the 161-test rules suite
was run to say so with a measurement.

### The five things the callable's contract forced on the route

Each of these is a design constraint the server already fixed, not a preference.

1. **Only changed fields are sent.** `assertProductUpdateAuthorized` reads its
   permission tier from the fields a payload *names*, not from the resulting diff. A
   form that resent every field would refuse a manager's name correction over a price
   nobody touched. So `buildUpdateIntent` compares each typed value against the stored
   product and carries only what differs — and a correction where nothing differs is
   refused locally as `product_unchanged`, which is the client half of the server's own
   refusal of a request that changes nothing.
2. **Every field is offered at once, in one dialog.** `readSellableProduct` validates
   the *resulting* document, so a refusal can name a field this correction never
   touched. A single-field edit could not honour "name every broken field in one
   request, or none".
3. **A manager is not offered price or cost at all.** The form says why, in place of
   the fields. Offering a field it knows will be refused teaches an operator only that
   the app guesses. The boundary is still enforced behind the surface —
   `_requireMonetaryRole` refuses rather than drops, the same way the create form
   already refuses a cost a manager types.
4. **Clearing a cost is its own act.** A checkbox, offered only when a cost is
   recorded, and the cost field's helper text says in as many words that leaving it
   blank keeps the stored figure. On the wire that is `cost: null`, the one place in
   this app where null means "remove this" rather than "leave it alone".
5. **One request ID per correction, held across a retry of that same correction.** See
   below — this turned out to need more than the plan asked for.

### The request ID is held against the correction, not just the attempt

The queued text said to hold one request ID across a retry. That is necessary and it
is not sufficient, and the reason is a **server gap this chunk found and did not
fix**, in line with the standing instruction that a gap found while wiring the route
is a finding to record.

`products.ts` builds the idempotency fingerprint from `productId`, `name`, `sku`,
`priceMinor`, and `categoryId`. ~~**`costMinor` is not in it.**~~ **Fixed 2026-08-08
by the bulk-change chunk, which was inside `functions/`: `costMinor` is now part of
`productUpdateFingerprintInput`, and absent, null, and a value all hash differently.**
So one request ID carrying two payloads that differ *only* in cost hashes identically,
and the second call is answered off the stored record with the new cost silently not
applied. Every other field would have been refused as `already-exists`. It is narrow —
it needs an unknown outcome followed by a changed mind about the cost alone — but it is
a silent wrong answer rather than a refusal, which is the worse kind. The client-side
protection below was kept: it is belt and braces now rather than the only guard, and a
second client would otherwise inherit nothing.

The route closes it from this side: the retained request ID is stored beside a
fingerprint of the exact correction it was issued for, so changing any field, cost
included, mints a fresh one. `test/inventory/catalog_management_panel_test.dart` pins
it with a cost-only retry, and the test says why in a comment rather than leaving the
next reader to work out which field it is really about.

**Two smaller server observations, both harmless today and both worth knowing before
bulk change reuses this callable:**

- ~~`UpdateProductRequest` in `products.ts` does not declare `cost`.~~ **Fixed
  2026-08-08.** It is typing only — the handler reads from
  `requireObject(request.data)`, a `Record<string, unknown>` — so behaviour was correct
  and the interface was merely incomplete documentation.
- ~~`UpdateProductResponse` echoes `name`, `sku`, `price`, `priceMinor`, and
  `categoryId`, but **not `cost`**.~~ **Fixed 2026-08-08: it now echoes `cost` and
  `costMinor`.** A cost that moved appeared in `changedFields` with no value beside it,
  so the client could reconcile four of the five fields against the request and not the
  fifth. The route still confirms a cost by re-reading the catalog and
  `TenantProductUpdateResult` still documents the hole — the Dart decoder ignores keys
  it was not built for, so the two new fields reach it and are not yet read. Closing
  the client half is a Flutter change and was out of that chunk's scope.

### The escape hatch for a malformed cost is not reachable from here, deliberately

"A stored cost too malformed for the callable to correct is cleared with `cost: null`"
is a real server guarantee and **this route cannot reach it**. `TenantProduct` is a
strict read model, and one product it refuses makes the whole page a read failure — so
a product with an unreadable cost never renders a row, and no row means no "Correct"
button. The same is true of every other `readSellableProduct` refusal:
`productUnreadable` and `needsOperator` are modelled and worded, and are reachable only
if the document changes between the page load and the call.

That is not a defect in either half. The server contract is right, the client's
strictness is right, and the intersection is an operator's job. It is recorded because
"the callable can do it" and "a person can do it" are different sentences, and this
board is built on the difference.

### Two smaller decisions worth not re-litigating

**A product filed under a category this page did not read is left where it is.**
Categories are one bounded page and a business may hold more, so requiring the current
category to be among the offered ones would make a name correction impossible for
every product filed past the first page. Moving a product still requires a category
this surface actually read, exactly as the create form does.

**Three sentences elsewhere on the route stopped being true and were changed.** The
catalog scope line, the add-product confirmation, and the retire confirmation all told
an operator that a name, code, and price are permanent. Each now branches on whether
this build carries the callable, so a build without it still reads correctly. The
retire confirmation additionally points at the correction, which is the thing it used
to say did not exist.

## Many products at once, previewed before they change - 2026-08-08

### Chunk chosen, and why the queued one was right

Took the queued chunk: **bulk change as the `updateProducts` server callable**.
Checked against the board first, as required. Its stated prerequisite had landed the
same day — the single-product edit surface — so the two permission tiers, the refusal
vocabulary, and the "only changed fields are sent" contract were all proved once on one
product rather than guessed at across four hundred. No unqueued capability the app
needs in order to function is missing: every remaining red row is blocked on a decision
(password reset on App Check), an interface nobody has shared (the printed body), a
schema that does not exist (subscription), its own reporting chunk (profit display), or
on this chunk landing first (spreadsheet import).

### Completed in this session

**A business can correct up to fifty products in one request, and see exactly what that
would do before it does it.** `updateProducts` is the twenty-fifth callable and the
forty-eighth export. It is N applications of `updateProduct`'s own decision executed on
the server — the same planner, the same price arithmetic, the same strict read of the
resulting document — plus everything a bulk change has to decide that one product at a
time never raises.

**No board row moved and none was meant to.** This is a server chunk with no Flutter
surface; "change many products at once" stays red until a route calls it, exactly as
`updateProduct` stayed red for a day. `firestore.rules` is untouched and the 161-test
rules suite was run to say so with a measurement rather than an assertion.

### The four properties, and why each is a decision rather than a consequence

1. **A preview is a mode, not a dry-run flag.** `mode` is required and has no default,
   because the failure modes are not symmetric: a preview mistaken for a commit is a
   report nobody acts on, and a commit mistaken for a preview changes four hundred
   products nobody agreed to. A preview reads exactly what a commit reads through
   exactly the same code and writes **nothing** — not the corrections, not the audit
   entries, and deliberately **not an idempotency record**. That last one is the point:
   it is what lets a client preview and then commit under one request ID, and because
   the commit's fingerprint covers the rows, a change edited between the two is refused
   as `already-exists` rather than quietly applied as something other than what was
   shown.
2. **Every broken row is named at once.** A row that cannot be parsed, a product that
   does not exist, a category that does not exist in this business, and a document too
   malformed to correct are all *outcomes* carried back beside the rows that worked. A
   row-at-a-time refusal turns a four-hundred-row change into four hundred round trips
   of discovery.
3. **Partial success is stated, never implied.** Every row comes back with `updated`,
   `unchanged`, or `failed`, its changed fields, its audit entry ID, and what the
   product now holds. Nothing is silently dropped and nothing is silently coerced.
4. **Bounded, and the caller chains it.** Fifty rows per request. There is no
   server-side cursor because there is no server-side collection to walk — the caller
   holds the rows — so what the server owes is a bound it will not exceed and a request
   that is independently idempotent, which is what makes a chain of them retryable at
   any point.

### What "already correct" had to mean, and why it is not a refusal here

One product at a time, a request that changes nothing is refused: it can only be a
caller defect, and answering `ok` would put an idempotency record and an audit entry
behind a request that did nothing. **In a bulk change it is the ordinary case.**
Re-running a four-hundred-row correction that half applied must be able to finish, and
it cannot if the rows that already landed take the whole request down with them.

So `planProductUpdate` gained one option, `allowUnchanged`, and `updateProduct` does not
pass it. The *resulting* document is still validated either way — a row that changes
nothing on a product no device can parse still fails — so "nothing to do here" never
became a way to skip the read model. There is a test for exactly that.

### Three defects that belong to the request, not to a row

Reporting these per row would have made the report itself wrong or the request
meaningless, so each takes the whole request down:

- **An unknown top-level key**, for the same reason `updateProduct` refuses one:
  dropping it silently would make "this never writes `quantity`" something a caller has
  to take on trust rather than something observable from outside.
- **More rows than the bound.** Applying the first fifty and reporting the rest as
  failed would read as partial success rather than as a caller that needs to chain, so
  the message says to send the rest as a further request with its own request ID.
- **A product named twice.** This is the one worth arguing. Two rows for one product are
  two conflicting intents, and there is **no honest outcome to report for either**: the
  second is planned against a document the first has already changed, so both rows would
  describe a before-and-after that never existed. The duplicate is recorded before the
  rest of the row is read, so a spelling mistake in one of the two cannot hide the
  ambiguity — a test pins that case specifically.

### Permission is decided over the whole request, before anything is read

`assertProductBatchAuthorized` collects the union of every row's requested fields and
**delegates the decision to `assertProductUpdateAuthorized`**, so the tier can never
drift from the one the single-product path enforces. A manager may correct names, codes,
and categories in bulk; naming a price or a cost anywhere in the request refuses all of
it.

What is added is the message. A rename of four hundred rows carrying three stray price
columns has to say *which three* or the refusal is not actionable, so the refusal names
the offending rows — as `rows[1], rows[2]`, matching the zero-based `index` every
outcome carries, and summarizing past ten as "and N more". Payload-path notation rather
than ordinals, because "row 3" beside an outcome indexed 3 is the kind of off-by-one
nobody notices until they correct the wrong product.

Deciding it up front rather than per row also means the preview refuses too. A manager
who previewed green and then hit a commit-time refusal would have learned only that the
app guesses.

### One `getAll`, because Firestore permits nothing else

A transaction may not read after its first write, so a per-row read-then-write loop is
not a slower version of this — it is a transaction that throws on its second row.
`applyProductBatchUpdate` therefore gathers every product and every distinct category
the request names into a single `getAll`, plans all rows, and only then writes. The
in-memory double enforces the read phase exactly as Firestore does, which is why this
was never in doubt.

Two consequences worth knowing:

- **A request whose every row was refused reads nothing at all.** `getAll()` with no
  document references is an error rather than an empty answer, so the writer guards it.
  There is a test.
- **`FakeFirestore` gained `getAll`**, which it did not have — the preview path is its
  first caller. The double's own rule is that nothing goes in without one, and it
  reproduces the no-references refusal rather than inventing an empty result.

### The write budget, and what the bound is actually set by

Each corrected row writes two documents — the product and its audit entry — and the
request adds one idempotency record. **Fifty rows is 101 writes against Firestore's
limit of 500.** The bound is nowhere near that limit and is not set by it: it is set by
wanting a transaction that fails on contention to be cheap to retry, and by matching
`TENANT_DISCOVERY_PAGE_SIZE`, the other bounded-and-chained page in this codebase.
Raising it costs retry latency long before it costs write budget, and that sentence is
in the source beside the constant.

### One audit entry per product, correlated without a new kind of record

Every corrected row writes `audit_logs/pu_<40 hex of sha256(identity, productId)>` with
the same `eventType: "product_updated"` and the same `mutatesQuantity: false` a single
correction writes, plus two fields a single correction does not carry: `batchId` and
`rowIndex`. "What did that bulk change do" is therefore answerable by querying
`audit_logs` for one `batchId`, and because a single-product correction carries neither
field, such a query matches only the rows of a bulk change. No batch summary document
was invented; the idempotency record already stores the whole response.

**The row's ID is derived from the product, not from its position.** Re-sending a
request with its rows reordered lands on the same documents rather than duplicating
every entry. A replay never reaches that code — the idempotency record answers it — and
when one does, the audit entry's `create` refuses it, which is what makes reusing a
deterministic ID safe. Both halves have tests.

**Order is nevertheless part of the fingerprint, deliberately.** Every outcome is
indexed by where its row sat, so answering a reordered retry off the stored record would
hand back indexes naming different rows. Refusing it as `already-exists` is the honest
answer, and the corrections themselves are unaffected for the reason above.

### The two findings this chunk inherited were both fixed, because it was inside `functions/`

`PLAN.md` queued both here explicitly, and both are retracted inline above at the text
that recorded them:

- **The idempotency fingerprint omitted `cost`.** Two payloads under one request ID
  differing *only* in cost hashed the same, so the second was answered off the stored
  record with the new cost silently not applied — a silent wrong answer where any other
  field would have been refused. It is now `productUpdateFingerprintInput`, an exported
  function so the property is testable rather than buried in a callable, and absent,
  `null`, and a value all hash differently. That distinction is the one that matters:
  omitting `cost` leaves a recorded cost alone and `cost: null` clears it.
- **`UpdateProductResponse` did not echo `cost`.** It now echoes `cost` and `costMinor`.
  The Dart decoder keeps unknown keys rather than refusing them, so the two new fields
  reach the client harmlessly and are not yet read — closing the client half is a
  Flutter change and out of scope here. `UpdateProductRequest` now declares `cost` too,
  which is typing only and changed nothing.

Changing what an existing request ID hashes to strands no in-flight retry, because
nothing is deployed anywhere. That is the only reason this was free.

### A name collision worth knowing about before someone greps for it

`MOBILE_BULK_UPDATE_IMPLEMENTATION.md` and `MOBILE_BULK_UPDATE_SETUP.md` both document
a method called **`updateProducts()`** — the previous app's client-side Firestore batch
in `lib/services/bulk_update_service.dart`, which writes the root `alcohol` collection
and is reachable from `lib/pos/goods.dart` alone. The new server callable has the same
name and does the structurally opposite thing. Those two documents are pre-migration
artifacts and were left alone; this paragraph is the pointer so a later reader does not
mistake one for the other or conclude the callable already existed.
