## Products imported from a spreadsheet, previewed before they exist - 2026-08-08

### Chunk chosen, and why the queued one was right

Took the queued chunk: **spreadsheet import as the `importProducts` server callable**.
Checked against the board first, as required. Its prerequisite had landed the same day —
`updateProducts` — so the required mode, the row bound, the per-row outcome report, the
authorization decided over every row before anything is read, and the preview that writes
nothing were all built and proved rather than guessed at. Import was always meant to be
taken second: it has to solve everything bulk change solved *plus* three problems bulk
change never faced, and none of those would have been easier to solve while also
inventing the preview.

No unqueued capability the app needs in order to function is missing. Every remaining red
row is blocked on a decision (password reset on App Check), an interface nobody has
shared (the printed body), a schema that does not exist (subscription), its own reporting
chunk (profit display), or on a Flutter surface that is deliberately one chunk covering
both halves of this feature.

### Completed in this session

**A business can create up to fifty products from a spreadsheet in one request, and see
exactly what that would create before any of it exists.** `importProducts` is the
twenty-sixth callable and the forty-ninth export. It reuses the bulk correction's
envelope wholesale — the same `ProductBatchMode`, the same required-mode reader, the same
`describeRows` for a refusal that names offending rows as payload paths — and it reuses
the validation that decides what a product may hold: an imported row's name, code, price,
and cost are read by `readProductUpdateInput`, and the document each row would create is
read back through `readSellableProduct` before anything is written. The two paths
therefore cannot drift about what a product is.

**No board row moved and none was meant to.** This is a server chunk with no Flutter
surface, so "import a catalog from a spreadsheet" stays red until a route calls it —
exactly as `updateProduct` stayed red for a day and as `updateProducts` has stayed red
since this morning. `firestore.rules` is untouched and the 161-test rules suite was run
to say so with a measurement rather than an assertion.

### The three new problems, and how each was answered

**1. A spreadsheet names "Bakery", not `ct_7f3a`.** A row names its category by
`categoryId` **or** by `categoryName`, never both — two ways of saying one thing have no
honest resolution when they disagree — and never neither, because a product must be filed
somewhere. A name is matched case-insensitively over collapsed whitespace, because
"bakery" and "Bakery" are one category to everybody who is not a computer.

The key is called `categoryName` and not `category`, deliberately. A stored product's
`category` is the **legacy alias for `categoryId`** and holds an ID; the previous app's
uploader wrote a display name into a field of that name, which is precisely the drift this
rewrite exists not to repeat.

**An unmatched name refuses the row. It does not create the category**, and that is the
decision this chunk had to make. A category is permanent here: the rules permit rename and
delete, and this app offers neither, for the orphaning reason the catalog decision records.
So "Bakry" typed once into a spreadsheet would become a grouping nobody can rename, nobody
can remove, and whose products every grouped report separates from the ones filed under
"Bakery". What makes refusing tolerable is the preview: a caller sees every unmatched name
at once, before anything is written, and the catalog surface already creates categories. If
category correction ever exists this is worth revisiting; until then, creating a category
from a typo is a worse answer than naming it.

**A name two categories share fails that row rather than guessing.** Nothing in this app
makes a category name unique — `allow create` on `categories` checks nothing at all — so
two "Bakery" categories are a state a business can reach, and the refusal says to name the
category by ID.

**2. The deterministic ID has to be per row, and position is the only identity a row
has.** The client's scheme is
`pd_<40 hex of sha256("createTenantProduct tenantId createdBy requestId")>`, scoped by
request — exactly right for one product and wrong for four hundred, which would all
collide on it. `productImportRowIds` digests the request identity and the row's
**position**, and returns all three documents that row is written at: `pd_` for the
product, `sa_` for its stock adjustment, `pi_` for its audit entry.

This is the one deterministic ID in this codebase derived from a position, and it is a
deliberate reversal of the neighbouring decision. `productBatchRowUpdateId` derives a row's
audit entry from the *product* it corrects, so re-sending a bulk correction with its rows
reordered lands on the same documents. An import has no product to derive from — that is
what an import is — so order becomes part of what a retry is recognised by, and the
fingerprint says so. A reordered retry answered off the stored record would report IDs
belonging to different products; one *not* answered off it would create the whole catalog
a second time. `already-exists` is the only honest outcome.

**3. Opening stock arrives with the ledger entry that says where it came from.** A row may
carry a `quantity`, and this is the only product payload in this codebase that may:
`updateProduct` refuses one outright, with a message naming `adjustStock`. That refusal is
not relaxed here, it is *satisfied* — the reason it exists is that a quantity written with
no `stock_movements` entry has no recorded origin, and this path writes that entry in the
same transaction.

Four documents per created row rather than a correction's two: the product, its audit
entry, and — only when the row opens holding stock — a `stock_adjustments` record and a
`stock_movements` entry, both in `adjustStock`'s own shape, field for field, because an
imported unit and an adjusted unit are the same unit and reconciliation reads one ledger.
`sourceType` is `product_import` and `adjustmentType` is `opening_balance`, which is the
type `adjustStock` already carries for exactly this. `previousQuantity` is `0` rather than
unknown: the product is being created in the same transaction, so it held nothing.

The product is created **holding** the opening quantity rather than created empty and then
adjusted. The recorded history is identical — the same ledger entry, the same before and
after — and it is one write fewer per row. Fifty rows is therefore at most 200 writes plus
one idempotency record, against Firestore's limit of 500, which is what the row bound had
to answer for.

**A row that opens holding nothing writes no ledger entry at all**, and its audit entry
says `mutatesQuantity: false`. Whenever that flag is true the entry names the
`adjustmentId` that says where the stock came from, and that pairing is what makes a
quantity acceptable in a product payload at all. There is a test for both halves.

### The one place import deliberately differs from correction: a price is not gated

`updateProduct` puts **price and cost** behind owner or administrator. `importProducts`
puts **only cost** there, and that is a decision rather than an oversight.

Changing a price silently alters what every subsequent sale records for a business that
will not notice until reconciliation, which is why correcting one is narrow. Setting the
*first* price is not that: it is creation, `allow create` on `products` already names the
operational three, and the catalog's own add-product form already lets a manager type a
price. An import that refused what the form beside it accepts would be a rule nobody could
explain.

Cost is gated for the reason it is gated everywhere — it is the business's margin written
down, and the create form refuses one from a manager too. The tier is delegated to
`assertProductUpdateAuthorized` over the single field `cost`, so neither the threshold nor
the wording can drift, and the decision is made over every row **before anything is
read**, so the preview refuses too. A manager who previewed green and then met a
commit-time refusal would learn only that the app guesses.

### Three decisions that are not re-derivable from what came before

**1. A product named twice is not a refusal here, which reverses the bulk correction's
rule.** `updateProducts` refuses a product named twice because two rows addressing one
*document* are two conflicting intents with no honest outcome to report for either. Two
import rows describing one product are not that: each creates its own document under its
own ID, and a shop legitimately stocking two products with one name and one code is a
state this app already permits and the till already refuses to resolve by scan. SKU
uniqueness is stated rather than enforced everywhere else in this system, and an import is
not the place to invent it — a check against fifty rows would not see the four hundred
already in the catalog, which is a guarantee the next request breaks.

**2. Re-running an import needs a new request ID, and that stocks the shelf twice.**
Stated rather than prevented, and tested rather than left to be discovered. The guard is
the request ID: a genuine retry under the same one is answered off the idempotency record
and lands on the same documents, which is already strictly better than the previous app's
uploader, which had no idempotency of any kind and duplicated the catalog on every retry.
A *fresh* request ID is a different request and creates the rows again. The preview is the
answer to that, not a duplicate check this app has never been able to make.

**3. An absent cost and an explicit `null` mean the same thing here, and hash the same.**
The opposite of `updateProduct`, where `null` clears a recorded cost and absence leaves it
alone. There is nothing to clear on a product that does not exist yet, so a blank
spreadsheet cell means the business did not say — and a null cost is therefore not a
monetary row, so a manager may send one.

### The category scan, and why exceeding it refuses the request

Resolving names means holding this business's categories in memory, and that read is
unbounded unless something bounds it. `MAXIMUM_IMPORT_CATEGORY_SCAN` is **500**, read as
`limit(501)` so "there are too many" is answered by the read itself rather than by a count
query nothing else in this codebase runs. Exceeding it refuses the **whole request**,
because the defect belongs to the business rather than to any row, and the message says
what to do instead: name each row's category by `categoryId`, which needs no scan at all.

Which read runs is decided by the rows rather than by a flag. A request naming every
category by ID reads exactly those documents through `getAll`; a request naming any
category by name scans instead, and that scan answers the ID rows too — so the two are
alternatives rather than both. A request whose every row was refused reads **nothing**,
because `getAll()` with no references is an error rather than an empty answer. All three
shapes have a test, including the one proving an ID-only request is unaffected by a
business holding 502 categories.

**One field is written that the catalog's own create form does not write: `updatedAt`.**
The nightly stock verification defers a product written in the last five minutes by
reading that field, and this is the one create path that can produce a product already
holding stock. Without it, an imported product could be compared against a ledger entry
Firestore has not yet made visible to the query that walks it.

### A literal NUL byte was repaired in `productBatch.ts`

`productBatchRowUpdateId` separated its two digest inputs with a **literal NUL byte**,
typed into the source on 2026-08-08 rather than written as an escape. This is exactly the
standing trap `PLAN.md` documents, from the other direction: `file` reported the module as
`data`, and `grep` reported it as "Binary file ... matches" and returned no lines from it
— a module hiding from every search of the repository.

It is now `\u0000`, written as an escape. **The digest is byte-identical** — a template
literal's `\u0000` is that same character — so no audit ID any bulk change would write has
moved, and the functions suite says so. A comment at the site now records that the
separator must stay a NUL rather than become a space, because turning it into one *would*
change every audit ID a bulk change addresses. Repaired with a small Node script replacing
the byte by index, which is what `PLAN.md` says is the way out: the editing tools cannot
anchor on a string that has to contain the byte.

Fixed here rather than left, because this module is now shared infrastructure — the import
path imports three things from it — and because a session that copied the pattern into the
new file would have copied the byte.

### Meaningful failures and their resolutions

No test failed that was not made to. The type checker caught the ordinary mistakes and one
real one: `assertProductUpdateAuthorized` takes a whole `ProductUpdateInput`, and handing
it an import row's own requested fields would have refused **every** import by a manager,
because those fields always include `price` and `price` is in `MONETARY_PRODUCT_FIELDS`.
That is what forced the price/cost split above to be stated as a decision rather than
inherited; the delegation now passes the single field `cost`.

Two things were changed after being written and before being run, both wrong answers
rather than compile errors:

- **A helper read the import ID back out of the document it had just asserted on**, which
  proves nothing at all. It now compares the audit entry's `importId` against the
  response's, which is the property worth having: one import is answerable as one thing.
- **Two tests in `products.test.ts` shared a name.** "a request whose every row was refused
  reads nothing at all" existed for the bulk correction already, and `node --test` reports
  both without complaint, so a failure in either would have been ambiguous. The import one
  is now "an import whose every row was refused reads nothing at all".

**And the NUL byte was met three times in one session, which is the part worth
recording.** Once in `productBatch.ts`, where the previous chunk left it. Once in **the new
`productImport.ts`**, whose `productImportRowIds` was written in the same shape and
acquired one of its own — found only because `grep` refused to search the file while
double-checking the separator convention, which is the same symptom as the first. And once
in *this handover*, where the sentence describing the first repair silently acquired two.
All three are fixed, and the last was caught by running `file` over the scratch copy before
it reached `HISTORY.md`.

**So the lesson is narrower and worse than the standing trap said.** It is not "typing a
control character into a test fixture"; it is writing a separator as a control character at
all, anywhere, source or prose. The escape has to be spelled out as six characters. `file`,
or `indexOf(0x00)`, is a one-second check and is now recorded in the traps as habitual.

The upside of finding the third one: all three digests in this feature area — the
idempotency identity, a bulk correction's audit ID, and an imported row's three IDs — now
separate their fields the same way, with the same escape and the same comment, so nobody
comparing them has to wonder which was deliberate. That was the intention behind the
accident, and it is now written down instead of implied.

## Both bulk halves reach a person - 2026-08-08

### What was built

**One screen, two callables, and the two board rows they were holding closed.**
`updateProducts` and `importProducts` had been built, tested, exported, and called by
nothing — two consecutive server chunks ending in the unreachable table, which `PLAN.md`
named as the limit. This chunk is the surface, and both rows are now green.

The route is `TenantBulkCatalogScreen`, reached from **"Manage catalog" → "Bulk changes and
import"** rather than from the landing route. It belongs beside the catalog for the reason
the catalog belongs beside the till: correcting many products starts by looking at them, and
the product list it needs is the list that route already shows.

**Four decisions the surface had to make, and the first was the open one.**

1. **Where the rows come from.** `PLAN.md` recommended it and this chunk accepted it
   unchanged: a **bulk correction reads its rows from the catalog the app already holds** —
   tick products on the route's own paged list, choose one field, preview — and an **import
   starts from delimited text** pasted into the screen. No package, no file picker, no
   binary format. `.xlsx` stays excluded, and nothing about the shape of this screen would
   have to change to add it later, because the parser is one function returning rows.
2. **A bulk correction is one field across many products, not a form.** Three reasons, and
   the first is the input: these rows come from products already on the device, so there is
   no column to read a per-product value out of. The second is that a name and a code belong
   to one product each — two products cannot share a corrected name, and a shared code is
   what the till refuses to resolve by scan. The third is authorization: the server decides
   permission over the **union** of every row's requested fields, so folding a price into a
   category move would refuse the whole request for a manager who never asked to change
   money. So the four things offered are: file under a category, set a unit price, set a unit
   cost, and remove the unit cost.
3. **A page is immutable once built, and a commit re-sends the very objects the preview
   sent.** Order is part of the server's request fingerprint, and a page keeps one request ID
   across its own preview and its own commit — which is exactly what the server's decision to
   write **no** idempotency record for a preview exists to allow. Rebuilding the plan for the
   commit would issue new IDs and could reorder rows, so the plan is held in state and
   anything that changes what it was built from throws it away.
4. **A commit is offered only after a preview that answered every page.** A rule, not
   caution: committing a page nobody previewed is the thing the preview exists to prevent,
   and a preview whose chain stopped has not described the whole change.

**The role asymmetry is honoured in two different ways on one screen, because the server
imposes two different rules.** A correction naming a price or a cost *anywhere* refuses the
whole request, so a manager is offered **no money correction at all** — the chips are absent
and `bulk-catalog-money-hidden` says why. An import **may** take a price from a manager,
because setting a first price is creation and the add-product form beside it already accepts
one, and must still refuse a cost — so a manager's sheet carrying a `cost` column is refused
**as a sheet**, before any row is read, which is where `assertProductImportAuthorized`
decides it. A manager who previewed green and then met a commit-time refusal would learn
only that the app guesses.

**The per-row report is the product.** Every row appears — `Created`, `Corrected`,
`Unchanged`, or `Refused` — with what it holds or would hold, or the exact refusal. A
correction is labelled by its **position in the selection** and an import by the **line of
the pasted sheet, header included**, because the server's index is page-local and neither of
those is what a person recognises: page-local index 0 of the second request is the
fifty-first product they ticked, and a person fixing a refusal is looking at their own file.

**Rows this client can refuse are refused before anything is sent, and still reported.** A
blank name, a spaced code, a price the till cannot represent, a negative opening balance, a
row naming a category twice or not at all, a row with fewer cells than its header — each is
that row's own refusal, carried in the report beside the server's outcomes, so every broken
row is named at once rather than found one round trip at a time. Every one of them is
validated by **the catalog surface's own helpers**: `tenantCatalogNormalizedName`,
`tenantCatalogNormalizedSku`, and `tenantCatalogPriceMinorUnits` were promoted from private
to public for exactly this, so a product created by an import, created by the add-product
form, and corrected one at a time cannot differ in what this client will write. A private
`_shared` wrapper converts their `TenantCatalogManagementException` into this boundary's own
and carries the code through unchanged.

**Sheet-level defects throw and row-level defects are reported, which is the split the
server already makes.** No header, a column this import does not read, one column twice, a
required column missing, no category column at all, more rows than the chain will hold — all
of them refuse the sheet, because reporting them per row would make the report itself wrong.
**A column nobody reads is refused rather than ignored**, so nothing a person supplied is
dropped without being mentioned.

**Quoting is the minimum a spreadsheet actually emits.** A double-quoted cell may hold the
delimiter and two quotes inside one are a literal quote. Without it a product called
`Bread, sliced` becomes two cells and shifts every column after it — a wrong import that
looks like a valid one. The delimiter is decided from the **header alone** (tab, comma, or
semicolon) so every row is split the same way; deciding it per row would let one row with a
stray tab be split differently from its neighbours.

**A half-answered chain is the ordinary case, not an error.** Pages are sent one after
another, a refusal stops the chain, and the report says how many requests answered — which
in a commit is how many were written. A page whose answer cannot be decoded is reported as
an **unknown outcome** rather than a failure, because the request was sent: in a commit it
may have been written, and only a re-read settles it.

**The duplicate-import hazard is stated where a person can see it.** The commit confirmation
says in as many words that running the sheet again creates the products a second time,
because nothing in this app makes a code unique and retiring a product is not an undo.

**The client half of the `cost` echo gap is closed.** `UpdateProductResponse` has echoed
`cost` and `costMinor` since earlier the same day; `TenantProductUpdateResult` now reads
both, proves they agree through the till's own conversion, and **reconciles them against the
correction** — a corrected cost must come back holding the requested figure and a cleared one
must come back null. The single-product route now states the new cost in its notice instead
of leaving it to the re-read. The shared reader, `tenantCatalogOptionalMoney`, is the one the
bulk decoders use for the same pair inside a per-row product.

### Meaningful failures and their resolutions

**Four, and three of them were the tests being right.**

1. **An enum cannot declare a constant called `name`.** The sheet-column enum's first two
   members were `name` and `category`; `name` collides with `Enum.name`, which every enum
   already has. They are `productName` and `categoryName` now, with a `label` field carrying
   the header a refusal should tell a person to type. Caught by the analyzer immediately.
2. **The shared validators throw the wrong exception type.** Promoting
   `tenantCatalogPriceMinorUnits` and its two neighbours meant the bulk boundary was raising
   `TenantCatalogManagementException` out of a function documented to raise
   `TenantBulkCatalogException`. Three unit tests caught it. The fix is the `_shared` wrapper
   above, which converts the type and carries the code through — deliberately not a second
   copy of the validation, which is the whole reason they were promoted.
3. **A page of the catalog cannot hold sixty products.** The chain test read sixty with
   `pageSize: 60`, and `readCollectionPage` bounds a page at fifty and throws `RangeError` —
   so the guard reported a failed read and the test could not find its own buttons. The fix
   made the test better than it was: it now ticks forty on one page, pages forward, and ticks
   twenty more, which is how a selection gets past fifty in reality and also proves the
   selection survives paging.
4. **A confirmation sentence was also a field's helper text.** A `textContaining` assertion on
   "keep the price they were sold at" matched twice, because the price field says it too. The
   assertion moved to a sentence only the confirmation carries. Worth recording as the
   ordinary hazard of writing the same true thing in two places.

One thing was changed after being written and before being run: the report first rendered a
category move as `Bakery -> cat-drinks`, taking the "after" from the server's echo. The page
now carries the `valueLabel` the confirmation uses, so it reads `Bakery -> Drinks`. That is
safe to display as what the row holds only because the decoder proves it — an outcome is
refused unless the product came back holding exactly the requested value, for a corrected row
and an unchanged one alike.

**The NUL trap was met twice more, and neither was written this session.** Running the
habitual check over the files this chunk touched found a **pre-existing literal NUL byte in
`lib/inventory/catalog_management_panel.dart`** — `_ProductEditDraft.fingerprint` joined its
fields on one, committed on 2026-08-07 and unnoticed for a day while `grep` reported the
1,400-line catalog route as "Binary file ... matches" and returned nothing from it. It is
repaired to a spelled-out escape, byte-identical in meaning, so no retained request ID
changes what it is held against. That is the **fifth** occurrence and the first in Dart, so
the trap's framing was wrong: it is not a `functions/` habit, it is whatever file is being
written.

**And then writing the paragraph you are reading produced two more, in `PLAN.md` and in
this file** — each time the sentence recording a repair came back holding a real NUL where
its `\u0000` should have been, and each time the same check caught it seconds later. **The
mechanism is now known and is worth more than the count**: writing the six-character escape
through a shell heredoc into a script turns it back into the byte, whatever quoting is used.
Build it as `chr(92) + 'u0000'`, or its equivalent, and concatenate. Both new Dart files were
checked too and neither carries one. This check has caught every occurrence ever caught
before a commit, and nothing else ever has.

**`.xlsx` and any binary spreadsheet format** stay excluded, and the recommendation this
chunk accepted is the reason: delimited text is the input a person already has, every
spreadsheet exports it, it survives a copy-and-paste, and it needs no package. Nothing about
the shape of this screen would change to add a picker later — the parser is one function from
text to rows.

**The 476 pre-existing analyzer issues** remain excluded and remain correct, for the reason

## Profit is shown, or refused, and never overstated - 2026-08-08

### What was chosen, and why

The queued chunk, taken unchanged: **a surface that shows profit and margin, and states how
much of it is unknown.** It was the only red board row not blocked on a decision, on somebody
else's interface, or on a sequencing call — the last one waiting on nothing but effort, in a
table this file has twice recorded emptying of exactly that kind of row.

Checked against the board before accepting it, as required. No capability the app needs in
order to function is missing and unqueued: no red row stops a business operating, the four
remaining reds are each blocked on something a coding session cannot resolve, and the amber
one is deliberate. So the queued chunk stood.

### What it turned out to be

**A display chunk, and the measurement says so.** `functions/` and `firestore.rules` were not
touched at all, and both suites were run over the finished tree to prove it rather than to
assert it: **409 functions tests and 161 rules tests, both unchanged.** Everything the surface
needs was already computed and already parsed:

- `aggregateSales` in `functions/src/operations/domain.ts` returns `profit` and
  `incompleteCostLineCount`, and `getSalesComparison` already sends both — for a whole
  business, for one member, and for one category, because the filter is applied before the
  aggregation rather than after it.
- `daily_metrics` already stores both, and `TenantDailyMetrics` already parsed both.
- `TenantSalesTotals` already parsed both.

So the answer to "whether anything on the server is missing" is **no**, with one qualification
that decided the whole design and is recorded below: **nothing reports how many sale lines
there were altogether**, only how many lacked a cost.

### The decision the chunk actually turned on

The `PLAN.md` question was what "unknown" looks like next to a figure — a count, a proportion,
a suppressed figure below some coverage, or all three. **A proportion is not available.**
Neither surface is told the total line count, so "96 lines have no cost" cannot be turned into
"96 of 4,000" without a server change, and a server change was out of scope for a display
chunk that had just measured the server complete.

That is not a limitation to work around; it is the argument. A line with no cost is counted by
the server as costing nothing, so a profit figure over incomplete data is an **upper bound**,
and with no total line count **how far above the truth it sits is unmeasurable**. An
unmeasurable overstatement is not a smaller version of the truth. So the rule is:

> **No profit figure is shown unless every sale line behind it carries a cost.**

An "at most" ceiling was considered and declined, and it is worth recording why, because it is
the plausible alternative. It is honest wording, but the number it decorates is still the
number a reader remembers, and the qualifier's weight is exactly the thing nothing here can
quantify: a period with two costed lines in five hundred produces a ceiling equal to the
takings, which is the 100%-margin failure this app already refused once. Suppression heals by
itself as costs are recorded; a ceiling does not stop being misleading as the data improves,
it just stops being *very* misleading.

### The three states, and why the third exists

`TenantProfitBasis` in the new `lib/reporting/profit_report.dart`:

1. **`complete`** — every line carried a cost. The figure is shown with its margin, and the
   note says so: *"Every sale line behind it carries a cost."* That positive sentence is not
   decoration. A reader cannot tell a complete figure from an overstated one by looking at it,
   so the completeness is stated wherever the figure is.
2. **`incomplete`** — at least one line carried none. No figure, no margin, and the count is
   inside the reason rather than beside it.
3. **`inconsistent`** — the profit exceeds the takings it was computed from. That means a
   negative total cost, and nothing that writes either figure can produce one: profit is
   revenue minus a sum of non-negative line costs. It is **ordered above `incomplete`**, the
   way `stockComparisonOutcome` orders its own causes most-specific-first, because an
   incomplete figure is at least the arithmetic it claims to be and this one is not — naming
   missing cost data for it would name a cause that does not explain it.

The basis is decided **from the figures themselves**, never from where they came, which is
what stops the reconciled daily summary and the server-added period totals disagreeing about
when a number may be believed. The cost the server must have subtracted is recovered as
`sales - profit` **in whole minor units**, which is exact rather than approximate because the
server adds money as integers.

A fourth candidate state was dropped: "no cost recorded at all", distinguishable because the
recovered cost would be zero. Under suppression it produces the same output as `incomplete`,
so it would have been a distinction with no consequence.

**A margin is withheld unless the figure it describes is shown**, and also when the period
took nothing — a margin on no takings is a division by zero, not a figure of zero. A
percentage is the most believed number on any report and it carries no units to warn a reader,
so it must never outlive the figure it was divided from.

### Who may see it

**Owner and administrator, and no rule changed.** This was not a fresh decision: the standing
product-cost decision of 2026-08-07 already said in as many words that what putting a buying
price behind owner/admin buys is that **no manager is *shown* a margin**. `daily_metrics` is
readable by owner, administrator, and manager, and `getSalesComparison` answers all three, so
a manager's device already holds every figure involved. This is a **surface boundary, not a
secrecy guarantee**, exactly as recording a cost is, and it is documented as one in the code.

`TenantProfitReport.allowedRoles` is restated rather than imported from
`TenantCatalogManagementRepository.costRoles`. It is deliberately identical, and it is this
domain's own decision about a different document — importing the inventory module into
reporting to borrow a two-element list would couple two areas over a coincidence of value.

**`firestore.rules` is untouched and was measured so.** The role decision needed no rule
because it removes nothing a manager could already read; it removes what a manager is shown.

### The redundancy that shaped the widgets

Both panels already carried a sentence naming the incomplete count, visible to every reporting
role. Adding a profit block that also names it gave an owner two sentences containing the same
number, which reads as two findings rather than one. So:

- **A session that may see profit gets `TenantProfitStatement` and nothing else** — the count
  lives inside the reason there is no figure.
- **A session that may not gets the standalone count sentence, exactly as before.**

Never both. The sales-totals sentence lost its trailing clause and is now word for word the
daily summary's — *"96 sale lines have no cost recorded."* — because it is the same fact about
the same sale lines over a different stretch of days, and the clause it dropped ("so no profit
figure is shown") explained something the reader who sees that sentence is not being shown
anyway.

`TenantProfitStatement` is shared by both surfaces so the two cannot word one fact
differently, and it takes a `keyPrefix` because the daily summary renders one per day.

### Files changed

```text

lib/reporting/profit_statement.dart       new — the shared figure-or-reason block
lib/reporting/daily_metrics.dart          profitReport getter; the "no screen displays it" comment retired
lib/reporting/daily_metrics_panel.dart    showProfit from the guarded session; statement or count, never both
lib/reporting/sales_totals.dart           profitReport getter; _minorUnits promoted to reportingMinorUnits
lib/reporting/sales_totals_panel.dart     showProfit from the guarded session; the cost sentence unified
lib/reporting/reporting.dart              both new files exported
test/reporting/profit_report_test.dart          new — 11
test/reporting/profit_statement_test.dart       new — 8
test/reporting/daily_metrics_test.dart          +1
test/reporting/daily_metrics_panel_test.dart    +2
test/reporting/sales_totals_test.dart           +1
test/reporting/sales_totals_panel_test.dart     +3
```

**One duplication was removed rather than added to.** `sales_totals.dart` held a private
`_minorUnits` used to check that the tender split adds up to the total it describes. The
profit basis needs the same rounding for the same reason, so it is now `reportingMinorUnits`
in `profit_report.dart` and the tender check calls it. Its doc comment records why it is
deliberately **not** `checkoutMinorUnitsFromMajor`: that one refuses an amount the till could
not price and exists to stop a bad price being recorded, while these figures are already
recorded, arrive from the server, and are only ever compared with each other.

### Meaningful failures and their resolutions

**One, and it was arithmetic in the test rather than in the code.** A new decoder test
asserted a 25% margin over the existing response fixture, whose takings are `4820.75`;
`1205.25` of that is 25.0013%, and `closeTo(25, 0.0001)` refused it. The figure was wrong, not
the tolerance — a looser tolerance would have hidden exactly the kind of disagreement the
whole minor-unit comparison exists to expose. The fixture now overrides both figures to
`4820.00` and `1205.00`.

Three existing tests changed role rather than expectation, and that is the part worth
recording. `incomplete cost data is named, and profit is not shown`, `a day with one of
everything reads in the singular`, and the two sales-totals cost-count tests all ran as an
**owner** and asserted the standalone count sentence. Under the new rule an owner is shown the
profit statement instead, so they now run as a **manager** — which is what they were always
really testing, since the sentence they assert is the one a session that may not see profit
gets. The owner's side of each is a new test beside it.

One process note, because it cost a cycle and the file already warns about the general shape:
**appending this entry through a quoted shell heredoc failed to parse** and wrote nothing. The
entry was written to a scratch file with the editing tools and appended with a three-line Node
script instead. And then writing the paragraph you are reading produced an eighth occurrence of the
control-character trap: the sentence naming it came back holding a real NUL where its
six-character escape should have been, this time written straight through the editing tools
rather than through a shell heredoc. The habitual check found it in seconds, as it always
has. **So the mechanism is wider than the last entry concluded** — it is not the heredoc, it
is writing that escape anywhere at all, and the only reliable way to put one into a file is
to build it as chr(92) followed by the four characters and concatenate.

## The password-reset worker runs against real Auth and real Firestore - 2026-08-08

Taken because the rule attached to the password-reset exclusion said to take it: the
profit-display session excluded password reset for a third consecutive chunk, and the standing
instruction is that a third exclusion is when the emulator integration test for
`deliverPasswordReset` gets written. It was checked against the board first and nothing the app
needs in order to function is missing and unqueued — the four red rows are password reset
(blocked on the App Check decision), the printed receipt body (blocked on an external service's
interface), suspicious-return scoring (sequenced after the first deployment on purpose), and
subscription (no schema on the server) — so the queued chunk stood.

**It resolves none of the App Check question and is not meant to.** What it covers is the half
of that area that was never blocked by anything: `deliverPasswordReset` carries no attestation
of any kind, and the public callable in front of it is seventeen lines of validate-and-enqueue.

### What was built

`rules-tests/test/password-reset-delivery.integration.test.js` — **11 tests**, joined to the
existing invitation suite rather than given a fourth demo project. The suite goes **12 → 23**.

| Test | What only real infrastructure proves |
| --- | --- |
| an eligible reset sends a real Auth link and stores only hashes | `generatePasswordResetLink` against a real Auth record; the whole sent-state document |
| an address changed in real Auth after the request writes nothing | a real `updateUser` between request and dispatch |
| a disabled real Auth identity writes nothing | `disabled` read off a real Auth record |
| an address real Auth does not know writes nothing | the error code real Auth actually raises for a missing user |
| a canonical root that is absent or not eligible writes nothing | the real `users/{uid}` read, absent and then disabled |
| a suppression under the previous key version is still found | the real `getAll` across a keyring rotation |
| a retryable provider failure leaves a retry the next attempt completes | the lease, the attempt counter, and the deletion sentinels |
| a permanent provider failure marks the identity unavailable | the non-retryable branch of `markFailure` |
| a repeated dispatch of a sent delivery does not send twice | the real transaction reading a terminal state |
| a continue URL that is not HTTPS refuses to build the gateway | the gateway constructor, which every fake replaced |
| no document any of these deliveries wrote holds an address or a link | the frozen guarantee, read back out of a real store |

### One production change, and the claim it retracts

`PLAN.md` said this chunk "changes no production code". ~~Retracted~~ — **it changed one
keyword.** `firestorePasswordResetDependencies` in `functions/src/email/passwordReset.ts` is now
exported, with a comment saying why. Nothing else about it moved: no signature, no behaviour, no
call site, and the functions suite held at 409 to say so.

The alternative was to rebuild those adapters inside the test, and that would have been a test of
the rebuild. The adapters **are** the untested half — the unit suite substitutes all eight
dependencies, so the Firestore transactions and the Auth gateway had never executed anywhere.
Exporting the seam is what makes the test test something.

### Eight decisions worth keeping

1. **It lives in the invitation suite, as `PLAN.md` recommended, and the recommendation held.**
   No new ports, no fourth demo project, no fourth copy of the compiled Functions build. Password
   reset and staff invitation share the delivery, suppression, and recipient-hash code both
   exercise. `node --test` gives each file its own process, so the new file brings up its own
   Admin app and cannot disturb the acceptance fixtures.
2. **What is dispatched is `processPasswordResetTask` over the real dependencies, which is
   `deliverPasswordReset`'s body minus three lines** — the keyring parsed out of its secret, the
   Brevo provider constructed out of its secrets, and the `getFirestore()`/`getAuth()` defaults.
   Those three are deliberately uncovered, and the reason is a repository trap rather than
   laziness: reaching them needs `functions/integration/index.js` to export an email function,
   and every parameter in `email/config.ts` would then have to be answered at emulator startup or
   the run hangs after "Serving at port ...". That fixture's seven exports reach
   `firebase-functions/params` not at all, which is an invariant the reconciliation fixture
   documents at length, and it is not worth spending on three lines whose parts are unit-tested
   separately.
3. **The seam is `fetch`, not the provider.** The test constructs the **real**
   `BrevoEmailProvider` over a stub `fetch`, so `requireProviderConfiguration`, the message body,
   the idempotency header, and the HTTP status mapping all run. That is what lets the failure
   tests drive `provider_http_503` and `provider_http_400` through the real mapping instead of
   throwing a hand-made `EmailProviderError`, and it is why "what reaches the seam" is an
   assertion rather than a claim. No live credential, no network call.
4. **Both the worker and the assertions use the Functions copy of firebase-admin**, reached
   through `createRequire` against `functions/package.json`, the way the acceptance suite already
   does for `revokePlatformAdmin`. The adapters compare `leaseExpiresAt instanceof Timestamp` and
   write `FieldValue` sentinels from `functions/node_modules`; a handle built from the
   `rules-tests` copy would fail those identity checks for a reason no assertion would explain.
5. **The keyring has two versions.** A single-key fixture cannot reach `allRecipientHashes`'
   whole point, so the suppression test writes its document under the **previous** version and
   the task is prepared under the current one. The delivery is then recorded under the current
   version while the suppression that stopped it was written under the previous — which is the
   behaviour a rotation depends on, and it had never run against a real `getAll`.
6. **The plaintext guarantee is a test, not a comment.** Every address, every mixed-case form,
   every local part, and every action link the Auth emulator minted is collected as the file
   runs, and the last test sweeps `email_deliveries`, `email_delivery_status`, and
   `email_suppressions` for all of them. UIDs are deliberately unrelated to the local parts they
   belong to — `pwreset-eligible` holds `delivery-eligible@...` — because a UID echoing a local
   part would make that sweep pass for the wrong reason.
7. **`PASSWORD_RESET_CONTINUE_URL` is declared in the runner env**, beside the invitation secret,
   rather than set inside the test: outside a deployed function `defineString(...).value()` is
   just `process.env`, and the suite's configuration belongs in one place. The one test that
   needs a different value overrides `process.env` and restores it in a `finally`, which is the
   shape this file already requires of anything that mutates state a sibling test reads.
8. **The sweep test is the one that fails under `INTEGRATION_TEST_NAME_PATTERN`**, and that is
   recorded in the file rather than worked around. Filtered down to itself it has nothing to
   sweep, and a sweep that finds nothing is exactly the result its three floors exist to refuse.

### What it found: nothing broken, and that is worth stating

No defect. The worker was correct, and every risk this class of test exists to catch came back
clean on the first run:

- **The deletion sentinels serialize.** `beginDelivery` writes `nextAttemptAt: FieldValue.delete()`
  inside a merged `set` that may be creating the document, and `markSent`/`markFailure` delete
  `leaseId`, `leaseExpiresAt`, and `lastErrorCode` in an `update`. This is precisely the shape
  that took `mergeSaleReconciliationJob` down on every sale it ever saw, invisibly to eleven
  sessions of green unit tests. Here it is fine, and now measured rather than assumed.
- **`generatePasswordResetLink` works against the Auth emulator**, returning a
  `mode=resetPassword` link carrying an `oobCode` and the configured continue URL.
- **Real Auth folds the address.** The records are created mixed-case, the requests arrive padded
  and upper-cased, and the hash the task carries still matches the hash derived from what Auth
  holds. That is the current-email HMAC recheck running for the first time against something
  other than a map.
- **A missing identity raises the code the gateway swallows.** `findByEmail` catches exactly
  `auth/user-not-found` and rethrows everything else; only real Auth can say which code an
  unknown address actually produces, and it produces that one.

The whole new file runs in **2.7 seconds**, of which the eligible send is 1.68 — the first Auth
call of the process. Nothing here waits on a cold trigger, because nothing here goes through the
task queue.

## The app is driven on Android against the emulators - 2026-08-08

### Completed in this session

**The queued "run the app against the emulators" chunk, taken on Android after the product
owner answered the one question standing in front of it.** `PLAN.md` had queued this eleven
times and named exactly one thing to ask before starting: whether a loopback-only Windows or
web run was worth doing in that form, or whether Android should be brought back into scope. The
answer was Android, and first. That reverses the standing "skip the Android build and Android
emulator tests" instruction for this session only, on an explicit instruction, and it is
recorded here so a later session does not read the reversal as drift.

**It changed no repository file.** No Dart, no `functions/`, no `firestore.rules`, no test. The
working tree at the end of the run held exactly the five user-owned edits it held at the start.
That is what a behavioural session is supposed to look like, and everything below is either an
observation or a finding.

**Five capability chunks landed on 2026-08-08 and not one of their routes had been seen outside
a widget test.** All five were driven on a real device against real Auth, real Firestore, and
real Functions. Every one of them worked. The findings are all at the edges.

### What was verified, end to end, against real infrastructure

Each of these was checked in the app *and* against Firestore through the Admin SDK, because a
screen saying a thing happened is not the same as it having happened.

- **A product is created holding nothing.** "Manage catalog" wrote
  `pd_231dfbe58ed1d6bac0729933c2f89e30ff2cff88` with `quantity: 0`, `cost: 15`, and **no
  `updatedAt`** - which is the documented asymmetry with import, confirmed from the other side
  for the first time.
- **A correction audits its before and after.** Price 65 to 70 and cost null to 45 on
  `prod-bread` produced `audit_logs/pu_1e4ff8b47756fc7d7bc25a0031b1fb5a9a76cd75` carrying
  `changes: [{price, 65, 70}, {cost, null, 45}]`, `mutatesQuantity: false`, the actor UID, and
  the request ID. The route sent only the two fields that moved.
- **A preview really writes nothing.** The bulk correction's preview reported "2 would be
  corrected" and neither `prod-mandazi` nor `prod-milk-500` had a `cost` field at that moment.
  Committing added `cost: 12` to both. The preview/commit split is real, not cosmetic.
- **The pasted spreadsheet was the strongest argument for this chunk and it held.** Three rows
  of comma-delimited text, header included, with a **quoted cell holding the delimiter** -
  `"Bread, sliced"` - parsed as one product named `Bread, sliced`. All three were created with
  their price, cost, category resolved by name, and opening quantity, plus three
  `stock_adjustments` carrying `sourceType: "product_import"`,
  `adjustmentType: "opening_balance"`, `previousQuantity: 0`, one shared
  `importId: im_72f70bae46efc371b972caf4ea274d94d18ad055`, and `rowIndex` 0/1/2. Rows were
  labelled **Line 2, Line 3, Line 4** - the line of the pasted sheet, header included, exactly
  as the standing decision requires.
- **A sale freezes the cost onto its line.** This is the central guarantee of the product-cost
  decision and it had never been observed outside a test. The stored sale carries
  `unitCostMinor: 4500` and `costMinor: 4500` beside `unitPriceMinor: 7000`, with receipt
  `CT-33C-20260808-0001` and `payloadSchemaVersion: 2`. It submitted automatically on save, and
  the landing panel read `Confirmed: 1` on return - so the 2026-08-04 defects (a sale that never
  submitted, and a stale pending-checkout panel) both stay fixed.
- **The profit rule is a role boundary and the two sessions see different sentences.** Same day,
  same data, verified by signing in twice:

  | Session | What the daily summary says for 2026-08-08 |
  | --- | --- |
  | Owner | `Sales: KES 70.00 over 1 transaction in 1 shift` / `Profit: KES 25.00, a margin of 35.7%.` / `Every sale line behind it carries a cost.` |
  | Manager | `Sales: KES 70.00 over 1 transaction in 1 shift` - and nothing else |

  70 minus 45 is 25, and 25/70 is 35.7%. The manager is shown no figure, no margin, and no cost
  sentence at all. The manager's landing route also omits "Checkout settings", which is the
  owner/admin gate showing up where it should.
- **Reconciliation works from both directions.** The sale trigger created
  `dirty_1786210200000` and it completed on its own within seconds. "Ask for a check" then
  created `rj_6c2768eafe98218477ad713e9cf9d6f6f538f15c` with `source: "manual"`, the owner's
  UID, and its own request ID; it completed, walking **11 products** - the whole catalog
  including the imports.
- **The stock route reads the ledger.** After the sale, White bread loaf shows
  `Recorded stock: 39` (down from 40) and one ledger entry, `-1 - Sale`, sourced to the
  checkout ID and timestamped.

### Findings, recorded rather than fixed

The chunk said to record what is found and fix only what blocks the run. Nothing blocked the
run, so nothing was fixed.

1. **The login screen shows a raw platform-channel name when the password is empty.** With a
   valid address and an empty password, the error rendered to the user is, verbatim:

   ```text
   "dev.flutter.pigeon.firebase_auth_platform_interface.FirebaseAuthHostApi.signInWithEmailAndPassword".
   ```

   A **wrong** password gives a proper sentence ("The password is invalid or the user does not
   have a password."), so this is specific to the empty-password path: the form does not require
   a non-empty password before calling Firebase, and the resulting platform exception's message
   is the channel name. **This supersedes the 2026-08-04 note**, which recorded the same string,
   said it "appeared only after a mistyped sign-in and did not recur on a clean run, so it was
   not chased". It is deterministic and it was reproduced twice, once by accident and once
   deliberately. It is the first thing a new user can see.
2. **That error survives editing the fields.** Clearing the address and retyping it left the red
   text in place. This is the other half of the same 2026-08-04 note and it also reproduces.
3. **The invitation refusal tells the user to do something that can never work.** A newly
   invited manager was offered in-app acceptance on the business selector, and it failed with
   "Invitation could not be accepted. Please try again." **The server was right to refuse.** The
   invitation carries `visibleAcceptanceAllowed: false`, set at
   `functions/src/staff/issuance.ts:310` as
   `!targetIdentity.newlyCreated && targetIdentity.emailVerified` - this identity was created by
   its own invitation, so tokenless acceptance is correctly barred and the token is mandatory.
   The defect is the sentence: retrying cannot ever succeed, and the message says to retry.
4. **Board row text corrected, not its colour.** "Accept a staff invitation" read "In-app for a
   verified identity". That is incomplete: the flag is decided **at invite time** and requires
   the identity to have *already existed and already been verified* when the invitation was
   issued. Verifying the address afterwards - which is exactly what this session did - does not
   change the stored flag. The row's text is updated in `PLAN.md`; it is still green, because an
   identity that already exists can still accept in-app.
5. **The add-product form asks for a category next to nothing.** The form ends with "Choose the
   category this product is filed under." and **no picker beside it**; the picker is the chip row
   about a thousand pixels above, under a heading called "Categories" that also serves as the
   list of existing categories. Tapping "Bakery" up there does work and the sentence becomes
   "Filed under Bakery.", after which "Add product" enables. The inconsistency is that the
   **"Correct" dialog has an inline category picker** right where it is needed, so one screen
   does it both ways.
6. **A category ID reaches the eye in two places.** The import preview says "filed under
   **cat-bakery**" for a row whose author typed `Bakery`, and "Manage catalog" lists Charcoal 2kg
   under **cat-not-cached** because the seed files it under a category that does not exist. The
   read-only catalog resolves names correctly in the same situation, so the resolution exists and
   these two surfaces do not use it.

### Meaningful failures and their resolutions

- **The Android emulator would not boot, and it was the environment rather than the AVD.** It
  died with `This AVD's configuration is missing a kernel file!`, resolving the system image
  against `ANDROID_SDK_ROOT`, which this machine sets to
  `C:\Users\BonifaceMasota\develop\android-sdk`. That tree's
  `system-images\android-35\google_apis\x86_64\` directory **is an empty stub**; the real image
  with `kernel-ranchu` is under `D:\android-emulator-sdk`. Exporting
  `ANDROID_SDK_ROOT=D:\android-emulator-sdk` for the emulator process alone booted it in 92
  seconds. Flutter's own `adb` stays at the `develop` path and is called by absolute path, so
  the two do not conflict. **This is new and is now a standing note** - the previous Android

- **Staff invitation email cannot be delivered against the local emulators at all.**
  `deliverStaffInvitation` fails with `EmailProviderError ... safeCode:

  That is a local fixture and is **not** evidence the acceptance path works; what this session

## The sign-in screen says something true - 2026-08-08

### Completed in this session

**The queued chunk, unchanged: findings 1 and 2 from the Android device run, and nothing
else.** It was checked against the status board and the frozen fifteen-step rollout before
being accepted. Nothing a shop needs in order to operate is missing and unqueued - the four
red rows are blocked on App Check, on a print service's interface, on the first deployment,
and on a schema the server does not have - so the queued chunk stood.

**What a user now sees when a sign-in fails is a sentence, and it is a property of the
shape rather than of care taken at each call site.** Three things changed and the first two
are the findings:

1. **An empty password, and an empty address, are refused by the form before Firebase is
   called.** An empty password is not a credential. `signInInputDefect` judges the address
   first, trims it, and deliberately does **not** trim the password: a space is a character
   a password may contain, so a password made of them is the server's to judge and the only
   thing this app knows is wrong is a password that is not there at all.
2. **A refusal is cleared the moment the input it describes stops being the input.** Keyed
   on the *text* rather than on the controller notification, because a
   `TextEditingController` also notifies when only the selection moves - which is what the
   password field's own reveal toggle does, and revealing a password answers nothing the
   refusal said. Both branches are pinned by a widget test.
3. **No exception can be rendered, by construction.** This is the part that is not in the
   two findings and is the reason the chunk was worth taking as written. See below.

### The bug class, not the code that produced it

The chunk said to treat "the error is a string nobody wrote" as the defect rather than
patching the one path that produced it. That decided the design:

- **`lib/tenancy/sign_in.dart` is a narrow boundary**, in the shape
  `email_delivery_status.dart` and `account_verification.dart` already use.
  `EmailPasswordSignIn` is an interface; `FirebaseEmailPasswordSignIn` is the adapter;
  `SignInException` carries **a code and nothing else**. The provider's `message` is dropped
  at the boundary, so no surface above it can display one even by mistake. The old screen
  rendered `e.message ?? "Login failed"`.
- **`signInSafeError` reads a code and never a message.** Anything that is not a
  `SignInException` - a platform channel error, a plugin defect, a programming mistake -
  answers with one fallback sentence that names no cause. Mapping only the code that caused
  the report would have left every other channel-level failure printing itself.
- **A wrong password, an unknown address, and a malformed credential give one identical
  sentence.** Firebase itself collapses them into `invalid-credential` once email
  enumeration protection is on, so distinguishing them here is a disclosure that survives
  only until that setting changes - and this app already closes enumeration deliberately on
  the password-reset endpoint. Five codes, one answer, pinned by a test that asserts the set
  of answers has size one.
- **This changed a path that was already working.** A wrong password used to render the
  provider's own sentence, "The password is invalid or the user does not have a password.",
  recorded verbatim in the previous entry. It now renders ours. That is deliberate: the
  provider's sentences are written for whoever is reading a log, they are not translated,
  and one of them was not a sentence at all.
- **`setPersistence` moved into the adapter**, so the screen holds no Firebase type at all.
  Its swallowed failure is unchanged and is now documented as the expected case rather than
  the exceptional one: persistence is a web concept and every other platform answers
  `unimplemented`.

### The mechanism behind finding 1, now known exactly

The previous entry said the platform exception's "message is the channel name". **Refined
rather than retracted:** the message is
`Unable to establish connection on channel: "<channel>".`, produced by
`_createConnectionError` in
`firebase_auth_platform_interface/lib/src/pigeon/messages.pigeon.dart`. What was recorded
verbatim from the device - the channel name in quotes followed by a full stop - is the tail
of that sentence, which is what fitted on screen. The exception is a **`PlatformException`,
not a `FirebaseAuthException`**, which is why the old screen's `on FirebaseAuthException`
branch never saw it and its `catch` branch was the one that had the honest wording. Both
test files construct that exact object, copied from the plugin source, rather than a
paraphrase - an assertion against a paraphrase would prove nothing.

### Also fixed, in the same file and named rather than smuggled

**`emailFocus.requestFocus()` in the post-frame callback had no `mounted` guard**, so a
screen disposed inside its first frame would request focus on a disposed `FocusNode`. One
line, in a method this chunk was already rewriting.

### Deliberately not done

**The chunk asked for one look at the sign-in screen on a device afterwards, and this
session did not do it**, because the session instruction says to skip the Android build and
Android emulator tests. That is a reversal of the 2026-08-08 device session's own reversal,
and it is stated rather than left silent: the fix is covered by 32 tests including the one
that would have caught the original defect, and it has not been looked at by a person. **It
is queued in `PLAN.md` as the first thing the next device run does.**

**No other finding from the device run was touched.** Findings 3, 4, 5, and 6 are queued
separately and on purpose.

### Files changed

lib/tenancy/sign_in.dart           (new: the boundary, the input rule, the messages)
lib/tenancy/tenancy.dart           (one export line)

`firestore.rules` and `functions/` were not touched at all.

## A refused invitation says what will actually work - 2026-08-08

### Completed in this session

**The queued chunk, unchanged: finding 3 from the Android device run, and nothing else.** It
was checked against the status board and the frozen fifteen-step rollout before being
accepted. Nothing a shop needs in order to operate is missing and unqueued - the four red
rows are blocked on App Check, on a print service's interface, on the first deployment, and
on a schema the server does not have - so the queued chunk stood. It is the same defect class
as the sign-in repair before it, on the other surface a stranger meets, and it is the last of
the three device findings that leaves a user with no way forward at all.

**"Invitation could not be accepted. Please try again." is gone from both acceptance
surfaces**, and what replaced it is not a better sentence but a boundary that makes the old
one impossible to write.

### The chunk's own premise was wrong, and checking it is the finding

`PLAN.md` queued this as *"`failed-precondition` is the case that matters and it is the one
the device hit"*, and attached an instruction to **check the server's actual code for this
refusal before wording it - do not guess it from the flag name.** That instruction paid for
itself immediately.

**The server throws `permission-denied`, not `failed-precondition`**, and it carries the
reason in `details`:

```ts
throw new HttpsError("permission-denied", "The invitation cannot be accepted.", {
  violation: acceptanceViolation,
});
```

`functions/src/staff/acceptance.ts:171`. The `violation` is one of **eight** tokens produced
by `invitationAcceptanceViolation` in `functions/src/staff/acceptancePolicy.ts`, and
`versioned_proof_required` - the one the device hit - is the last of them. So a client
branching on the code alone could not have told the device's refusal apart from six other
permanent refusals and from a rejected HMAC proof. **The code was never enough; the detail
always was, and nothing had ever read it.** The superseded claim is retracted inline in
`PLAN.md` at the text that made it.

`failed-precondition` is a real answer from these callables, but it is a different one: the
five-minute recent-authentication rule, a missing root record, or an inactive business.

### One module, because it is one server function

`acceptTenantInvitation` and `acceptVisibleTenantInvitation` are two `onCall` wrappers over a
single `acceptInvitation`, refusing through a single policy function. So the client mapping is
a single module, `lib/tenancy/invitation_acceptance_failure.dart`, imported by both. Two
copies would be two ways to word one server decision and the first divergence would be
invisible - which is the same reasoning that put `planProductUpdate` behind one function for
the single and bulk correction paths.

It holds four things:

- **`InvitationAcceptanceViolation`**, a one-for-one mirror of the server's union, pinned by a
  test asserting the eight wire values as a set. A token drifting silently is exactly how a
  refusal would fall back to the vague sentence without anybody noticing.
- **`InvitationAcceptanceMode`**, `token` or `visible`, mirroring the server's own mode
  parameter. It is carried because the server branches on it: a `permission-denied` naming no
  violation means a rejected proof on one path and an ineligible signed-in identity on the
  other, and one sentence covering both would be vague on purpose.
- **`InvitationAcceptanceException`**, carrying **a code and a violation, and no message**.
  Same shape and same reason as `SignInException` the session before: the provider's sentence
  is written for a log reader, is not translated, and is sometimes not a sentence at all. The
  violation may cross because it is a server-authored enumerated token rather than prose - the
  rule that no string this app did not write reaches a user is unchanged.
- **`invitationAcceptanceSafeError`**, the mapping.

### The rule, which is what the defect actually violated

> **Only a failure this app knows to be transient may invite a retry.**

Every violation the server's policy produces is permanent *for the invitation it refused* - a
flag fixed at invite time, a consumed token, a cancelled invitation, a suspended business - so
none of them says "try again", and each names the one thing that can move the user forward
instead. Exactly two answers offer a retry, `unavailable`/`deadline-exceeded` and
`resource-exhausted`, because for those two a retry is the answer. A test asserts that
partition over seventeen codes and both modes rather than describing it.

**The sentence for the case the device hit** sends the user to the emailed link and names the
one action that can produce another one:

> This invitation has to be opened from the link in your invitation email, so it cannot be
> accepted here. Ask your administrator to send the invitation again if you no longer have
> that email.

That last clause is not padding: `resendStaffInvitation` exists, so it is a real path rather
than sympathy.

### Four decisions that are not obvious from the finding

1. **`versioned_proof_required` is permanent and the wording says so without saying why.**
   `visibleAcceptanceAllowed` is decided once, at invite time, by `!newlyCreated &&
   emailVerified` in `functions/src/staff/issuance.ts:310`. Verifying the address afterwards
   does not change it. The sentence therefore does not tell the user to verify anything - that
   advice would be true-sounding, actionable, and useless, which is the same failure mode as
   "Please try again" wearing different clothes.
2. **`email_unverified` is unreachable today and is mapped anyway.** The server's own
   `mode === "visible" && emailVerified !== true` guard throws before the policy function is
   consulted, so nothing produces that token. It is modelled because the server declares it;
   dropping it would make a later server change answer the fallback silently. Recorded here so
   the next reader does not delete it as dead code.
3. **`fromWireOrNull` is tolerant, and it is the one tolerant thing in the file.** An older
   client meeting a violation a later server adds must degrade to the code-level sentence, not
   turn a refusal into an unrenderable failure. Shape is judged strictly and content
   permissively, in that order: only a string, at `violation`, inside a map, naming a token
   this client knows.
4. **The fallback offers no retry either.** `SignInException`'s fallback does, because a user
   staring at a sign-in screen has nothing else to do. Here there is somebody to ask, an
   acceptance that failed for an unmodelled reason is far more often a policy refusal than a
   blip, and the button is still on screen for anyone who wants to retry anyway. So it names
   the administrator and stops.

### `catch (_)` was the defect; the sentence was the symptom

Both surfaces discarded the error entirely - `tenant_visible_invitation_acceptance.dart:326`
and `tenant_invitation_acceptance.dart:318` - and **neither adapter converted anything**, so
there was no code to discard in the first place. Both halves had to be built:

- `FirebaseAcceptVisibleTenantInvitationCallable` and `FirebaseAcceptTenantInvitationCallable`
  now catch `FirebaseFunctionsException` and throw `InvitationAcceptanceException`, reading
  the violation out of `details`. Before this they each had **no `try`/`catch` at all**, unlike
  `FirebaseSendAccountVerificationCallable` beside them.
- Both forms now `catch (error)` and map it.

The client-side refusal above them - "This invitation cannot be accepted here.", set when
`createIntent` throws - was left alone. It is already a sentence this app wrote and it already
promises nothing.

### Deliberately not done

**Nobody has looked at this on a device either.** The session instruction says to skip the
Android build and the Android emulator, so this is 19 tests and no eyes, exactly as the
sign-in repair was. **The debt is now two chunks deep and both are queued against the next
device run**: the sign-in screen first, then a refused invitation.

**The server was not touched and must not be.** The server is right to refuse; only the
sentence was wrong. `functions/src/staff/issuance.ts`, `acceptance.ts`, and `acceptancePolicy.ts`
were read and left alone.

**Findings 4 and 5 were not touched**, and are queued together as the next chunk. Finding 6 is
an environment limitation rather than a product defect and stays where it is - it is also why
this repair cannot be exercised end to end on the emulators, since the identity that hits
`versioned_proof_required` is precisely the one whose invitation email never arrives locally.

**The other surfaces that say "Please try again." were left alone**, and there are seven of
them - staff invitation, resend, cancellation, email replacement, staff status, staff update,

## The design system's token layer, wired to nothing - 2026-08-11

### Completed in this session

**`design.md` §11 step 1, taken additively**: every role, type role, spacing value, radius,
spring, duration and density value the specification names now exists in
`lib/ui/tokens.dart` as one `ThemeExtension`, `spiritTheme` registers it, and **nothing
reads it**. `DESIGN-AUDIT.md` §6 decision 1 is what made that the shape of the chunk: the
audit found that conforming the token layer in place would repaint roughly forty button call
sites, every caption, every card, every form and every chip at once, so step 1's "changes no
pixels" claim was unachievable as written. Making it additive restores the claim and makes
each later diff attributable to one component.

**The pass condition was an empty screenshot diff and it was measured rather than asserted.**
101 images, regenerated with the registration in place and again with it backed out, hashed
both times: byte-for-byte identical. See the test section for why that comparison had to be
run against a same-day set.

### The one question the token layer could not avoid, and the answer

`design.md` §3 gives `density.comfortable` and `density.compact` different body roles, but
`bodyMedium` is a single global value and **all 756 bare `Text(` call sites** in the migrated
tree resolve to it through `DefaultTextStyle`. One `ThemeData` cannot hold two body sizes, so
the token layer had to choose a structure - and the choice decides whether those 756 sites are
ever edited, and therefore the shape of steps 6 and 8. `DESIGN-AUDIT.md` §6 lists it as the
one item still needing a decision that "is not cosmetic in any sense".

**Answered by the product owner this session: a nested `Theme` per screen.** A back-office
screen wraps its subtree in a `Theme` built from `Theme.of(context).copyWith(...)` carrying the
compact `AppTokens` and a `bodyMedium` swapped to that density's body role. It keeps §3's
"density is a property of the surface, chosen by the screen" literal, and it edits none of the
756 sites. Reading the role explicitly at every call site was the other correct answer and was
declined because it eventually edits all of them.

**What is in this chunk is the deciding half, not the mechanism.** `AppDensity` holds both
value sets, `bodyRole` is the seam a nested `Theme` reads, and `pointerOnly` carries §3's rule
that a touch device never gets 32px targets whatever its width - as data, so the widget that
eventually resolves density cannot forget it. The widget itself arrives with the first compact
screen; step 1 changes no pixels and no screen is compact yet. A widget test exercises the seam
end to end, so the decision is proved rather than described.

### Two traps in `ThemeExtension`, one of which fails silently

1. **A field called `type` breaks the extension.** `ThemeExtension` declares
   `Object get type`, and it is the key `ThemeData.extensions` is stored and looked up under.
   The first draft of `AppTokens` held the type roles in a field named `type`, which overrides
   it - so the map would have been keyed by an `AppTypeRoles` instance and
   `Theme.of(context).extension<AppTokens>()` would have answered `null` for ever, with
   nothing failing to compile. The roles are reached as `typography`, the reason is written at
   the field, and a test asserts `AppTokens.dark.type == AppTokens`.
2. **A `Theme` built from a fresh `ThemeData` drops every extension.** `AppTokens.of` therefore
   **throws** rather than falling back to the defaults: a compact screen silently rendered at
   comfortable spacing looks like a layout bug rather than the wiring one it is. The
   `FlutterError` names `copyWith`, which is the fix, and a widget test asserts it.

### What the token layer proved about the specification

Step 1 exists to prove the roles map onto what exists before anything moves, and it found two
things in `design.md` and one in `DESIGN-AUDIT.md`. Both document corrections were made here,
in that order, because `design.md` §0 puts the document first.

1. **`text.primary`'s published contrast was rounded the wrong way.** §2.1's table said
   17.2 / 15.2 against base and raised; white on `#0D1F16` measures **17.147**, which rounds to
   17.1. The cell now reads 17.1. It is a rounding slip rather than a wrong colour, and it is
   worth recording because **`DESIGN-AUDIT.md` §1.3 recomputed 17.15, printed it beside the
   claim of 17.2, and concluded "The contrast figures in §2.1 are correct"** - so an independent
   recomputation had already looked straight at it. The test asserts the measurement matches the
   published figure to within 0.05 rather than merely clearing a floor, which is what caught it:
   the first run failed by 0.0528.
2. **The spacing scale was named two incompatible ways.** §2.3 described it by index -
   "`space.1` = 4 through `space.16` = 64" - while §3 asks for a section gap of `space.24` and
   §5.2 for padding of `space.20` and `space.16`, which are values. The two collide on the name
   `space.16`: 64 under one reading, 16 under the other. **Only the value reading is coherent**,
   because under the index reading §3 gives the *compact* density a larger section gap than the
   comfortable one, and `space.24` is not on the scale at all. §2.3 now states the value naming
   and says why. No value changed; the permitted set is the same ten.

### Three things recorded rather than resolved, because resolving them means inventing a value

1. **§2.1's container borders do not clear §9's 3:1 for a UI boundary.** Measured against
   `surface.base`: `border.subtle` 1.38, `border.strong` 1.97, and the five status borders
   between 1.38 and 2.04. §9 makes 3:1 pass/fail for "UI boundaries". **The one boundary that
   carries information on its own - the focus ring - clears it at 11.71**, and it is the only
   one §9 names with a value; a status is a container plus an icon plus a word, so its border is
   decoration rather than signal. That is an argument, not a resolution: either §9's boundary row
   means something narrower than every border, or ten colours need to become lighter. The values
   are pinned by tests and the ratios are in the file; nothing was invented.
2. **`mono` has no family, and cannot have one yet.** §2.2 opens with "One family - Roboto" and
   its last row says "monospace", and this app bundles no font at all - `lib/theme.dart` names
   none, deliberately, and the screenshot harness injects Roboto itself, which is why the harness
   is currently more branded than the app. So `mono` carries its 13 / 18 / 400 metrics, names no
   family like the eleven roles above it, and **is not yet fit for the job §2.2 gives it**. A
   test asserts every role's family is null, so the day the question is answered that assertion
   fails deliberately.
3. **`sage.100` `#A0BCAC` is the one §2.1 primitive this file does not carry.** No role consumes
   it. A colour nothing can reach is a value waiting to be picked up by a widget that needed a
   role instead, so it goes in when a role wants it, and the reason is written where it would
   have been.

### The screenshot diff needs a same-day baseline, and that is new

Regenerating the set produced **39 of 101 images differing from the set on disk**, which was
generated yesterday. **None of it is this chunk**: with the registration in place and with it
backed out, all 101 hash identically. The cause is the harness working as documented -
`tool/screenshots/fakes.dart` derives its business dates from `DateTime.now()` because the daily
summary and reconciliation compute a business date the same way and read by exact path, and
`screenshots/README.md` says in as many words that re-running on another day produces the same

The consequence is a working practice rather than a defect: **a step's screenshot diff is only
attributable if the baseline was generated the same day**, or the review will show 39 moved
images nobody changed. Every migration step's step 4 depends on this. Recorded in `PLAN.md`
under standing traps.
