## Two contradictions closed, and five components written down before anyone builds them - 2026-08-16

A short follow-on to the batch above, in the same session. The product owner was asked the three
blocking questions it raised and answered all three: **drop "filled" from §7**, **keep the section
head at `title.md` and correct §2.2**, and **draft the five component specifications**.

### The two amendments, and why neither moved a pixel

`design.md` is at **v0.6**. Both changes went to the *document*, because in both cases the code was
already resolving a contradiction the document could not see.

**§7's filled destructive confirm never existed.** §2.1's `action.destructive` row is a transparent
container with a `#FF5C6C` label and border; there is no filled variant anywhere. §7 asked for one
in a single word. The two exits were a fifth action role — which needs a container colour and a
label colour that clears §9 on it — or deleting the word. The word went. **The rule that replaces
it is worth more than the deletion**: a confirm button takes the tier of the action that opened the
dialog, which makes §8 rule 4's "the verb persists" hold in shape as well as in words and stops
twelve call sites each choosing.

**§2.2's section head was the half that was wrong.** `title.lg` is *also* `PageHeader`'s screen
title at §4.1's `compact` band, so a section head sharing the role put two headings of identical
weight on a phone, one under the other — which is what §7's "Title appears once" exists to prevent.
Eleven migrated screens had been drawing `title.md` since step 6. The row moved. A band-dependent
answer was considered and refused: a heading whose *role* changes on resize is a rule nobody could
look up, and §4.3's own principle is that a **form** changes with the band while the role does not.

**The status line was corrected in the same pass.** It had read v0.4 through the whole of v0.5, and
`PLAN.md` carried it as the product owner's to fix. A specification whose header disagrees with its
own changelog is the failure this document exists to prevent, one level up.

**Nothing in `lib/` changed except two comments**, both of which described a contradiction that no
longer exists. Suite unchanged; no image moved. That is the outcome an amendment of this kind should
have, and it is the evidence that the code had the better reading of both rows.

### The proposal

`DESIGN-PROPOSAL-COMPONENTS.md`, a new file, **explicitly not binding and explicitly not built**.
Five components, each with the call-site count measured on the day rather than carried:
`ConfirmDialog` **12** across 9 files, `FilterChipBar` **20** across 5, `QuantityStepper` 1,
`AppSheet` 1, `RollingNumber` 0.

**It proposes an order that is not §5.1's priority order**, and says why: §5.1 gives
`QuantityStepper` priority 1 because the defect is bad, and the count says `ConfirmDialog` and
`FilterChipBar` are the whole app while the other three are the till alone.

**Three things it refuses to answer, flagged ⚠ rather than decided.** Whether a confirmation is
dismissible by its scrim; the **chip radius**, where §2.3 says `radius.sm` and the theme's
`chipTheme` says `StadiumBorder` and `PLAN.md` has carried the disagreement since 2026-08-13; and
whether the till's tender chooser is a filter at all — it is drawn as `ChoiceChip`s but a filter
narrows a list you are looking at and a tender is a fact you are recording, and it carries a rule no
filter has, which is that there is deliberately no default.

**Two things it argues against itself on, which is the point of writing it down.** `AppSheet` is the
only one of the five that is genuinely hard — §2.4 asks a sheet to settle on release *velocity* and
`DraggableScrollableSheet` settles on position, so it cannot be a restyle — and it is proposed as
its own chunk, built last. And `RollingNumber` **fixes nothing**: no accessibility failure, no
missing capability, no duplicated code. The proposal says to cut it if anything else needs the time.

### The rule worth keeping out of this one

**When the document and the code disagree, find out which one is resolving a contradiction.** Both
amendments here looked at first like the code drifting from the spec, and both turned out to be the
spec contradicting itself somewhere else — §7 against §2.1, and §2.2 against §7. A session that had
"corrected" the code towards the document would have shipped two regressions and called them
compliance.

## Five components, seven decisions, and the reskin runs out of things it can do alone - 2026-08-16

**Fifteen commits in one session, at the product owner's direction to "finish up the reskin".** It
did not finish, and what it reached instead is a cleaner statement of what is left: every §11 step
except **12** is now either done or blocked on nothing, and 12 is blocked on six decisions this
session deliberately did not take.

**`design.md` moved three versions - v0.6, v0.7, v0.8 - and eleven product-owner decisions are in
them.** That is the headline for a future reader: the specification changed more than the code did,
because most of what was blocking was a document contradicting itself or asking for something it had
not defined.

### The three amendments, and why each one is the document's fault rather than the code's

**v0.6, two self-contradictions.** §7 asked for a *filled* destructive confirm and §2.1 defines no
filled destructive container - the word was withdrawn rather than a fifth action role added. §2.2
gave a section head `title.lg`, which is *also* `PageHeader`'s screen title at `compact`, so a phone
got two headings of identical weight and §7's "Title appears once" had nothing to stand on; the row
moved to `title.md`, which eleven migrated screens had already drawn since step 6.

**v0.7, six decisions in one pass.** A chip is `radius.pill`, closing a disagreement with
`chipTheme` the code had carried since 2026-08-13. The app **bundles Roboto and Roboto Mono** - it
bundled nothing at all before this. The eight §6.4 assets are **Lottie, sourced** rather than
natively drawn or authored in Rive. The device tier stops gating the assets. **There is a character
and it is a shop cat.** And §4.4 gained the home's top bar while §5.2 gained `ShiftBanner` and
`SyncIndicator`, both drawn from the product owner's own mockups.

**v0.8, one sentence and the most expensive one in the file.** A sheet settles on the **nearest
detent** rather than on release velocity. Flutter settles on position; honouring the old rule meant
hand-writing a gesture recogniser and a settling simulation that §10 says no test here can prove.
What the rule was protecting survives - follows the finger, rubber-bands, more than two positions,
dragged rather than tapped.

**Every one of those amendments left the code alone.** v0.6 changed two comments. v0.7's chip row
changed nothing, because the theme was already right. That is the property an amendment of this kind
should have, and it is the evidence the code had the better reading.

### The seven components

| Component | Call sites | What it replaced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ConfirmDialog` | 8 | Twelve hand-built `AlertDialog`s, each choosing surface, radius, order and tier again |
| `FilterChipBar` | 5 files, 20 chips | Five hand-built `Wrap`s, **none of which honoured §4.3** |
| `EmptyState` | 6 | `No products found.` and five more bare sentences |
| `QuantityStepper` | 1 | §5.1's "minus + delete, no plus" |
| `AppSheet` | 2 | `showModalBottomSheet` with Material's own chrome |
| `ShiftBanner` | 1 | A panel with five controls and seven lines of prose |
| `SyncIndicator` | 2 | §5.1's "five-line offline queue list" |

**§4.3 is the one that was actually missing on the chips, and it is worth stating separately from the
styling.** That table gives `FilterChips` "horizontal scroll, one line" at `compact` and "wrap" above
it. No screen did this - all five wrapped at every band, so a phone showing three choosers spent
eight rows on filters before the figures they filter began.

### The confirm's tier is inherited, and that is the rule worth carrying

A dialog opened by a `destructive` button confirms with `destructive`; one opened by a `primary`
button confirms with `primary`. §8 rule 4 asks that the verb persists from button to dialog to
confirmation, and a confirm that changed *appearance* on the way would break that in shape while
keeping it in words. It also removes the one decision twelve call sites were each making separately.

### Six defects that only a rendering could find

The session's own tally, because they are the argument for §10's "the screenshot diff is the review
artefact" and every one of them passed its widget tests first.

1. **A `StatLine` on the compact cart bar overflowed at 411.** It is a label column and a
   right-aligned figure column sized for a card; a strip with one figure has no column to line up
   with.
2. **`QuantityStepper`'s well was sized from the till's ceiling of 1,000,000** - seven digits, a
   215-pixel control, and about 77 pixels left for a product name inside a 420-wide cart pane. Every
   line wrapped to four rows. Capped at four digits.
3. **The stepper's error sat inside its 76-pixel well**, wrapped to six lines, and shoved the two
   buttons out of alignment with the number they change.
4. **An empty label string still reserved its sixteen-pixel row**, putting both buttons above the
   number. `AppFieldWell` draws no label row for an empty label now.
5. **The empty-state mark's flaps pivoted about the centre of the top edge**, so they splayed from
   one point and the box drew as a crown.
6. **"Signed in as Owner" appeared twice on the home** once the role reached the header. `design.md`
   v0.7 predicted exactly this for the business name and said what to do.

**Two of those - 2 and 3 - surfaced as *tests failing to find the save button*.** The symptom was
three steps from the cause, and no widget test could have named it.

### The Lottie files, audited rather than eyeballed

Four landed, 62KB of a 120KB budget, and each was read for its actual colour count:

| File | Colours | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `approved.json` (the cat) | 1 - pure black | line art, one delegate tints it |
| `upload.json` | 2 | line art |
| `sync.json` | 3, none of them this palette's | tintable, three delegates |
| ~~`empty.json`~~ | 7 beiges and oranges | **failed the rule, removed** |

**Asset 6 is drawn instead.** The sourced file failed, and the alternative already in the repository -
`images/empty.gif` - was measured rather than judged: **244KB** against a 120KB budget for every
external asset combined, **150 x 150** of raster, **252 colours** so it cannot be tinted at all, and
**77 frames looping forever** where §6.4's budget reads "idle loops on an operational screen: 0" and
an empty state is a screen somebody is reading. `_BoxPainter` is sixty lines, has no payload, no
licence, and reads both its colours from the theme on every build.

**§6.4 now splits by what an asset *is***: a state indicator nobody needs to be charmed by is drawn,
and anything with character is sourced.

### The font, which was the oldest untrue sentence in the repository

`lib/theme.dart` named no family, so every string rendered in whatever face the device defaulted to,
and §2.2's `mono` role carried its metrics while naming nothing - meaning SKUs and receipt numbers,
the one place §2.2 insists on monospace, rendered proportionally. **The screenshot harness injects
Roboto itself**, so every capture ever reviewed was of a more branded app than the one that shipped.

Bundling it moved **zero images**, which is the proof: the app now matches its own pictures rather
than the other way round.

**One assertion failed and it was written to fail.** `tokens_test.dart` read "no type role names a
family, including mono", with a comment saying that when the family was settled this would be the
test that broke, deliberately. It broke.

**`mono` still has no readers**, and that is the half left: the role is defined, has metrics, now has
a face, and no screen applies it.

### A blocker I called wrongly, and the correction

**I told the product owner the home's top bar needed data the route was not given, and estimated an
hour of plumbing.** They pushed back. Half of it was wrong.

`CheckoutPendingEvidencePanel` **already held the counts** - it reads them itself and always did. So
restyling *that widget* into `SyncIndicator` plus `SyncQueuePanel` is a pure visual change, and the
badge is then in reach of the toolbar without the number being hoisted anywhere. There was never an
hour in it.

What *was* blocked is only the member's name, and the fix is smaller than the estimate too: Firebase
has `currentUser.displayName` loaded already, so the shell takes a callback and hands it down. It is
frequently null, so the subtitle falls back to the role alone.

**The lesson is the one this file keeps relearning from the other side.** A coupling that looks like
"this needs a new read" is worth grepping before it is worth writing down: the data was one widget
away, and the widget was already reading it.

### The shift, and the two decisions that were the product owner's

The old panel showed up to five controls and seven lines at once. `ShiftBanner` gives one status, one
line, one action - so the rewiring was a redistribution, and two of the calls were taken by the
product owner rather than guessed:

- **The counted-cash field lives in the sheet**, not on the banner. That makes closing a two-surface
  operation, which is the stated cost.
- **Close shift is the banner's action and Cancel cash count is in the sheet**, because §1 argues a
  reversal should not sit beside the thing it reverses.

**Together they mean the banner's *Close shift* opens the sheet rather than closing outright.** §8
rule 4 makes that read correctly - the verb persists onto the control that finishes it - and it is
recorded here because it is a real extra step on the app's most consequential operation.

**The third decision was taken by rule rather than by picking**: a warning promotes the detail line.
An error, a shift open elsewhere, or unsynchronized sales become the line and turn the status
`attention`. `PLAN.md` records a real device run where this surface said "Confirmed sales: 0" beside a
drawer holding two unsynchronized sales, so that warning had to keep a place on the surface.

**One copy defect introduced and caught**: the unsynchronized-sales sentence was reworded while being
moved. Moving a fact between surfaces is a visual change and rewording it is not; the sentence is
restored verbatim.

**And the `ensureVisible` trap again, from the direction that hides it.** The sheet's controls start
below its `half` detent, so a tap on *Close shift* landed on nothing, **silently never reached the
server**, and the test failed three lines later on an unrelated assertion.

### What this session did not do, and why

- **Step 12** - the accessibility audit - is blocked on six decisions the product owner has not taken.
- **The `mono` sweep** was deferred by the product owner explicitly.
- **Printing** was raised and is still blocked on the print service's interface, which has not been

### The rule worth keeping out of all of this

**When the document and the code disagree, find out which one is resolving a contradiction.** Three
amendments this session looked at first like the code drifting from the specification, and all three
turned out to be the specification contradicting itself somewhere else - §7 against §2.1, §2.2
against §7, §2.4 against what the framework can do. A session that had "corrected" the code towards
the document would have shipped three regressions and called them compliance.

## Three states, a dialog that holds a form, and a page bar that stops moving - 2026-08-16

**The queued chunk was the whole remaining tail of the reskin, batched as one at the product owner's
direction.** Five items. **Four landed; item 4, `MotionAsset` and the Lottie files, did not** - see
its own section for why that is a stopping point rather than a failure, and for what the next session
inherits.

`PLAN.md` said "if it splits, **split it after item 2**, because items 1 and 2 together close every
unmigrated surface in the app". That line was right about the split point and wrong about which side
of it the work would run out on: items 1, 2, 3 and most of 5 fit, and the one that did not is the one
with a file format in it.

**What it finishes:** §11 step **7**, which had been "all but `RollingNumber`" since the previous
session, and the last three unmigrated surfaces in the app. **Every route, every dialog and every
full-page state in the migrated tree is now drawn from the token layer.**

### Item 1 - `LoadingState` and `ErrorState`, and the guard was the real call site

Both are in `lib/ui/states.dart` beside `EmptyState`, which is now three components in one file
because a screen that has one of them has all three: a read either has not answered, answered with
nothing, or failed.

**`ErrorState` is §7's *failure to read a record* pattern, all four parts of it.** *"`status.problem`
badge, the record's identifier in `mono`, a plain statement of what could not be read, and - this
matters - what is still true despite it."* What it replaced on `TenantBootstrapFailure` had **one** of
the four: a 48px `Icons.error_outline` - hue and a glyph, no word, which is precisely what §9 rules
out - two unstyled `Text`s at Material's defaults, and four hardcoded numbers.

**`status` is a parameter, and `PlatformRouteUnavailable` is why.** §7 writes the pattern for a read
that failed and §2.1's `problem` is "difference found, **unreadable**, out of stock". Nothing failed
on that screen: this build has no platform console, which §2.1's `neutral` - "archived, retired,
closed" - describes exactly. Painting it red would send somebody looking for a fault that does not
exist.

**No animated mark on either, and that is §6.4 quoting itself.** Its banned list reads *"animated
illustrations on error and failed-to-read states. A person looking at '2 sale lines could not be read'
needs information, not a sad mascot."* The badge does the work the illustration would have.

**`LoadingState` requires its message, and the routing shell is the argument.** §5.1's row is "bare
`CircularProgressIndicator`" and the word doing the work is *bare*. One `_RoutingProgress` covered
**four** phases - `waitingForAuth`, `bootstrapping`, `openingTenant`, `signingOut` - with one
identical spinner, and only one of those is worth waiting for if you meant one of the others. It takes
a sentence per phase now.

**The surface that actually mattered was not on the queue entry's list.** `PLAN.md` named
`TenantBootstrapFailure` and `PlatformRouteUnavailable`. The bigger one is **`TenantRouteGuard`'s
three defaults**, which every guarded route in the app renders unless it passes its own: a bare
spinner, and two sentences - `Tenant access unavailable.` and `Tenant data unavailable.` - that named
a *tenant* to a shopkeeper. That is §8 rule 1, and the step-11 copy pass could not see it because it
greps screens rather than the frame under them. **Nine assertions across eight test files were right
about the old copy and were updated.**

**One sentence in the queue entry was wrong and is corrected here.** It said the two components would
"replace the bare `CircularProgressIndicator` **and the `SizedBox.shrink()`** that every
`TenantRouteGuard` currently passes as a loading state". Only two panels pass `shrink()` - the shift
panel and the checkout evidence strip - and **both do it deliberately**: the guard's loading widget
replaces the whole subtree, so a panel that re-reads on a signal would blink a spinner over content it
already has. That is a standing trap in `PLAN.md`, and the `??` in the guard is now commented so a
later session does not "finish the migration" by taking them away.

**Three platform queues got all three states at once**, which was not on the list either. The
archival, lifecycle and review queues each hand-built a loading spinner, an error column and an empty
sentence - **nine surfaces, three components**, and they are the reason `09a` through `09d` all moved.

**Neither surface became an `AppScaffold`, and that is a decision rather than an unfinished
migration.** `AppScaffold` requires a title and draws a `PageHeader` for it; these are not pages and
have no name. Giving them one would put a heading above a centred state and break §7's "title appears
once" in the only way that section did not anticipate - by inventing the title. The three remaining
raw `Scaffold`s in the shell are hosts for a state, not unmigrated routes, and `PLAN.md`'s step-5a
entry is corrected to say so.

### Item 2 - `AppDialog`, and one dialog surface instead of two

**`DESIGN-PROPOSAL-COMPONENTS.md` §1 split this out on purpose**, and the entry is worth quoting
because it is the reason this was cheap: *"`ConfirmDialog` refuses children - it takes strings and two
actions - and the three form-bearing dialogs stay `AlertDialog` until somebody specifies `AppDialog`.
Flagging this rather than quietly widening the component is the whole point of writing it down
first."*

**Every value in it is read off a row `design.md` already has** except one, and that one is derived
rather than invented: the **width**. §4.3's `Form` row is "single column, **720 max**" and §4.2 gives
"reading and forms" the same 720, so `AppDialog.maximumWidth` is `AppLayout.reading`. What it replaces
is `SizedBox(width: 440)` in the business switcher - the only width any dialog in this app ever
stated, chosen by one call site for itself, and matching nothing in the document.

**`ConfirmDialog` moved onto the same frame rather than keeping a copy of it.** The four surface
values - `surface.overlay`, `radius.lg`, `space.24`, the trailing `Wrap` of actions - were about to be
written a second time, which is how a system ends up with two dialogs that differ by four pixels
nobody chose. `_DialogFrame` is private, both components use it, and **`ConfirmDialog`'s rendering is
unchanged**: its ten tests and its six captures all hold, which is the evidence.

**Four call sites, not the three the queue entry named.** Correcting a product, the business switcher,
the set-default confirmation, **and the reconciliation amend-shift dialog**, which no list had. The
stock-adjustment dialog the entry named had already become a `ConfirmDialog` in the previous session -
so the entry was working from a count that was one session stale in both directions.

**The set-default dialog takes no title and no actions**, and that is the case a component which
always drew a title row would get wrong: `TenantDefaultForm` carries its own heading and its own two
controls, so the dialog around it is the surface and nothing else. §7's "title appears once" arriving
inside a dialog.

**Two of the four stop being dismissible by a tap on the scrim, and that is a decision rather than a
side effect.** `ConfirmDialog` already records the rule: a stray tap outside a *question* lands on
cancel, which is the safe answer. A stray tap outside a **form** throws away everything typed into it.
`DESIGN-PROPOSAL-COMPONENTS.md` §1's open question 1 proposed exactly this split, and it is recorded
in `PLAN.md` for ratification rather than buried here.

**`showAppDialog` also paints §2.1's `surface.scrim`**, where four call sites had been getting
Material's `black54` by saying nothing.

**The parameter is `content`, not `child`, and the reason is a lint.**
`sort_child_properties_last` requires a `child` argument to be written last, and on these call sites
the child is a hundred-line form with two buttons after it - so the lint would push `actions` below a
block nobody scrolls past. `AlertDialog` calls the same slot `content` for the same reason.

### Item 3 - `RollingNumber`, and §6.3 turning out to be a layout requirement

**§6.2 gives it two rows and only one of them has anywhere to go.** *"Total recalculates - digits
roll; only changed digits move, `spring.smooth`"* is the till's total. *"Quantity change - digit rolls
vertically"* has **no call site**: the only quantity a person changes is inside `QuantityStepper`,
which is an editable `AppTextField` they type into, and rolling glyphs under a caret is not a thing
that can be done. `RollingNumberSpring.snappy` carries the row so it stays findable; nothing reads it.

**The first version was wrong and six checkout tests said so in one run.** It returned the roll
*instead of* the `Text`, so `checkout-total` did not exist while the spring was moving - and
`checkout_cart_panel_test.dart`'s `_settle` is six pumps of 10ms, which is well inside
`spring.smooth`. The tests were right and the component was wrong: **a total that cannot be read
mid-roll is a total that is briefly not stated**, which is §6.3 in as many words. It draws the
committed figure on every frame now, painted or not, with the roll as an overlay above it. **Not one
of the seven existing `StatTile` call sites had to change**, and `14-new-sale` and
`15-new-sale-with-a-cart` did not move a pixel - which is the proof that at rest the component is
exactly the `Text` it replaced.

**`Opacity` drops its subtree's semantics at zero.** So the first fix held for the eye and failed for
a screen reader - the reader §6.3's rule is really about. `alwaysIncludeSemantics: true` is not a
formality on this component.

**A roll between two figures of different length is wider than the figure it covers.** `KES 120.50` →
`KES 0.00` pads to ten positions over an eight-character box: a **57-pixel** `RenderFlex` overflow,
which is exactly two glyphs of `numeric.hero`. The overlay is clipped and left-aligned now, so the
figure's left edge stays where the layout put it and the positions rolling away spill off the end.

**One test prediction was wrong in the component's favour**, which is a first for this file.
`99.00` → `100.00` was written expecting all six positions to move; it moves **three**. Right-aligned
padding leaves `.00` under `.00`, so the minor units hold still and only the shillings roll.

**Interruptibility is a generation counter, not a restart.** The drive's target is an integer index
into a list of strings; a change arriving mid-roll appends and retargets, so the spring carries
through the intervening generation from its live position and velocity. The list is pruned to one
entry every time the spring settles, which is what stops a till that rings four hundred sales a shift
from holding four hundred strings.

**The compact cart bar's total deliberately does not roll.** Its string alternates between a figure
and the sentence `Total unavailable`, and it sits in an `Expanded` that has to ellipsize at 411 - a
defect that file already records against `StatLine`. One rolling total per till.

### Item 5 - `Pagination` and `AppTabs`, and `LedgerEntry` having nowhere to go

**`Pagination` is thirteen screens, two shapes, two tiers and two label sets.** Eleven drew a `Wrap`
of two buttons labelled `Previous page` / `Next page`; two drew a `Row` with `Previous` / `Page N` /
`Next` at `tertiary`. §5.1's row is "low-contrast Previous / **Page N** / Next", so eleven of the
thirteen were never the component this document describes - **they never told a person which page they
were on.**

**The bar always draws both controls now.** Eleven hid `Previous` on the first page and `Next` on the
last, so the control a person was about to press slid sideways when the other one vanished. §5's
matrix has a `disabled` row for exactly this; the callbacks are untouched, a disabled control does
what an absent one did, and **two tests that asserted the control was absent now assert it is present
and disabled** - the stronger of the two claims.

**`secondary`, and the tree had already decided.** `stock_adjustment_panel` had written the reasoning
into its own comment - *"§2.1 permits exactly one primary per screen region and on this route that is
`Adjust stock`; 'Next page' competing with it for the eye is the tier system not being applied rather
than a taste call. The same repoint is made on every paginated feed"* - and eleven of the thirteen
already drew it. The catalog and the bulk route were the outliers at `tertiary` and moved to match.

**One finding the sweep surfaced:** the stock panel's `Manual adjustments` button was sitting *inside*
the page bar's `Wrap`. It is not pagination; it opens another route. It was there because the `Wrap`
was where the buttons happened to be, and a component owning its own form is what made that visible.

**The labels stay noun phrases, and that was settled rather than deferred.** §5.2 says a button label
is "always a verb phrase naming the effect", and `Previous page` names a destination. The reading that
survives is that §5.2's rule is written about controls that *act on a record* - *Save*, *Correct*,
*Retire* - and for a navigation control the destination **is** the effect. Keeping the copy also keeps
thirteen screens' strings unchanged, which is the difference between a component migration and a copy
pass.

**`AppTabs` fixes a §9 failure nobody had listed.** A Material text tab is **46** logical pixels high
- `_kTabHeight` in the SDK - and §9's touch-target row is 48 × 48, pass/fail. The four tabs on the
platform route have been two short since they were written, and no audit caught it because §9's own
"known current failures" list names `Correct` / `Retire` and `Previous` / `Next` and stops. The height
comes from `density.minimumTapTarget` now, so it is the same 48 every other control is measured
against.

**Its indicator weight is read rather than chosen.** `design.md` states exactly one stroke width
anywhere - §2.1's focus ring at 2px - so the indicator takes that token instead of Material's
coincidentally-equal default. If the ring ever moves, the indicator moves with it, which a literal `2`
would not.

**It wraps `TabBar` rather than redrawing one**, on exactly the argument `AppScaffold` made about
`AppBar`: `TabBar` owns the `TabController` handshake, the indicator's travel and the scroll-into-view
of a selected tab, and hand-drawing it would move selection behaviour into a visual change.

**`LedgerEntry` was not built, and the reason is that it has no call site.** §5.1 gives it "hand-built
ledger rows", and **all five** of the screens that had them - the product ledger, the movement feed,
the adjustment feed, the activity log and the shift-amendment feed - became `RecordList`s in step 6's
sweep on 2026-08-13. **§4.3's contract absorbed §5.1's row and nobody noticed.** Building it now would
put a component in `PLAN.md`'s "Built, tested, and still unreachable" table *on purpose*, which is the
one thing that table exists to prevent. Whether §5.1 should lose the row is the product owner's and is
recorded as an open decision.

### Item 4 - `MotionAsset`, not built, and what the next session inherits

**Stopped rather than started badly.** It is the only item of the five with a *file format* in it, and
the reading done for it turned up a question that cannot be answered by writing code:

- `approved.json` is one colour and `upload.json` is two, so a single wildcard value delegate tints
  either. **`sync.json` has three** - `#00B8FF`, `#F4B624` and white - and `assets/lottie/README.md`
  already records that it "needs three". A `lottie` value delegate addresses a **named layer**, so
  three delegates means knowing three layer names inside that file; a wildcard would flatten all three
  of the sync glyph's states into one colour, which is the opposite of what asset 4 is for.
- Two of the three call sites - `SyncIndicator` and the top bar's queue button - are components that
  shipped on 2026-08-16 with their own matrices and their own captures, so wiring an asset into them
  re-shoots those images.

**Nothing in this session was blocked on it, and nothing else in §11 is either.** It is queued behind
printing at the product owner's direction, with the layer-name question named - which is more than the
entry it replaces had.

### One mistake worth recording, because it nearly went into the commit

**`dart format lib/` reformatted the whole legacy tree.** 124 files under `lib/pos/**`,
`lib/screens/**`, `lib/services/**`, `lib/model/**` and `lib/constants/**` - every one of them
read-only under `claude.md` hard rule 3 - came back modified, and `flutter analyze` over `lib` jumped
from 475 to 491 while the churn was in the tree. They were reverted from a list built by subtracting
this chunk's own edits from `git diff --name-only`.

**The lesson is one word in a command.** `dart format lib/` and `dart format <the files you edited>`
look equally harmless and are not. Every earlier chunk in this file formatted named files; this one
reached for the directory because it had edited twenty-two of them, and a directory in this repository
contains 410 files a chunk may not touch.

**A second, smaller version of the same mistake cost a full-suite run.** The screenshot baseline dance
moves this chunk's new files aside and back; the restore keyed them by **basename**, and
`test/ui/pagination_test.dart` and `tool/screenshots/pagination_test.dart` share one. Three unit-test
files came back as their harness namesakes and the suite failed with `Method not found:
'screenshotCase'`. The three were rewritten. **Key a save-and-restore by path, never by basename** -
this repository has three pairs that collide, and it will have more.

## Printing gets its plumbing, and the exclusion that blocked it was five days stale - 2026-08-17

**The chunk is printing, Phase 1, and the correction is worth more than the code.** Four consecutive
chunks carried an exclusion reading *"blocked on the print service's interface, which has not been
shared"*. `docs/printer_transport.md` has been in this repository since **2026-08-11**, committed in
`1262476` alongside `design.md` and `claude.md`, and it is a complete 384-line design: the seam, the
platform matrix, the configuration document, the durable job queue, the failure vocabulary and the
required tests.

**Nobody opened it for five days because the exclusion list said not to.** That is precisely the
failure mode `prompt.md`'s "do not silently inherit the exclusion list" was written about, and it is
the first time it has actually fired. The product owner's own answer when asked was *"I already
shared the interface and we picked what we deemed best from it"* — which is what the document is.

### What was built

Four files for the transport, because §1.1 asks for four:

- **`checkout_print_transport_base.dart`** — the contract, and nothing else. No `dart:io`, no
  Flutter, no state, so both platform implementations and every test fake depend on it without
  dragging a platform in. `PrinterEndpoint`, `PrinterTransportKind`,
  `PrinterTransportCapability`, `PrinterTransportException`, `PrinterTransportCode` and the
  `PrinterTransport` interface.
- **`checkout_print_transport_io.dart`** — one `dart:io` socket per job, covering all five Phase 1
  targets.
- **`checkout_print_transport_unsupported.dart`** — throws `transport_unsupported`. §1.1's whole
  point: *"a new platform target fails loudly at first print instead of quietly dropping
  receipts"*.
- **`checkout_print_transport.dart`** — the conditional-import shim. **There is no `js_interop`
  branch and that is not an omission**: §1.1's example lists one, but a conditional import naming a
  file that does not exist will not compile, so `_web` gets its branch on the day it gets its file.
  Until then the *default* import is the stub, which is the same outcome — a web build throws rather
  than dropping a receipt. **Forty lines that make Phase 2 a new file instead of a refactor of every
  call site.**

Plus **`checkout_print_configuration.dart`**, the tenant document, and **`checkout_print_jobs.dart`**,
the durable queue, and **`checkout_print_failures.dart`**, the eight codes as eight sentences.

### The four decisions inside it that are worth defending

**A connect timeout is inferred from elapsed time, not from an errno.** `docs/printer_transport.md`
§2 records, verified against the borrowed repo at commit `95b07d4`, that its `on TimeoutException`
around `Socket.connect(timeout:)` is a **dead branch** — the SDK throws `SocketException` (errno
10060 on Windows) — so its more helpful message never renders. Reading `osError` instead would trade
one platform assumption for another: the code differs on POSIX, and when the SDK's own timer fires
first there is no code at all. **Elapsed time is the one signal that means the same thing
everywhere**, so `_open` records a start instant and compares.

**`flush` is where a stalled printer is discovered, not `add`.** `Socket.add` is buffered and returns
immediately, so a transport that timed only the write call would report success for a payload still
sitting in the send buffer against a printer with its cover open. The timeout wraps `flush`.

**Serialization is keyed by endpoint, not by job.** One ESC/POS printer accepts one connection on
`:9100` and two concurrent jobs interleave or get refused — but a shop with a counter printer and a
kitchen printer should not have the second wait on the first. The mutex is the outbox's own
`_operationTails` pattern with the address as the key, and there is a test for each half.

**The reprint writes its audit line *before* re-queueing.** A reprint that was not recorded never
happens; the opposite order loses the audit line exactly when it matters, which is a crash
mid-reprint. There is a test that a refused audit leaves the job `printed`.

### Two traps the tests found, both real

**A `Future`-returning method that throws synchronously.** `enqueue` validated its receipt number and
its payload before returning a future, so `await queue.enqueue(...)` inside a `try` caught it and
`queue.enqueue(...).catchError(...)` did not. Two tests written the natural way failed, and the fix
is one keyword: the method is `async`. `reprint`'s transition guard had the same shape and moved with
it.

**A record that did not equal its own persisted form.** Hive stores `createdAtMs`, so a re-read loses
the microseconds a `DateTime` carries — and a caller comparing what `enqueue` returned with what
`read` answers found two different timestamps for one job. The clock is truncated to the millisecond
the record stores, in `_now()`, so the in-memory record and the durable one are the same value.
**This is the kind of defect that never fails loudly**: it would have surfaced one day as a
deduplication that quietly stopped deduplicating.

### What is deliberately not built

**The receipt body**, and this is the document's own scope line rather than a shortcut:
*"In scope: getting a finished byte payload to a printer… Out of scope: building the bytes."*
`flutter_esc_pos_utils`' `Generator` builds them and is already a dependency. What does not exist is
the **layout** — and `design.md` §12 is explicit that a receipt "is a design surface with its own
constraints and will not inherit from this document". Inventing one here would be inventing the
product owner's design.

**The consequence is stated rather than discovered: this slice is built and unreachable.** Nothing on
the sale path calls `enqueue`, because nothing produces bytes. It enters `PLAN.md`'s "Built, tested,
and still unreachable" table with exactly one bounded reason and the reason queued, which is the good
kind of entry that table records — the life `updateProduct` had for one day.

**Phase 2, the web transport.** The shim resolves to the stub and printing throws
`transport_unsupported` on web. Correct deferred behaviour.

**`receipt_reprinted` as an audit event.** `audit_log.dart` states that "server code is its only
writer", so it is a Cloud Function and a server chunk. `HivePrintJobQueue.reprint` takes the seam it will
land on as a **required** argument, so a reprint cannot happen unaudited by omission.

**Deleting the legacy print paths.** `pos/pos.dart`, `Receipt_service.dart` and
`thermal_printer_service.dart` are the only remaining record of the Flask contract in §5, and
`docs/printer_transport.md` §10 decision 3 says Phase 1 lands *before* they go. They are also under
the read-only hard rule.

### One decision the next chunk must have answered

**`docs/printer_transport.md` §10 decision 1 — one printer per device, or several?** That document
calls it "the most consequential question left". This chunk built the shape the document *assumes* —
the endpoint is tenant configuration — and the two items above it are safe either way. Kitchen-plus-
counter routing makes the endpoint a **per-job property**, which changes the durable record rather
than just the transport. The job record already carries `host` and `port` per job, so the migration is
smaller than it would have been; what it would change is where they come from.

### The rules needed no change, and that was checked rather than assumed

`firestore.rules` already carries `match /configuration/{documentId}` with read for active staff and
write for owner and admin, so `configuration/printer` is covered by the same wildcard
`configuration/checkout` is. **The queue entry written for this chunk predicted a rules change and a
rules test and was wrong**, which is worth recording next to the six mis-counted figures: the
prediction was made from the shape of the work rather than from the file.

```text
lib/checkout/checkout_print_transport_io.dart           new
lib/checkout/checkout_print_transport_unsupported.dart  new
```

`lib/` was edited except the barrel.

### Tests

```text
flutter test --no-pub --concurrency=1 --reporter=failures-only
+2146: All tests passed!
```

**+47, and every one of §9's nine required coverage lines has a test**: endpoint validation including
eleven hosts that must be refused; every failure code asserted by code rather than message; the
`dart:io` transport against a real `ServerSocket` that accepts, that stalls, and that refuses; the
unsupported stub throwing rather than no-oping; every legal transition and the illegal ones; two
`send` calls for one receipt producing one delivery; two concurrent jobs to one endpoint never
overlapping; a malformed durable record throwing rather than resetting and an absent configuration
refusing rather than defaulting; and a job interrupted in `printing` resuming as the same job.

**The recovery test simulates the crash by writing the record rather than by hanging a transport**,
and that is the honest simulation: after a process dies the only thing that exists is the box, and a
test that kept the original `run` alive would still be holding the endpoint mutex it died inside. A
separate test proves that a real send does leave the record in `printing` for the whole of its
duration, which is the state the first one starts from.

**The four server suites ran after the previous commit and before this one**, clearing the carry
counter from its limit of 2: functions **409**, rules **161**, reconciliation **10**, invitations
**23**.

**Both integration suites had to be run twice, and the reason is a trap this file already carries.**
The first pass piped each suite through `tail -14`, which kept `cancelled / skipped / todo /
duration_ms` and cut `ℹ tests N` and `ℹ pass N` off the top of the block. `PLAN.md`'s standing trap
is explicit that an exit code proves nothing here — a Firestore port collision makes a suite run no
test at all and still exit 0 — so "exited successfully" was not evidence and the two were run again
for their counts. **A filter that keeps the wrong four lines is the same defect as trusting the exit
code**, and the second run's command greps for `^ℹ` instead.

## A receipt gets a body, and a shop name with a macron stops crashing the sale - 2026-08-17

**The chunk is printing's second half — the receipt body and the piece that dispatches it — taken at
the product owner's direction to "finish printing" after the plumbing landed the same day.** Two of
its four items ran. **The two that did not are surfaces**, and they are named at the end.

**Two assumptions were stated rather than blocked on**, because the product owner reaffirmed the
request after both were raised:

1. **`design.md` §12 says a receipt "will not inherit from this document".** Read here as *the token
   layer does not apply to paper*, not as *no layout may exist*. A thermal printer has no colour, no
   radius and no type scale; it has a column count, three emphasis levels and a cut. So the structure
   is derived from the roll and the wording from §8's content rules, and **no token is read anywhere
   in the file**. Every printed string lives in one `ReceiptWords` class so replacing the copy is an
   edit rather than an excavation.
2. **One printer per device**, which is `docs/printer_transport.md`'s own stated assumption. Per-job
   routing remains a change to where `host` and `port` come from rather than to the record.

### The finding, which is worse than the one it was written to catch

**A shop called `Mũgumo Stores` did not print badly. It threw.**

`docs/printer_transport.md` §2 warns that the borrowed repository "Latin-1 encodes bytes `0x80`–`0xFF`
and never emits `ESC t`, so every non-ASCII character prints as the printer's default code page
instead". That is a **cosmetic** defect: mojibake on paper. The test written for it found something
else — `Generator` encodes with `latin1` by default and `latin1.encode` **raises** on U+0169:

```text
Invalid argument (string): Contains invalid characters.: "Mũgumo Stores"
```

So the receipt formatter, called on a sale path, would have thrown for a business name that is
ordinary Gĩkũyũ orthography in the market this app is built for. **An exception on the sale path is
not a printing defect, it is a lost sale**, and nothing in the design document predicted it because
the document is about the transport rather than about the encoder.

**`ReceiptText.forPrinter` is the answer and it is deliberately lossy.** A thermal printer genuinely
has no glyph for `ũ` in any single-byte code page this app selects, so there is no correct rendering
to preserve — the choice is between a legible substitution and a failed sale. Letters with a Latin
base lose their mark (`ũ` → `u`, `ĩ` → `i`, and the curly quotes a word processor inserts); anything
else becomes `?`, which reads as *this printer could not draw that* rather than as a missing letter.
**Nothing is silently dropped**, because a name shortened without trace is a name a customer cannot
match to the shop.

### What was built

**`checkout_receipt_body.dart`** — the ESC/POS body. `ESC t` is emitted before a single printable
character, which is the one command the design document singles out, and there is a test that asserts
its byte position is *before* the shop name rather than merely present. Two rows per sale line rather
than one, because a 32-column line cannot hold `2 x Maize flour 2kg` and `KES 271.00` side by side
without truncating the product name to about twelve characters — and the name is what a customer
checks. **The shape does not change with the roll**: a receipt with two layouts is two things to
reason about and nobody compares them side by side.

**A cut only where `hasCutter` says so.** A cut command to a printer without one is ignored by some
models and prints a control character on others; feed lines are what a person tears against.

**`checkout_print_dispatch.dart`** — the one call that turns a committed sale into a receipt on its
way to paper, and the piece that made the slice reachable at all. Four subsystems each did one thing
and none knew about the others; a screen wiring them together would have had to make five decisions
that belong in one place.

### The three decisions in the dispatcher

**It never throws for a printing reason.** §6.3's rule — *"no animation may sit between an input and
its record"* — is the same argument with a larger consequence: a receipt that can break a checkout is
a paper jam that can lose a sale. Every transport and queue failure comes back as a result carrying a
code. There is a test that loops **all eight** codes and asserts none of them escapes. A malformed
*durable* record is the single exception and propagates, because that means the box cannot be
trusted, which is not a printing problem.

**When no printer is configured it refuses and writes no job.** A job needs an address and
`docs/printer_transport.md` §6 forbids guessing one. **The receipt is not lost, and the reason is
structural**: the sale is durable and the job key is the receipt number the sale already carries, so
queueing it later produces the *same* job rather than a second delivery. There is a test for exactly
that recovery. This is what makes refusing safe rather than lossy, and it is why the endpoint was not
made nullable to avoid refusing.

**A retry re-sends the bytes the sale produced, never new ones.** A receipt retried after a price
change has to print what was **charged**. That is why `retry` is a separate entry point from
`dispatch` rather than a flag on it.

### The copy defect only a preview could find, and there will never be a picture

**The footer was 34 characters on a 32-column roll.** `Keep this receipt to return an item` does not
fail on a narrow roll — it **wraps**, leaving a centred sentence with the word `em` on the line under
it, which reads as a broken printer rather than as copy. It is now `Keep this receipt for returns`,
which is 29.

**It was found by decoding a receipt and printing it**, in a throwaway test deleted afterwards, which
is the closest thing to a screenshot that paper can have. §10 says the harness cannot see motion;
it also cannot see paper, and it never will — no viewport renders ESC/POS.

**So the review is arithmetic**, and it is now an assertion:
`ReceiptWords.longestLineFits` measures every fixed string against the narrowest roll. Product names
and shop names are excluded deliberately — those are the shopkeeper's and wrap by design. **This is
the only invariant in the slice that copy can break in complete silence**, which is exactly why it
is a test rather than a comment.

### What is left, and it is one coherent chunk rather than three loose ends

**Three surfaces, and none of them is built:**

1. **Printer setup** — owner and admin, writing `configuration/printer`, with a Firestore merge
   writer shaped like `FirebaseTenantCheckoutConfigurationWriter`. `PrinterTransport.probe` is a
   first-class operation for exactly this screen: *is this printer reachable?* without wasting paper.
   `PrinterTransportCapability.endpointIsPrinter` decides whether the address field is shown at all.
2. **The sale-path call site.** `CheckoutDraftService.saveDraft` is the seam and the dispatcher takes
   what it needs, but **wiring it before setup exists would add a call that can only ever refuse** —
   which is worse than not wiring it. These two land together or not at all.
3. **The queue's own surface** — what a person sees when a receipt did not print. The eight sentences
   exist; where they appear and what *Send again* attaches to does not.

**"Print a receipt" therefore stays red**, and the row says why. Green means a person could do it in
a running app today, and today nobody can tell the app where the printer is.

**One question inside `pending()` is recorded rather than answered**: one malformed record throws for
the whole listing, which is the fail-closed rule but is the one place it is uncomfortable — an
unreadable job hides every readable one from the surface that would show them. The chunk that builds
that surface should decide deliberately, and the honest third answer is a listing that returns the
good records *and* the count of unreadable ones, the way the profit display already states how many
lines it could not use.

```text
lib/checkout/checkout_print_dispatch.dart    new — CheckoutPrintDispatcher and its three outcomes
lib/checkout/checkout.dart                   two exports

test/checkout/checkout_receipt_body_test.dart   new, 14
test/checkout/checkout_print_dispatch_test.dart new, 12
```

Nothing existing in `lib/` was edited except the barrel, and nothing under `functions/`,
`firestore.rules` or `rules-tests/` was touched.

### Tests

```text
flutter test --no-pub --concurrency=1 --reporter=failures-only
+2172: All tests passed!
```

**+26**, taking the printing slice to **73 tests across five files**. Two failed on their first run
and both were the tests being right: the crash on a non-Latin-1 shop name, and a fixture that built a
sale payload with a made-up hash where `CheckoutSalePayload` checks that the hash describes the exact
payload it was given.

**One test was rewritten rather than kept, and the reason is worth recording.** It asserted that a
receipt states *Not recorded* where a sale carries no tender — by building a sale with none. That
payload does not exist: `CheckoutSalePayload` refuses it outright with *"tender must name one of the
recorded payment methods"*. So the branch is defensive, the assertion moved onto the mapping itself,
and the comment says which. **A test that cannot construct its own premise is testing the wrong
thing.**

## Printing reaches paper, and six faults wearing one sentence - 2026-08-18

**What shipped is the composition, not the engine.** Everything under printing had been built and
tested since 2026-08-17 and **nothing called any of it**. This session wired it: `main.dart` opens
the encrypted job box under its own key, loads `CapabilityProfile` once because a formatter must not
do I/O, builds the platform transport and `CheckoutPrintDispatcher`, and hands `CheckoutDraftService`
the `onSaved` hook it was written for. The routing shell gained two routes — **Printer**, owner and
admin, and **Receipts waiting**, which carries no role list because the person who discovers a
receipt did not come out is whoever is standing at the till. The queue card states its own depth,
which is §4.4's *"a card states its own condition"* and the one example that section names.

**The till now says when a receipt did not print, and that is the defect worth recording.**
`CheckoutSavedDraft.receiptPrintFailure` was produced by the draft service, asserted in four tests,
returned to the screen and **discarded there**. A cashier whose printer was off saw a sale that
looked perfect. It is a second `Callout` rather than a sentence folded into the first, because a
printer fault must never read as a lost sale — and **only a failure is drawn**: `null` means *sent*
and also means *this build queues no receipts*, so a confirmation would assert something the till
cannot distinguish. Where it printed, the paper is the proof.

**A real printer was dialled for the first time.** `192.168.100.20:9100`, a live ESC/POS unit on the
shop LAN. Everything below the app worked on the first attempt — the transport, the queue, the
formatter, the dispatcher — and a receipt came out, rung up through the till's own UI by
`tool/printer_till_smoke.dart`, which taps a product tile, taps a tender, taps *Save*, and prints
what that press produced through `createPrinterTransport()` and `CheckoutReceiptBody`.

### Six faults, one sentence, and that is the finding

Reaching that printer took six unrelated failures. **Five were environmental and every one of them
reported to the person as the same words.** In order:

1. **A Fortinet VPN kill-switch ate the entire LAN.** ARP resolved, routing was correct, binding the
   socket to the Wi-Fi source changed nothing — and the gateway did not answer either, while the
   internet did. It was also killing `flutter test`'s own loopback channel, so every suite had been
   dying with `Connection closed before test suite loaded` and a VM stack dump. One cause, two
   symptoms that looked nothing alike.
2. **The system drive was full** — 50 MB free of 173 GB — which crashed the Dart compiler mid-suite
   with `errno 112` and stalled the Firestore emulator download. Two Flutter commands at once was
   enough to exhaust it.
3. **Android refused cleartext** to a LAN address the debug allowlist did not name. The allowlist
   already predicted this case in its own comment.
4. **The functions emulator never started** because it was waiting on an interactive prompt for
   `EMAIL_SENDER_ADDRESS`, which nothing surfaced.
5. **`cloud_functions` 6.0.5 treats an unavailable App Check token as fatal**, so no callable could
   leave the device at all.
6. **A 26-byte HMAC placeholder** where `cursorSecret()` demands 32.

**Every one of these rendered as "We could not open your business account. Check your connection."**
The screen states a sentence this app wrote and deliberately prints no exception at a shopkeeper,
which is right — and it left a device run with nothing whatever to read. `_showFailure` now
`debugPrint`s the error it is about to hide. One line, debug only, and it is the difference between
a diagnosis and six hours of guessing.

### Two platform defects, neither of them a printing defect

- **`INTERNET` was declared only in `src/debug`**, where the Flutter template puts it for hot reload.
  Every debug build had it; no release build had ever been checked. Nothing this app depends on
  declares it either. It is now in the manifest that ships.
- **iOS had no `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription`.** iOS 14 and later refuse a connection to another
  device on the local network without it, and the refusal arrives as an ordinary socket error — so a
  printer that is switched on and working would have reported *"the printer did not answer"*.

### The Firebase upgrade, and why it is defensible

Resolving `cloud_functions` to 6.3.6 moved **19 packages**, including `firebase_core` 4.3.0 → 4.13.0.
The whole data layer moved. It is defensible for exactly one reason: the full suite went **2172 →
2213 with not one existing assertion changed**. The constraint was never widened — the pubspec's own
`^6.0.5` already permitted 6.3.6 and pub had simply not been asked.

### What this leaves behind, recorded rather than fixed

- **A print job is never deleted.** The box grows without bound and `pending()` scans every key on
  each home build. A retention policy is a decision, not an implementation detail.
- **The queue panel truncates its reason to one line**, hiding the half that says what to do. That is
  `RecordList`'s contract rather than the panel's, so it ripples.
- **App Check is disabled on project 299444269776.** A release build installs no provider at all, so
  the callable path that 6.3.6 now tolerates is tolerating a permanent absence.
- **`Print a receipt` is amber, not green.** A phone configured the printer through the new route and
  rang up sales; nobody has yet watched paper come out of it in the running app.

```text
                                                bootstrap failure now logged
```

## A receipt that lost its last digit, and a package whose two numbers disagree - 2026-08-18

**Printing went green, and the hour between amber and green is the whole of this entry.** The wiring
landed earlier the same day; a phone then configured its printer through the new **Printer** route,
rang up sales, and paper came out. The paper was wrong. Every right-aligned value had lost its final
character — `KES 271.0`, `CT-8F8-20260818-004`, `Wanjik`, `Cas` — and each product name was sharing a
line with its own price, which the formatter deliberately puts on the line below.

### Four wrong theories, and what each one cost

**This is recorded because the diagnosis was the expensive part, not the fix.**

1. **"The roll is 58mm and the layout is 48."** Wrong, and it cost a bad instruction: the setting was
   changed to 32 columns, which made it worse. The correction came from the operator noticing the
   dashed rules had gone *short* — a rule is drawn left-to-right from the margin, so its length
   measures the paper. **The rules were the instrument all along.**
2. **"It is a 42-column 80mm mechanism."** 80mm rolls exist at 576 dots and at 512, which is 48
   columns and 42. Ruled out by printing a ruler: markers of exactly 32, 42 and 48 characters, each
   ending in its own number. `48` printed whole.
3. **"The printer reserves a right margin the generator does not know about."** Ruled out by printing
   `KES 271.00` three times — flush to column 48, one short, two short. **All three printed whole.**
   The paper was never the constraint.
4. **"The line is 49 characters."** Ruled out by measuring the payload instead of the paper — and the
   first version of that tool reported an off-by-one that belonged to **the tool**, because it skipped
   `ESC $ nL nH` as three bytes rather than four. A diagnostic that guesses a control sequence's
   length invents the defect it is looking for.

### What it actually was

`flutter_esc_pos_utils` reports `PaperSize.mm80.width` as **558 dots** while treating that same roll
as **48 characters** — and 48 characters of Font A is **576** dots. **The package's own two numbers
disagree by a character and a half.** On top of that, `Generator.text` emits an absolute print
position *and* a justification command for the same line, so a right-aligned amount is told both
*start at dot 0* and *right-align*. Each printer resolves that contradiction its own way; this one
slid the text to its edge and sliced it, and swallowed a line feed while doing it — which is why the
name and the price arrived together.

Dumping the byte stream with a correct skip table made it plain, because the positions are visible:

```text
<@0>Receipt<@320>CT-8F8-20260818-0042
<@0>KES 271.00            <- position 0, and also told to right-align
```

### The fix, and why it is padding rather than arithmetic

`CheckoutReceiptBody` now pads every line to the roll's character count and **positions nothing**.
`_pair` puts a label left and a value hard right; `_right` right-aligns money; `_centred` centres the
heading at double width; `_rule` replaces `generator.hr()` so that even the rules are built the same
way as the rows they separate. Emphasis moved from half a line to the whole line — the receipt number
row and the TOTAL row are bold outright — because emphasising one half of a line requires two writes
to it, and two writes to one line is precisely what was mis-positioning them.

The only geometry left is *"this roll is N characters"*, and N is a figure a person can verify with
`tool/printer_width_ruler.dart`.

### The tests were green throughout, and that is the finding

`checkout_receipt_body_test.dart` had **14 passing tests while the defect was on the paper**, because
every one of them asserted on the decoded *text* and the fault was in the *geometry*. It is now **22**.
The eight new ones assert the contract that was missing: no line exceeds the roll, a rule fills it
exactly, every money line ends at the last column, and a price is never on its name's line.

**A suite that reads the words cannot see the shape.** That is the transferable lesson, and it is why
these tests parse the control sequences by their real lengths rather than stripping them.

### Two other things the evening found

- **The receipt showed no business name.** Not a layout fault: there was no `configuration/branding`
  document, so `TenantBrandingRepository.load` returned null and the heading correctly fell back to
  `ReceiptWords.unnamedBusiness` — *"Sales receipt"*. The dev seed now writes one.
- **A queued print job stores its bytes, not its sale.** Changing the paper width does not re-lay-out
  anything already in *Receipts waiting*, so a retry after a width change reprints the old width. That
  is deliberate — a receipt reprinted after a price change must still say what was charged — but it
  made the width experiments read as though nothing had changed.

### Files changed

```text
lib/checkout/checkout_receipt_body.dart      _columns, _pair, _right, _centred, _rule;
                                             row() and PosColumn no longer used
test/checkout/checkout_receipt_body_test.dart  14 -> 22, the width contract
rules-tests/scripts/seed-dev-emulator.js     a branding document, so a shop can name itself
PLAN.md                                      Print a receipt: red -> green

tool/printer_width_ruler.dart                new - measures the roll, and the right margin
tool/printer_payload_dump.dart               new - measures the payload, with a correct skip table
tool/printer_row_probe.dart                  new - measures the generator's primitives alone
```

Nothing under `functions/src`, `firestore.rules` or `rules-tests/test` was touched; the seed script is
a development fixture and no rule or handler moved, so the four server suites did not need to run.

The product owner changed the redesign approach after the Flutter-led layout system proved too
prescriptive. Stitch now owns proposed visual composition, while active code remains authoritative
for behavior, data, RBAC, offline semantics, and reachable routes. Root `DESIGN.md` is retained as

different boundary: approved semantic values must still enter Flutter through a reusable theme
extension rather than hardcoded screen values.

This was an audit and setup run only. No Stitch screen was generated, edited, renamed, moved,
grouped, archived, or deleted, and no product code changed.

### What was audited
